output:
Course Title: Programming for Everybody (Getting Started with Python)

Course Description
“Programming for Everybody” is an introductory, zero-prerequisite course that teaches the fundamentals of computer programming through the Python language. By the end of the course, students will be able to read, write, debug, and reason about simple Python programs and will have a solid foundation for more advanced study in computer science, data analysis, web development, or automation.

Chapter-by-Chapter Syllabus

Chapter 1 – Why Program?  
Purpose: Introduce the idea of programming as a tool for problem solving and creativity. Discuss how software powers everyday technology, what programmers actually do, and the advantages of learning Python as a first language.

Chapter 2 – Installing and Using Python  
Purpose: Guide students through installing the Python interpreter and a code editor (or using an online notebook). Students write and run their first “Hello, world!” program and learn how to use the interactive prompt.

Chapter 3 – Variables, Expressions, and Statements  
Purpose: Explain how computers store data in memory. Students learn about variables, numeric and string literals, basic arithmetic, assignment, and simple input/output so they can create small computational scripts.

Chapter 4 – Conditional Execution  
Purpose: Teach decision-making in code using boolean logic. Students master if, elif, else statements and comparison operators to control program flow.

Chapter 5 – Functions  
Purpose: Introduce code reuse and modularity. Students define, call, and document functions, understand parameters and return values, and explore Python’s built-in functions.

Chapter 6 – Loops and Iteration  
Purpose: Cover while and for loops for repeated execution. Emphasize loop control (break, continue) and typical patterns such as counting, searching, and summing.

Chapter 7 – Strings  
Purpose: Dive deeper into text processing. Students slice, concatenate, format, and iterate over strings, and learn common string methods and escape sequences.

Chapter 8 – Files  
Purpose: Show how programs interact with external data. Students open, read, write, and close files, process line-oriented text, and handle simple file errors.

Chapter 9 – Lists and Tuples  
Purpose: Present Python’s ordered collections. Students learn list creation, indexing, slicing, mutability versus immutability, and common list/tuple operations for data aggregation.

Chapter 10 – Dictionaries and Sets  
Purpose: Introduce key–value and unordered collections. Students build dictionaries, perform lookups, count frequencies, and understand set operations to manage unique items.

Chapter 11 – Error Handling and Exceptions  
Purpose: Make programs robust. Students discover try/except blocks, built-in exceptions, and strategies for graceful failure and debugging.

Chapter 12 – Modules and Standard Library  
Purpose: Teach code organization and reuse through modules. Students import and leverage popular standard-library modules (math, random, datetime, os, sys) to extend program capabilities.

Chapter 13 – Working with Data on the Web (APIs & JSON)  
Purpose: Provide a first look at retrieving and parsing data from the internet. Students use urllib/requests to fetch web data, parse JSON, and integrate external information into programs.

Chapter 14 – Object-Oriented Programming Basics  
Purpose: Offer an optional introduction to classes, objects, attributes, and methods. Students see how OOP supports larger, more complex software design.

Chapter 15 – Project Week & Capstone  
Purpose: Students apply everything learned by planning, coding, and presenting a small individual or group project—examples include a text game, data-scraping script, or personal finance calculator.

Appendices & Supplementary Material  
A. Command-Line Basics  
B. Style Guide (PEP 8 overview)  
C. Next Steps in Python and Computer Science

Grading & Assessments (suggested)  
• Weekly programming exercises (40%)  
• Quizzes on conceptual understanding (20%)  
• Mid-course practical exam (15%)  
• Final capstone project (25%)

By following this chapter roadmap, students progress from zero knowledge to confidently writing small but meaningful Python programs, ready for deeper study or immediate practical use.

Video Brainstorm for the Topic  
“In spite of the fact that procrastination feels bad to you, why do you do it?”

1. The Science of Self-Sabotage  
   • Animated explainer that unpacks how the limbic system overrides the prefrontal cortex, leading to short-term relief and long-term regret.

2. “A Day in the Life of My Inner Procrastinator”  
   • Comedy sketch in which two characters—“Me” and “Future Me”—argue all day about whether to work or watch Netflix.

3. The Dopamine Trap: Why Your Brain Loves to Delay  
   • Whiteboard video teaching how micro-bursts of dopamine from scrolling social media feel safer than tackling uncertain tasks.

4. 30-Day Anti-Procrastination Experiment  
   • Vlog series documenting your attempt at eliminating one procrastination trigger per week and tracking mood, sleep, and productivity data.

5. Reaction Video: Watching Students Cram for Finals  
   • Record live reactions and commentary while students describe their last-minute study habits; follow up with a psychologist’s analysis.

6. Procrastination & Perfectionism: Two Sides of the Same Coin  
   • Sit-down discussion with a licensed therapist exploring how fear of imperfection fuels avoidance.

7. Myth-Busting: “I Work Better Under Pressure”  
   • Use time-lapse experiments to show performance differences between early starters and last-minute rushers.

8. Guided “2-Minute Start” Technique  
   • Real-time tutorial where viewers pick a task, set a timer for two minutes, and begin together on screen.

9. The History of Procrastination  
   • Documentary-style video tracing references from ancient philosophers (Seneca, Hesiod) to modern productivity gurus.

10. Desk Makeover for Focus  
   • Before-and-after transformation emphasizing environmental design to reduce distraction triggers.

11. Interview with a Neuroscientist  
   • Q&A covering how chronic procrastination can rewire neural pathways, plus evidence-based ways to reverse it.

12. “Procrastination Nations”: Cultural Differences  
   • Compare attitudes toward time management in Japan, Germany, and the U.S. via street interviews or remote calls.

13. Gamifying Your To-Do List  
   • Demo several productivity apps that turn tasks into RPG-style quests; evaluate which actually reduce delay.

14. The Emotional Cost: A Storytelling Episode  
   • Personal stories submitted by subscribers about missed opportunities because of procrastination, followed by coping tips.

15. Live Study With Me – Body-Double Technique  
   • Host real-time focus sessions where viewers work alongside you in silence to harness social accountability.

16. “I Tried Mel Robbins’ 5-Second Rule for a Week”  
   • Challenge video testing the famous countdown method; include pre- and post-metrics on output and stress.

17. From Chaos to Calendar Blocking  
   • Screen-share tutorial on converting a chaotic to-do list into a color-coded calendar, highlighting psychological benefits.

18. Procrastination & Mental Health  
   • Panel discussion with a psychiatrist and life coach on how anxiety, ADHD, and depression intersect with delay.

19. The Economics of Putting Things Off  
   • Infographic-rich breakdown of how procrastination costs billions in lost productivity at schools and workplaces.

20. ASMR for Focus  
   • Experiment with an ASMR soundscape designed to reduce anxiety and encourage viewers to start their postponed tasks while listening.

These ideas span multiple formats—educational explainer, comedic sketch, challenge vlog, interview, and live stream—to engage diverse audiences while diving into why we procrastinate even when it feels bad.

Because “The Great Gatsby” blends Jazz-Age glamour, sharp social satire, and a haunting love story, readers who enjoyed it often appreciate novels that share one or more of those qualities. Here are some recommendations:

1. “This Side of Paradise” by F. Scott Fitzgerald  
   Fitzgerald’s debut novel charts the restless life and loves of Princeton student Amory Blaine, capturing the same wit, decadence, and generational longing found in Gatsby.

2. “The Beautiful and Damned” by F. Scott Fitzgerald  
   Another Fitzgerald classic, this story follows Anthony and Gloria Patch as their marriage and fortunes unravel—an exploration of excess and moral decline in 1920s New York.

3. “Tender Is the Night” by F. Scott Fitzgerald  
   Set on the French Riviera, it portrays the glamorous but fragile marriage of Dick and Nicole Diver, offering a more mature, bittersweet take on wealth, obsession, and disillusionment.

4. “The Sun Also Rises” by Ernest Hemingway  
   Hemingway’s sparse prose depicts a group of expatriates drifting through Paris and Spain after World War I, grappling with lost ideals and aimless desire—echoes of Gatsby’s postwar malaise.

5. “The Age of Innocence” by Edith Wharton  
   A piercing look at New York high society decades before Gatsby, this novel shows how rigid social codes can thwart passion and individual happiness.

6. “Revolutionary Road” by Richard Yates  
   Set in 1950s suburbia, it offers a mid-century update on the dissection of the American Dream through the unraveling marriage of Frank and April Wheeler.

7. “Rules of Civility” by Amor Towles  
   A modern novel steeped in 1930s Manhattan elegance, it follows ambitious young Katey Kontent as she navigates class, romance, and reinvention—capturing the glamour and melancholy Gatsby fans savor.

8. “A Moveable Feast” by Ernest Hemingway  
   Though nonfiction, this memoir of 1920s Paris immerses readers in the expatriate literary scene that shaped Fitzgerald and gives vivid context to Gatsby’s era.

Is the answer in the generated text correct for the equation in the given input?

To find the roots of  
x³ − 4x² + 6x − 24 = 0

1. Look for an integer root (Rational Root Theorem).  
   Test x = 4:  
   4³ − 4·4² + 6·4 − 24 = 64 − 64 + 24 − 24 = 0.  
   So x = 4 is a root.

2. Factor out (x − 4).  
   Use synthetic division with 4:

   Coefficients: 1 −4 6 −24  
   Bring down 1.  
   4·1 → 4; −4 + 4 → 0  
   4·0 → 0; 6 + 0 → 6  
   4·6 → 24; −24 + 24 → 0  

   The quotient is x² + 6, so  
   x³ − 4x² + 6x − 24 = (x − 4)(x² + 6).

3. Solve x² + 6 = 0:  
   x² = −6 ⟹ x = ±i√6.

Final solutions:  
x = 4, x = i√6, x = −i√6

9-Day Family-Friendly Morocco Itinerary  
(Activity level: light → moderate; plenty of breaks and options to shorten/skip)

–––––––––––– DAY-BY-DAY PLAN ––––––––––––

DAY 1 – Arrive Casablanca  
• AM Land at Mohammed V Intl. Airport, private transfer to hotel near the Corniche.  
• Mid-day Stretch legs with a seaside promenade walk; quick visit to Rick’s Café for lunch (make kids feel like movie stars).  
• PM Guided visit of the spectacular Hassan II Mosque (family audio guides available; elevators for anyone who tires easily).  
• Evening Early dinner of seafood on the waterfront; relax & recover from jet-lag.

DAY 2 – Casablanca ➜ Rabat (1 hr 15 min drive)  
• 09:00 Depart for Rabat.  
• 10:30 Check-in, drop bags.  
• 11:00 Kasbah des Oudaias treasure hunt—short walks, great ocean views, colorful alleys perfect for photos.  
• Lunch Café Maure: mint tea & almond pastries overlooking the Bou Regreg river.  
• PM Quick stops: Hassan Tower & Mausoleum of Mohammed V (easy, flat paths).  
• Optional Cycle or take a horse-drawn carriage along the palm-lined waterfront.  
• Evening Family stroll through the medina; try grilled sardines at a local stall.

DAY 3 – Rabat ➜ Chefchaouen (4 hrs)  
• 08:30 Scenic drive through the Rif Mountains (plenty of restroom/photo stops).  
• Check-in at a riad inside the “Blue City.”  
• Late PM Leisurely wander through indigo lanes; older kids can climb 10 min to the Spanish Mosque for sunset.  
• Dinner Tagine on a rooftop with panoramic mountain views.

DAY 4 – Chefchaouen ➜ Volubilis ➜ Fes (4 hrs total with stops)  
• 09:00 Depart for Roman ruins of Volubilis.  
• 11:00 Guided one-hour walk among mosaics (flat terrain, shade trees, cafés near entrance).  
• Picnic or café lunch in nearby Moulay Idriss (inexpensive local fare).  
• 15:30 Arrive Fes; settle into traditional riad.  
• Early evening Demonstration of traditional pottery—hands-on for kids.

DAY 5 – Fes: Imperial City & Crafts  
• AM Half-day medina tour with licensed guide: tanneries viewing terrace, Nejjarine Fountain, Bou Inania Madrasa. Pace is slow; tuk-tuk pickup available if needed.  
• Lunch Family-run eatery in the medina (try pastilla).  
• PM Free time at riad pool/terrace OR optional visit to Jnan Sbil Garden for mellow stroll & paddle boats.  
• Evening Cooking workshop—prepare your own couscous dinner.

DAY 6 – Fes ➜ Middle Atlas ➜ Sahara (Merzouga) (7 hrs with scenic stops)  
• 08:00 Drive via cedar forests of Ifrane & Azrou; pause to see Barbary macaque monkeys, picnic among cedars.  
• Mid-day Lunch in Midelt (apple country).  
• Late PM Arrive Merzouga; switch to 4×4 or camel for 1-hr sunset ride to desert camp (moderate activity; can opt for 4×4 only).  
• Evening Sand-dune sunset, stargazing, Berber drumming around campfire; overnight in en-suite tent with real beds.

DAY 7 – Sahara ➜ Todra Gorge ➜ Dades Valley (4 hrs)  
• Early AM Optional sunrise dune walk (15-20 min).  
• 09:00 Drive to Tinghir; short, flat walk along Todra River palm groves to the 300 m-high gorge walls.  
• Lunch Riverside café (grilled brochettes, fresh salads).  
• PM Continue to Dades Valley; check into kasbah-style hotel with pool and garden.  
• Relaxation Family board-game time or short hike behind the hotel to “Monkey Fingers” rock formations (30 min round-trip).

DAY 8 – Dades ➜ Ouarzazate ➜ Aït Ben Haddou ➜ Marrakech (5–6 hrs)  
• 08:30 Depart via the Road of 1,000 Kasbahs.  
• 10:30 Stop at Ouarzazate’s Atlas Studios (sets from Aladdin & Game of Thrones—fun photo-ops).  
• Noon Explore UNESCO ksar of Aït Ben Haddou (45-min guided climb; mule hire available).  
• Lunch Terrace restaurant overlooking the adobe village.  
• PM Cross the High Atlas on scenic Tizi n’Tichka Pass with plenty of scenic stops.  
• 18:00 Arrive Marrakech; settle into riad with courtyard pool.

DAY 9 – Marrakech Highlights & Departure  
• AM Horse-drawn caleche ride around the 12th-century ramparts to avoid too much walking.  
• Visit Majorelle Garden & YSL Museum (pre-book skip-the-line tickets).  
• Lunch Street-food tasting in Jemaa el-Fnaa (opt for rooftop café if crowds feel intense).  
• PM Shop for last-minute souvenirs in the souks OR relax at riad/nearby hammam (kid-friendly sessions available).  
• Transfer to Marrakech Menara Airport for evening flight OR add an extra night if schedules allow.

–––––––––––– WHAT MAKES IT LIGHT–MODERATE ––––––––––––
• Daily walks kept to 1–3 hrs max, with transport or animal rides as alternatives.  
• Mid-day breaks at hotels / cafés to avoid peak heat.  
• Scenic drives broken up with frequent stops.  
• Kids’ activities: pottery, cooking class, dunes, movie sets, monkeys.  

–––––––––––– OPTIONAL EXTRAS / SWAPS ––––––––––––
• Replace Sahara overnight with two nights in Agafay Desert (closer to Marrakech) for shorter drive.  
• Add a beach day in Essaouira after Marrakech if you can extend the trip.  
• Trade Chefchaouen for a full day in Meknes if you prefer less mountain driving.

Have an amazing Moroccan adventure!

Leg Raises

Target areas: Lower abdominals, hip flexors (also engages quadriceps and lower back stabilizers)

Equipment: An exercise mat or padded floor

Step-by-step instructions
1. Starting position  
   • Lie flat on your back on the mat.  
   • Extend both legs straight and keep them together.  
   • Place your arms flat on the floor alongside your body, palms facing down for support.  
   • Engage your core by drawing your bellybutton toward your spine and keep your lower back gently pressed into the floor.

2. The movement  
   • Inhale.  
   • While keeping your legs straight and together, slowly lift them off the floor, using your abdominal muscles to control the motion.  
   • Continue raising your legs until they form roughly a 90-degree angle with your torso (or as high as comfortable without lifting your lower back off the mat).  
   • Pause briefly at the top.

3. Descent  
   • Exhale.  
   • Slowly lower your legs back toward the floor in a controlled manner.  
   • Stop just before your heels touch the ground (1–2 in / 3–5 cm above the floor) to keep tension on the abs.  
   • Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.

Reps & sets
• Beginners: 2–3 sets of 8–10 reps  
• Intermediate/advanced: 3–4 sets of 12–15 reps  
Rest 30–60 seconds between sets.

Technique tips
• Keep your lower back in contact with the mat throughout the movement; if it arches, raise your legs less high or bend your knees slightly.  
• Move slowly—momentum reduces the exercise’s effectiveness and increases injury risk.  
• Exhale on the way down to help maintain core engagement.  
• Keep your neck relaxed; avoid tensing or lifting the head.

Common mistakes to avoid
• Letting the lower back lift off the mat (risking strain).  
• Swinging the legs or using momentum.  
• Holding your breath.  
• Dropping the legs too quickly.

Modifications & progressions
• Easier: Perform bent-knee leg raises (knees at 90°) or single-leg raises.  
• Harder: Add ankle weights, hold a light medicine ball between your feet, or finish each rep with a hip lift (raise your hips an inch off the floor at the top).  
• Alternative equipment: Do hanging leg raises from a pull-up bar for an advanced variation.

Safety note
If you feel pain (not to be confused with normal muscle fatigue) in your lower back or hip flexors, stop the exercise and consult a fitness professional for corrections or alternatives.

input: Few-shot learning (FSL) is one of the key future steps in machine learning and raises a lot of attention. In this paper, we focus on the FSL problem of dialogue understanding, which contains two closely related tasks: intent detection and slot filling. Dialogue understanding has been proven to benefit a lot from jointly learning the two sub-tasks. However, such joint learning becomes challenging in the few-shot scenarios: on the one hand, the sparsity of samples greatly magnifies the difficulty of modeling the connection between the two tasks; on the other hand, how to jointly learn multiple tasks in the few-shot setting is still less investigated. In response to this, we introduce FewJoint, the first FSL benchmark for joint dialogue understanding. FewJoint provides a new corpus with 59 different dialogue domains from real industrial API and a code platform to ease FSL experiment set-up, which are expected to advance the research of this field. Further, we find that insufficient performance of the few-shot setting often leads to noisy sharing between two sub-task and disturbs joint learning. To tackle this, we guide slot with explicit intent information and propose a novel trust gating mechanism that blocks low-confidence intent information to ensure high quality sharing. Besides, we introduce a Reptile-based meta-learning strategy to achieve better generalization in unseen few-shot domains. In the experiments, the proposed method brings significant improvements on two datasets and achieve new state-of-the-art performance.

output: The paper addresses few-shot joint dialogue understanding (intent detection + slot filling). It introduces FewJoint, the first benchmark for this setting, offering a corpus of 59 real-world domains and supporting code. To combat data sparsity and noisy task sharing, the authors guide slot filling with intent cues and add a trust-gating module that filters low-confidence intent signals. A Reptile-based meta-learning strategy further improves cross-domain generalization. The proposed approach attains state-of-the-art results on two datasets.

instruction: Write a step-by-step guide for resolving GitHub merge conflicts.
decomposed_questions: Does the generated text include steps to resolve GitHub merge conflicts?
Are the generated steps presented in a step-by-step manner?
output:
Step-by-Step Guide to Resolving GitHub Merge Conflicts

1. Understand the Conflict  
   • A merge conflict occurs when Git cannot automatically reconcile differences between two branches.  
   • Conflicts typically arise when the same lines of code in the same file have been changed in two branches.

2. Reproduce the Conflict Locally  
   • Open a terminal (or Git Bash).  
   • Clone or pull the latest copy of the repository:  
     ```bash
     git pull origin main   # or your default branch
     ```  
   • Check out the branch you want to merge:  
     ```bash
     git checkout feature-branch
     ```

3. Start the Merge and Trigger the Conflict  
   • Attempt to merge your branch into the target branch locally:  
     ```bash
     git merge main   # or merge the target branch into your feature branch
     ```  
   • Git reports which files have conflicts and pauses the merge process.

4. Identify the Conflicted Files  
   • Run `git status` to see a list of files with conflicts, marked as “both modified.”

5. Open Conflicted Files in an Editor  
   • Conflicted regions are marked like this:  
     ```
     <<<<<<< HEAD
     code from your current branch
     =======
     code from the branch being merged
     >>>>>>> main
     ```  
   • Everything between `<<<<<<<` and `=======` comes from your branch (HEAD).  
   • Everything between `=======` and `>>>>>>>` comes from the other branch.

6. Decide How to Resolve Each Conflict  
   Two main strategies:  
   A. Accept Either Version  
      • Keep your change OR the other branch’s change.  
   B. Combine Changes  
      • Integrate the two snippets manually or rewrite them into a new unified version.

7. Edit and Remove Conflict Markers  
   • Delete all `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` lines.  
   • Ensure the remaining code compiles and meets project style guidelines.

8. Test Locally  
   • Run unit tests, build commands, or start the application to verify that your resolution works.

9. Stage the Resolved Files  
   ```bash
   git add path/to/conflicted-file
   ```

10. Complete the Merge  
    • After staging all resolved files, finalize the merge with:  
      ```bash
      git commit
      ```  
    • Git opens a default merge commit message. Adjust if desired, then save and exit.

11. Push the Changes Back to GitHub  
    ```bash
    git push origin feature-branch
    ```

12. Update the Pull Request (If Applicable)  
    • GitHub will automatically update your pull request.  
    • Verify the PR now shows no conflicts.  
    • Request reviews or approvals as needed.

13. Clean Up Local Branches (Optional)  
    • If the branch is merged and no longer needed:  
      ```bash
      git checkout main
      git pull origin main
      git branch -d feature-branch          # delete local
      git push origin --delete feature-branch  # delete remote
      ```

14. Prevent Future Conflicts  
    • Rebase or merge the target branch into your working branch frequently.  
    • Communicate with team members about overlapping work.  
    • Use smaller, focused pull requests to minimize divergence.

Quick Tips  
• Use tools: VS Code, GitHub Desktop, or GitKraken provide visual merge editors.  
• Run `git log --merge` to display commits involved in the conflict.  
• If you need to start over, abort the merge: `git merge --abort`.

Here are seven quick, nutrient-packed dinners—one for every weeknight—that require minimal prep and cook time. Each can be on the table in about 30 minutes (often less).

1. Sheet-Pan Lemon Herb Salmon & Vegetables  
   • Toss broccoli florets, halved cherry tomatoes, and thin zucchini rounds with olive oil, salt, pepper, garlic powder, and dried oregano on a sheet pan.  
   • Nestle salmon fillets among the veggies, brush with a lemon-olive-oil mixture, and sprinkle with fresh or dried dill.  
   • Roast at 400 °F (200 °C) for 15–18 min until salmon flakes easily.  
   Why it’s healthy: Omega-3s from salmon, fiber-rich veggies, minimal added fat.

2. 15-Minute Chickpea & Spinach Coconut Curry  
   • Sauté diced onion, garlic, and ginger in a pot. Add curry powder and a pinch of chili flakes.  
   • Stir in a can of rinsed chickpeas, a can of light coconut milk, and 2 cups baby spinach. Simmer 5-7 min.  
   • Finish with a squeeze of lime and chopped cilantro. Serve over microwavable brown rice.  
   Why it’s healthy: Plant protein, iron-rich spinach, dairy-free, naturally gluten-free.

3. Greek Yogurt Chicken Lettuce Wraps  
   • Shred or dice rotisserie chicken. Mix with plain Greek yogurt, diced cucumber, cherry tomatoes, olives, crumbled feta, lemon juice, and oregano.  
   • Spoon into sturdy romaine or butter-lettuce leaves.  
   • Serve with whole-grain pita chips or quinoa tabbouleh on the side.  
   Why it’s healthy: Lean protein, probiotics from yogurt, low-carb swap for tortillas.

4. 20-Minute Veggie-Packed Fried “Rice” (Cauliflower or Brown Rice)  
   • Heat sesame oil in a large skillet, scramble two eggs, then push to the side.  
   • Add a frozen veggie mix (peas, carrots, corn, green beans) plus diced bell pepper; cook 5 min.  
   • Stir in cauliflower rice or pre-cooked brown rice, low-sodium soy sauce, and a drizzle of sriracha. Finish with sliced green onions.  
   Why it’s healthy: Lower-carb option with cauliflower; customizable veggies; high protein from eggs.

5. One-Pot Lentil & Vegetable Pasta  
   • In a pot, combine 8 oz whole-grain or lentil pasta, 1 can diced tomatoes, 2 cups vegetable broth, sliced zucchini, mushrooms, and spinach.  
   • Simmer uncovered, stirring occasionally, 10–12 min until pasta is al dente and liquid is mostly absorbed.  
   • Stir in a spoon of pesto or fresh basil, plus grated Parmesan if desired.  
   Why it’s healthy: High fiber, plant protein from lentil pasta, only one pot to clean.

6. Turkey & Avocado Stuffed Sweet Potatoes  
   • Microwave or roast 4 medium sweet potatoes until tender.  
   • Meanwhile, sauté lean ground turkey with taco seasoning, black beans, and corn.  
   • Split sweet potatoes, mash interiors lightly, fill with turkey mixture, and top with diced avocado and salsa.  
   Why it’s healthy: Complex carbs, lean protein, healthy fats, gluten-free.

7. Quick Miso-Ginger Soba Noodle Bowl  
   • Cook soba noodles (buckwheat) according to package, drain and rinse.  
   • In the same pot, whisk 2 Tbsp white miso, 1 tsp grated ginger, 1 Tbsp rice vinegar, 1 Tbsp soy sauce, and 1 cup hot water to form a light broth.

instruction: Describe how to prepare the given food in your own words. Note down the ingredients you will need and the steps you will take to prepare them.
decomposed_questions: Does the generated text include the necessary ingredients for the preparation of the specified food in the given input?

Chewy Chocolate Chip Cookies  

Ingredients (makes about 24 cookies)
• 2 ¼ cups (280 g) all-purpose flour  
• 1 teaspoon baking soda  
• ½ teaspoon table salt  
• ¾ cup (170 g) unsalted butter, melted and cooled to room temperature  
• 1 cup (200 g) packed light-brown sugar  
• ½ cup (100 g) granulated sugar  
• 1 large egg + 1 large egg yolk, at room temperature  
• 2 teaspoons pure vanilla extract  
• 1 ½–2 cups (260–340 g) semisweet chocolate chips  
• Optional: ½ cup chopped walnuts or pecans  

Steps  

1. Pre-Mix Prep  
   • Melt the butter, then set it aside 10–15 minutes so it’s no longer hot.  
   • Preheat your oven to 350 °F / 175 °C. Line two baking sheets with parchment or silicone mats.

2. Combine Dry Ingredients  
   • In a medium bowl whisk the flour, baking soda, and salt. Set aside.

3. Make the Wet Base  
   • In a large mixing bowl whisk (or beat with a mixer) the melted butter, brown sugar, and granulated sugar until the mixture looks thick and glossy, about 1 minute.  
   • Add the egg, then the extra yolk, beating after each addition. Mix in the vanilla.

4. Bring Wet and Dry Together  
   • Add the dry ingredients to the wet mixture. Stir with a spatula or low-speed mixer just until you no longer see streaks of flour—do not over-mix.

5. Fold in the Chips (and Nuts)  
   • Gently stir in the chocolate chips and nuts if using. The dough will be soft.

6. Chill (Optional but Helps Chewiness)  
   • Cover the bowl and refrigerate 30 minutes to 1 hour. This rests the flour, firms the butter, and yields thicker, chewier cookies.

7. Portion  
   • Scoop heaping tablespoonfuls (about 2 tablespoons each) of dough, rolling them into balls. Place them on the prepared sheets, leaving 2 inches between.

8. Bake  
   • Bake 9–11 minutes, rotating sheets halfway through. The edges should look set and lightly golden; centers will still appear soft and puffy—that’s perfect for chewiness.

9. Cool  
   • Let cookies rest on the baking sheet 5 minutes (they finish setting), then transfer to a wire rack to cool completely.

10. Serve or Store  
   • Enjoy warm with a cold glass of milk, or store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 5 days. Freeze extras for longer storage.

Tips for Extra Chew  
• Use more brown sugar than white; its molasses content adds moisture.  
• Adding an egg yolk without the white increases fat, giving a fudgier texture.  
• Slight under-baking and allowing residual heat to finish the centers keeps them soft.

West-Coast Mini–Road-Trip  
Route: San Diego ➜ Los Angeles (≈130 miles / 210 km)  
Ideal pace: 2–4 leisurely days so you can linger in the beach towns, eat well, and catch sunsets.

DAY 1 – SAN DIEGO → LA JOLLA → ENCINITAS (35 mi)

1. La Jolla (20 min north of downtown San Diego)  
   • Start with coffee and ocean-view breakfast at Brockton Villa or Caroline’s Seaside Café.  
   • Stroll the coast walk to La Jolla Cove; watch sea lions on the rocks.  
   • Optional kayak or snorkel tour through the Sea Caves (garibaldi fish & leopard sharks in summer).  

2. Torrey Pines State Natural Reserve (5 min north)  
   • Short hikes to Broken Hill or Razor Point for dramatic cliffs and Pacific panoramas.  
   • If you’re a golfer, squeeze in nine holes at the world-famous Torrey Pines Golf Course next door.

3. Encinitas / Cardiff-by-the-Sea (20 min farther)  
   • Lunch at Taco Stand or Las Olas for classic SoCal fish tacos.  
   • Walk the meditation gardens at the Self-Realization Fellowship for Zen ocean views.  
   • Surf or watch pros at Swami’s break; sunsets here are legendary.  
   • Overnight in an oceanfront inn (e.g., Cape Rey Hilton in Carlsbad if you want resort amenities).

DAY 2 – CARLSBAD → OCEANSIDE → SAN CLEMENTE (35 mi)

4. Carlsbad  
   • Morning stop at the Flower Fields (Mar–May) or LEGOLAND (if traveling with kids).  
   • Grab craft coffee and a pastry in Carlsbad Village; pop into the small boutiques.

5. Oceanside (15 min)  
   • Rent cruiser bikes at Wheel Fun Rentals, pedal the Strand and out onto the historic wooden pier.  
   • Tour the California Surf Museum or snap photos at the “Top Gun” House (newly restored).  
   • Lunch: fresh poke at The Plot or tacos at Hello Betty.  

6. San Onofre & San Clemente (20 min)  
   • Detour into San Onofre State Beach for a laid-back beach session or beginner-friendly surf at “San O.”  
   • Continue to San Clemente Pier: sunset walk and dinner at Fisherman’s Restaurant (clam chowder + pier view).  
   • Overnight at Casa Tropicana or an Airbnb Spanish-style casita downtown.

DAY 3 – DANA POINT → LAGUNA BEACH → NEWPORT/HUNTINGTON (45 mi)

7. Dana Point (15 min)  
   • Morning whale-watching cruise (gray whales: Dec–Apr; blue whales: May–Oct) or stand-up paddleboard in the harbor.  
   • Quick hike to the Dana Point Headlands for coastal bluffs and wildflowers.  

8. Laguna Beach (15 min)  
   • Art vibe: browse small galleries on Forest Ave., visit the Laguna Art Museum.  
   • Swim at Crescent Bay or explore tide-pools at Crystal Cove State Park.  
   • Lunch: Nick’s Laguna or casual Urth Caffé.  

9. Newport Beach / Balboa Peninsula (20 min)  
   • Ride the tiny Balboa Island Ferry ($1.25) and grab a frozen banana (local icon).  
   • Rent a Duffy electric boat to cruise Newport Harbor with a picnic.  

10. Huntington Beach (a.k.a. “Surf City,” 15 min)  
    • Stroll the 1,850-foot pier; watch sunset surfers.  
    • Tuesday evenings host Surf City Nights street fair (live music & food trucks).  
    • Overnight at the Shorebreak or an oceanfront campsite at Bolsa Chica (if you snag a res).

DAY 4 – LONG BEACH → SANTA MONICA → LOS ANGELES (25–40 mi)

11. Long Beach (30 min)  
    • Brunch in Retro Row (4th Street).  
    • Tour the historic Queen Mary or the world-class Aquarium of the Pacific.  
    • Street-art walk through Downtown’s East Village Arts District.

12. Palos Verdes Peninsula (Optional scenic loop)  
    • Detour along Palos Verdes Drive for clifftop vistas at Point Vicente Lighthouse and Abalone Cove tide pools.

13. Santa Monica & Venice (30 min)  
    • Ride the Ferris wheel on Santa Monica Pier, then walk/bike the 2.5-mi Strand to Venice Beach.  
    • People-watch at Muscle Beach, explore Abbot Kinney Blvd for boutiques and gourmet food trucks.  

14. Downtown/Griffith Park, Los Angeles (finish)  
    • Wrap up with sunset at Griffith Observatory—city lights one way, Pacific glow the other.  
    • Celebrate the trip with tacos in Echo Park (try Guisados) or sushi in Little Tokyo.

TIPS & EXTRAS  
• Best season: Late spring to early fall for beach weather; avoid holiday-weekend traffic if you can.  
• Car choice: A convertible or sunroof SUV lets you enjoy the coastal air; book early for better rates.  
• Parking apps (ParkMobile, SpotHero) help avoid hefty beach-town fees.  
• Pack layers—mornings/evenings can be cool even in summer.  
• Leave room in your schedule for spontaneous stops: roadside farm stands in Carlsbad, dolphin sightings off Cardiff, or a surprise beach bonfire at Dockweiler Beach just south of LAX.

From postcard-perfect coves to historic piers and taco shacks, this slow-roll from San Diego to L.A. packs in classic SoCal surf culture, art, wildlife, and food—all within 130 miles of sun-washed Pacific shoreline. Enjoy the ride!

addressId is the primary key column for this table.
Each row of this table contains information about the city and state of one person with ID = PersonId.
Write an SQL query to report the first name, last name, city, and state of each person in the Person table. If the address of a personId is not present in the Address table, report null instead.
Return the result table in any order.

select FirstName, LastName, City, State

Explanation of the solution  

1.  What has to be reported  
   •  Every row that exists in table Person.  
   •  Along with that row we have to show the columns coming from table Address (city and state) that belong to the same personId.  
   •  When a person has no record in Address we still have to output the Person row and put NULL in the address columns.  

2.  Relational-algebra point of view  
   The requirement corresponds to a left (or left-outer) join: keep the whole left table (Person) and, when a matching tuple exists in the right table (Address), append its columns; otherwise append NULLs.

3.  SQL query that realises it  

```
SELECT  p.firstName ,
        p.lastName ,
        a.city ,
        a.state
FROM    Person  AS p
LEFT JOIN Address AS a
       ON p.personId = a.personId;
```

4.  Why it works  
   •  The `LEFT JOIN` first builds every row from Person (`p`).  
   •  For each of those rows it looks in Address (`a`) for rows having the same `personId`.  
   •  If such a row exists, the columns `city` and `state` are taken from it.  
   •  If no row is found, the join still outputs the Person row, placing NULL in the columns that come from Address, which is exactly what the problem asks for.  

5.  Complexity  
   A join is executed by the database engine with its own chosen method (hash join, nested-loop, merge join, etc.). Logically the query scans each table once, therefore the complexity is O(|Person| + |Address|).  

The implementation supplied in the prompt is already the concise and correct solution that fulfils these requirements.

Below is a thorough, safety-minded walk-through for turning an empty aluminum beer (or soda) can into a small demonstration-grade steam engine. Read the entire guide before beginning so you can gather all parts, understand the workflow, and prepare the workspace.

────────────────────────────
1. General Safety and Legal Notice
────────────────────────────
• Pressurized steam, even at relatively low pressures, can cause burns or propel objects violently.  
• Always wear eye protection, heat-resistant gloves, and long sleeves.  
• Work in a well-ventilated area on a stable, non-flammable surface, away from children and pets.  
• Have a fire extinguisher nearby.  
• Do not scale this design up without engineering calculations; the thin aluminum walls of a can limit safe pressure.  
• You alone are responsible for any injuries or damage that might result from attempting this project.

────────────────────────────
2. Materials
────────────────────────────
1. One empty 12-oz (330 mL) aluminum can (no dents or deep scratches).  
2. ~30 cm (12 in) of soft copper tubing, 3–4 mm outer diameter (refrigeration tubing works well).  
3. One 10–20 mL plastic syringe or the barrel of a retractable ball-point pen (for cylinder).  
4. One snug-fitting wooden or plastic dowel (for piston), length ≈ cylinder length + 20 mm.  
5. Small hose or silicone tubing (to connect boiler to cylinder).  
6. Thin sheet metal or sturdy wire for a small crank arm.  
7. A flywheel (e.g., metal jar lid, skateboard bearing with weight epoxy-bonded, or a toy car wheel).  
8. Two pieces of 1–2 mm steel wire or small nails to form the crankshaft axle.  
9. Small screws, nuts, washers, and scrap plywood or aluminum angle for the frame.  
10. Two-part epoxy rated ≥ 120 °C (or high-temperature RTV silicone).  
11. PTFE tape or high-temp thread sealant (optional, helps seal joints).  
12. Simple heat source: spirit burner, tea-light, or small gas torch.  
13. Tools: drill with bits 1–5 mm, needle files, hobby knife, fine sandpaper, pliers, tubing cutter, hacksaw, center punch/awl, permanent marker, small hammer.

────────────────────────────
3. Overall Layout
────────────────────────────
Boiler: the beer can holds water and generates steam.  
Cylinder/Piston: converts steam energy into linear motion.  
Crankshaft/Flywheel: converts linear motion to rotary motion and stores inertia.  
Frame/Base: keeps everything aligned and at a safe distance from the flame.

────────────────────────────
4. Preparing the Boiler (Beer Can)
────────────────────────────
Step 4.1  Clean & inspect  
• Rinse the can thoroughly; remove any sharp tabs.  
• Check for cracks or deep dents; discard flawed cans.

Step 4.2  Create a steam outlet  
• Measure ~15 mm from the top rim; mark a spot.  
• Center-punch lightly to prevent drill bit wandering.  
• Drill a 4 mm (or matching tubing OD) hole slowly; support the opposite surface with scrap wood to avoid tearing.  
• Deburr with a file or hobby knife.

Step 4.3  Fit the copper outlet tube  
• Cut a 6–8 cm length of copper tubing.  
• Slightly flare the interior end with a tapered awl or carefully using round-nose pliers; this prevents it from slipping out.  
• Insert tube through the drilled hole so the flared end sits inside.  
• From the outside, seat it flush; seal thoroughly with high-temp epoxy or solder designed for aluminum-copper (if you have the correct flux). Epoxy is easiest—rough the surfaces, degrease, apply, let cure 24 h.  
• Slip a short length (2–3 cm) of silicone hose over the tube’s outer end; we will couple this to the cylinder later.

Step 4.4  Add a fill/drain hole  
• In the can’s top, punch/drill a ~3 mm hole offset from the pull-tab opening. This will accept a tiny self-tapping screw as a plug.  
• Degrease the screw threads and wrap with PTFE tape for a better seal.

Step 4.5  Optional safety vent  
• To avoid over-pressure, lightly puncture a second tiny hole (≈1 mm) near the fill plug. If pressure climbs too high, it will vent steam. Alternately, use a low-pressure relief valve salvaged from a pressure cooker.

────────────────────────────
5. Building the Cylinder–Piston Assembly
────────────────────────────
Step 5.1  Prepare the cylinder  
• Use a plastic syringe barrel or a pen barrel (remove ink).  
• Trim to ~50–60 mm length.  
• Smooth inside with fine dowel + sandpaper if needed.

Step 5.2  Make the piston  
• Turn or sand the wooden/plastic dowel to a sliding but airtight fit inside the cylinder.  
• Wrap one end with PTFE tape and a thin coat of petroleum jelly to improve sealing and reduce friction.  
• Drill a 1 mm pilot hole through the piston’s center; insert a stiff steel wire (e.g., paperclip) as a piston rod, epoxying in place. Leave ~40 mm protruding.

Step 5.3  Cylinder head & steam port  
• Cut a 1–2 mm thick disk of plastic/metal to cap the rear of the cylinder (away from rod). Drill a 4 mm hole off-center for the steam inlet.  
• Insert a short stub of copper tube into that hole; seal with epoxy.  
• Press-fit or epoxy the head onto the cylinder, ensuring alignment.

Step 5.4  Guides and bushings  
• Drill the front end cap of the cylinder just wide enough for smooth, low-leakage motion of the piston rod.  
• Glue the front head onto the cylinder, leaving the rod free.

────────────────────────────
6. Crankshaft and Flywheel
────────────────────────────
Step 6.1  Crankshaft layout  
• Bend a 1.5–2 mm steel wire into an ‘S’ shape or assemble with two right-angle bends so that the crank throw (offset) is about 10–12 mm.

Step 6.2  Attach piston rod to crank  
• Drill a 1 mm hole in the crank throw end, insert the piston rod, and secure with a tiny bend or solder/epoxy sleeve.

Step 6.3  Mount the flywheel  
• Drill the flywheel’s center to accept the main axle.  
• Press-fit or epoxy to the axle, ensuring it spins true.

────────────────────────────
7. Engine Frame / Base
────────────────────────────
Step 7.1  Layout  
• On a piece of plywood or aluminum plate (~15 × 10 cm), mark positions for:  
  – Boiler (beer can).  
  – Cylinder (line up with crankshaft).  
  – Crankshaft bearings (two small blocks with holes or salvaged bearings).

Step 7.2  Fabricate supports  
• Cut two L-shaped angle-bracket supports or blocks for the crankshaft.  
• Drill holes for the axle ends; ream lightly for smooth rotation.

Step 7.3  Fasten components  
• Use screws or epoxy to secure the can horizontally. Keep the steam outlet uppermost so liquid water doesn’t splash straight into the steam line.  
• Mount the cylinder on a small wooden spacer so its centerline matches the crankshaft height.  
• Align piston rod with crank throw; fine-tune by shimming.

────────────────────────────
8. Linkage & Timing
────────────────────────────
A simple “oscillating” cylinder will automatically admit and exhaust steam as it rocks; however, with a fixed cylinder you need a valve. For simplicity, we’ll let the piston itself act as both power and exhaust ports:

Step 8.1  Port locations  
• Drill a second tiny 2 mm hole near the cylinder’s midpoint on the upper side; this becomes an exhaust vent (open to air).  
• Steam enters from rear port; when piston moves forward, exhaust escapes via the front vent, and vice versa.

Step 8.2  Align steam hose  
• Connect the hose from boiler outlet to the cylinder inlet stub. Secure with wire twist or small zip-tie.

────────────────────────────
9. Pressure Testing (Cold)
────────────────────────────
• Before firing, fill the can halfway with water; insert & snug the screw plug.  
• Submerge the can in a bucket of warm water.  
• Using a hand pump or blowing gently through the steam tube, add mild pressure and look for bubbles (leaks).  
• Fix leaks with more epoxy or PTFE tape; allow to cure.

────────────────────────────
10. First Firing & Tuning
────────────────────────────
Step 10.1  Steam production  
• Fill can to ≈ 1/3 with water; tighten plug.  
• Position heat source under the can’s bottom, not directly under sidewall.  
• Wait for gentle steam to exit the copper tube.

Step 10.2  Spin-up  
• With gloves, rotate the flywheel by hand; once condensation blows out and steam flow steadies, the engine should start cycling.  
• If it stalls:  
  – Check for air leaks.  
  – Ensure piston moves freely (apply a drop of light oil).  
  – Verify that steam hose isn’t kinked.

Step 10.3  Run-in  
• Let the engine run for short intervals (30–60 s) at first.  
• Monitor can temperature and pressure; never let it boil dry. Refill only after full cooling or through a remote reservoir.

────────────────────────────
11. Improvements & Variations
────────────────────────────
• Add a simple mechanical governor (rubber band belt to a spindle) to drive small loads like a toy generator LED.  
• Replace the cylinder with a metal hypodermic needle and brass tubing for higher durability.  
• Use a spring-loaded safety valve in the can’s lid for better over-pressure protection.  
• Insulate the boiler with fiberglass cloth to improve efficiency (keep external surface < 100 °C to avoid epoxy failure).

────────────────────────────
12. Shutdown & Maintenance
────────────────────────────
• Extinguish the flame first; allow the can to cool completely before opening.  
• Drain remaining water; inspect internal surfaces for pitting or cracks.  
• Store the engine dry to prevent corrosion.  
• Replace any softened epoxy seals before next use.

By following these steps methodically—and respecting the limitations of a thin aluminum can—you can build a modest tabletop steam engine that demonstrates conversion of heat energy to mechanical work. Always favor caution: if in doubt about integrity or safety, rebuild or reinforce rather than risk a rupture.

Sweet-&-Savory Kale Skillet with Creamy Almond-Tamari Sauce  
Serves 2 as a light dinner or 4 as a side

Ingredients  
• 1 large bunch kale (about 10 oz / 280 g), stems removed, leaves torn into bite-size pieces  
• 3 Tbsp smooth almond butter  
• 2 Tbsp tamari (or soy sauce)  
• 1 Tbsp apple cider vinegar  
• 1 Tbsp agave nectar  
• 2–3 Tbsp water (to adjust sauce consistency)  
• 1 Tbsp neutral or sesame oil for sautéing  
Optional pantry boosts (use if you have them): 1 minced garlic clove, a pinch of red-pepper flakes, toasted sesame seeds for garnish.

Method  
1. Prep the kale  
   Rinse the kale and shake or pat dry. Tear or slice leaves into bite-size pieces; discard thick stems.

2. Make the almond-tamari sauce  
   In a small bowl whisk together almond butter, tamari, apple cider vinegar, agave nectar and 2 Tbsp water until smooth. If it still feels thick, drip in another teaspoon of water at a time until pourable (about the texture of heavy cream). Taste and adjust—add a touch more agave for sweetness or a splash more vinegar for brightness.

3. Sauté the kale  
   Heat the oil in a large skillet over medium-high. (Add garlic or red-pepper flakes now if using and sauté 30 sec.) Pile in the kale. Toss with tongs until the leaves turn glossy and begin wilting, 3–4 min. If the pan looks dry, splash in a tablespoon of water to create steam and speed wilting.

4. Sauce & finish  
   Reduce heat to low, give the almond-tamari sauce a quick stir, then pour it over the kale. Toss for about 1 minute, just until the greens are evenly coated and the sauce clings to the leaves.

5. Serve  
   Transfer to plates or a shallow bowl. Sprinkle with sesame seeds or more red-pepper flakes if desired. Pair with rice, noodles or crusty bread for a heartier meal.

Flavor profile  
• Earthy kale gets savory depth from tamari, creamy richness from almond butter, zing from cider vinegar and a delicate sweetness from agave—an umami-bright combo that feels dinner-worthy yet comes together in 15 minutes.

Tips for adjusting your travel plans to a sudden temperature change:

1. Re-check the latest forecasts for each stop. Conditions may shift again; plan day-to-day rather than locking everything in too far ahead.
2. Pack and dress in layers. Light, moisture-wicking base layers, a warm mid-layer (fleece or sweater) and a wind-/water-resistant outer shell let you strip down or bundle up as temperatures swing.
3. Swap or add versatile clothing items instead of overpacking: a packable down jacket, convertible pants/shorts, a lightweight scarf or buff, and thermal socks/gloves take little space but cover big ranges.
4. Adjust activity timing. If it suddenly turns hot, move strenuous sightseeing or hiking to early morning/evening and leave indoor museums or cafés for the midday heat. If it turns cold, flip that schedule.
5. Revisit lodging choices. Cold snap? Look for accommodations with reliable heating; unexpected heat? Check for air-conditioning or at least fans.
6. Review transportation plans. Extreme heat can strain car engines and rail/air schedules; cold can bring icy roads or flight delays. Build extra buffer time into connections and consider travel insurance.
7. Hydration and nutrition: warm drinks and calorie-dense snacks help in cold; electrolytes and plenty of water are vital in heat.
8. Protect electronics and medication. Battery life drops in cold; high heat can damage devices. Keep medications within recommended temperature ranges.
9. Know local emergency numbers and nearby clinics. Temperature extremes increase risks of heatstroke or hypothermia.
10. Stay flexible: keep cancellation policies handy, and have a Plan B (alternate indoor attractions, shorter routes, or additional rest days) so the trip remains enjoyable whatever the thermometer says.

input:
Mathematics and art are related in a variety of ways. Mathematics has itself been described as an art motivated by beauty. Mathematics can be discerned in arts such as music, dance, painting, architecture, sculpture, and textiles. This article focuses, however, on mathematics in the visual arts.
Mathematics and art have a long historical relationship. Artists have used mathematics since the 4th century BC when the Greek sculptor Polykleitos wrote his Canon, prescribing proportions conjectured to have been based on the ratio 1:√2 for the ideal male nude. Persistent popular claims have been made for the use of the golden ratio in ancient art and architecture, without reliable evidence. In the Italian Renaissance, Luca Pacioli wrote the influential treatise De divina proportione (1509), illustrated with woodcuts by Leonardo da Vinci, on the use of the golden ratio in art. Another Italian painter, Piero della Francesca, developed Euclid's ideas on perspective in treatises such as De Prospectiva Pingendi, and in his paintings. The engraver Albrecht Dürer made many references to mathematics in his work Melencolia I. In modern times, the graphic artist M. C. Escher made intensive use of tessellation and hyperbolic geometry, with the help of the mathematician H. S. M. Coxeter, while the De Stijl movement led by Theo van Doesburg and Piet Mondrian explicitly embraced geometrical forms. Mathematics has inspired textile arts such as quilting, knitting, cross-stitch, crochet, embroidery, weaving, Turkish and other carpet-making, as well as kilim. In Islamic art, symmetries are evident in forms as varied as Persian girih and Moroccan zellige tilework, Mughal jali pierced stone screens, and widespread muqarnas vaulting.

output:
Word: adversity  
Core meaning: a state or period of serious, often prolonged, misfortune, hardship, or difficulty.

Possible synonyms and how they differ from “adversity”

1. Hardship  
   • Focuses on the tangible, practical difficulties (poverty, lack of resources, arduous labor).  
   • Slightly less dramatic; can describe everyday struggles as well as major crises.

2. Misfortune  
   • Stresses the element of bad luck or chance rather than sustained struggle.  
   • Can denote a single unlucky incident (“a misfortune”) rather than an ongoing condition.

3. Difficulty  
   • Very broad and often milder; covers anything that is hard to do, from a math problem to a crisis.  
   • Does not necessarily imply suffering; can be temporary or minor.

4. Trial  
   • Connotes a test of character or faith; often used in moral or religious contexts (“trials and tribulations”).  
   • Suggests the experience has a purpose or lesson.

5. Tribulation  
   • Literary / biblical register.  
   • Implies prolonged, severe suffering, usually with emotional or spiritual overtones.

6. Calamity  
   • Highlights a sudden, often large-scale disaster (natural or man-made).  
   • More dramatic and specific than the broad state of “adversity.”

7. Affliction  
   • Centers on the pain or distress itself, frequently used for illness or personal woes.  
   • Less about external circumstances, more about the suffering they cause.

8. Setback  
   • Indicates a temporary reversal or delay in progress rather than a sweeping period of hardship.  
   • Often used in business or project contexts (“a financial setback”).

9. Reverse (chiefly BrE, formal/dated)  
   • Means a defeat or reversal of fortune.  
   • Sounds archaic and is common in historical or literary writing.

10. Distress  
    • Emphasizes the emotional or mental aspect of suffering.  
    • Can describe immediate pain or anxiety, not necessarily a long-term adverse state.

Summary  
“Adversity” suggests an extended, serious condition of unfavorable circumstances. Each synonym above overlaps with that idea but tilts the emphasis toward luck (misfortune), scale (calamity), emotional impact (distress), temporary obstacles (setback), or moral testing (trial/tribulation).

STUDY NOTES  
Subject: History of the United States (c. 15,000 BCE – Present)

I. Indigenous & Pre-Colonial North America  
• First Peoples arrive via Bering Land Bridge c. 15,000 BCE; develop diverse cultures (e.g., Pueblo, Mississippian, Iroquois, Powhatan, Cherokee).  
• Sophisticated societies with trade networks, agriculture (maize, beans, squash), mound cities, and complex governance.  
Key Point: U.S. history predates European contact by millennia and begins with Indigenous nations whose sovereignty and cultures remain central today.

II. Age of Exploration & Colonial Foundations (1492-1763)  
• 1492: Columbus initiates sustained European contact in the Caribbean; Spain, France, the Netherlands, and Britain compete for territory.  
• 1607: Jamestown, first permanent English settlement; 1620: Plymouth founded by Pilgrims.  
• 1619: First Africans arrive in Virginia—roots of chattel slavery.  
• Colonial economy: New England (shipping, small farms), Middle Colonies (grain, trade), South (plantation agriculture: tobacco, rice, indigo).  
• Political/ideological seeds: Mayflower Compact, Virginia House of Burgesses, notion of “rights of Englishmen,” Great Awakening.  
• French & Indian War (1754-63) drives France from mainland North America; sets stage for colonial grievances over taxation.

III. American Revolution & Early Republic (1763-1815)  
• “No taxation without representation,” Stamp Act, Boston Tea Party, Intolerable Acts.  
• 1776: Declaration of Independence (Thomas Jefferson main drafter).  
• 1781: British surrender at Yorktown; 1783 Treaty of Paris recognizes U.S. independence.  
• Articles of Confederation prove weak; 1787 Constitutional Convention drafts U.S. Constitution—federalism, separation of powers, checks & balances.  
• Bill of Rights (1791) protects civil liberties.  
• First Party System: Federalists (Hamilton) vs. Democratic-Republicans (Jefferson).  
• 1803: Louisiana Purchase doubles U.S. territory; principle of judicial review from Marbury v. Madison (1803).  
• 1812-15: War of 1812 reinforces U.S. sovereignty, fosters nationalism.

IV. Expansion, Reform & Sectional Conflict (1815-1860)  
• “Era of Good Feelings,” then rise of Jacksonian Democracy (expanded white male suffrage, spoils system, Trail of Tears).  
• Manifest Destiny drives westward push: Texas Annexation (1845), Oregon Territory (1846), Mexican-American War (1846-48) → Mexican Cession (CA, NM, AZ, etc.).  
• Market Revolution: canals, railroads, telegraph transform economy; early industrialization in Northeast.  
• Second Great Awakening spurs reform—abolitionism (Garrison, Douglass, Tubman), women’s rights (Seneca Falls, 1848), temperance, public schools.  
• Sectional crises: Missouri Compromise (1820), Compromise of 1850, Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854), Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857).  
Key Point: Expansion intensified the debate over slavery, making conflict increasingly unavoidable.

V. Civil War & Reconstruction (1861-1877)  
• 1860: Abraham Lincoln elected; seven Deep South states secede → Confederate States of America.  
• 1861-65: Civil War—Union victory at Gettysburg, Vicksburg; Emancipation Proclamation (1863) redefines war aims.  
• 13th Amendment (abolition of slavery), 14th (citizenship/equal protection), 15th (voting rights for Black men).  
• Reconstruction: Freedmen’s Bureau, Black political participation, rise of sharecropping; ended by Compromise of 1877, rise of Jim Crow segregation.  
Key Point: Reconstruction attempted interracial democracy but was undermined by violence (KKK), Supreme Court decisions, and Northern retreat.

VI. Industrialization, Immigration & the Gilded Age (1870s-1900)  
• Rapid growth of steel, railroads, oil; rise of trusts (Carnegie, Rockefeller).  
• Massive immigration from Southern/Eastern Europe; nativism and Chinese Exclusion Act (1882).  
• Labor conflicts: Great Railroad Strike (1877), Haymarket (1886), Homestead (1892), Pullman (1894).  
• Urbanization, political machines (Tammany Hall), social gospel, Populist movement (farmers vs. railroads, call for silver coinage).

VII. Progressive Era & World War I (1900-1919)  
• Reformers (T. Roosevelt, Taft, Wilson) target monopolies (Sherman/Clayton Antitrust Acts), conservation, consumer protection (FDA).  
• 16th-19th Amendments: income tax, direct election of senators, Prohibition, women’s suffrage (1920).  
• 1917-18: U.S. enters WWI; Wilson’s Fourteen Points, League of Nations debate; Treaty of Versailles rejected by Senate.  
Key Point: Progressives expanded federal power to address industrial society’s ills while WWI projected U.S. power abroad.

VIII. Roaring Twenties, Great Depression & New Deal (1920-1941)  
• Economic boom, mass culture: jazz, Harlem Renaissance, radio, automobiles.  
• Nativism resurfaces: Red Scare, National Origins Act (1924), resurgence of KKK.  
• 1929 Stock Market Crash → Great Depression; unemployment peaks near 25%.  
• FDR’s New Deal: relief (CCC, WPA), recovery (NRA, AAA), reform (Social Security, SEC, FDIC).  
• Court-packing plan controversy; New Deal coalition reshapes politics.

IX. World War II & Early Cold War (1941-1960)  
• 1941: Pearl Harbor; U.S. joins Allies. Mobilization ends Depression; G.I. Bill passes (1944).  
• Home Front: internment of Japanese Americans (Korematsu v. U.S.).  
• Atomic bombs on Hiroshima & Nagasaki (Aug 1945); U.S. emerges as superpower.  
• Cold War begins: containment (Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, NATO), Berlin Airlift, Korean War (1950-53), McCarthyism.  
• Domestic prosperity; baby boom; suburbanization; beginnings of Civil Rights activism (Brown v. Board, 1954; Montgomery Bus Boycott, 1955).

X. Civil Rights Era & Social Upheaval (1960-1975)  
• 1960 election: JFK’s New Frontier; Cuban Missile Crisis (1962).  
• Civil Rights Movement: sit-ins, Freedom Rides, March on Washington (1963), Civil Rights Act (1964), Voting Rights Act (1965), Fair Housing Act (1968).  
• Great Society (LBJ): Medicare, Medicaid, War on Poverty.  
• Vietnam War escalates; anti-war protests; 1968 Tet Offensive erodes support.  
• 1960s-70s social movements: women’s liberation (NOW, Roe v. Wade 1973), environmentalism (EPA, Earth Day 1970), Native American activism (AIM).  
• 1970s: détente with USSR/China (Nixon); Watergate → Nixon resigns 1974; economic stagflation, energy crisis.

XI. Late 20th Century (1975-2000)  
• 1980s Reagan era: supply-side economics, tax cuts, military buildup, conservative resurgence, Iran-Contra scandal.  
• 1991: Cold War ends; Soviet Union dissolves; U.S. emerges as sole superpower (Bush 41).  
• Persian Gulf War (1990-91) liberates Kuwait.  
• 1990s Clinton years: economic expansion, NAFTA, tech boom, welfare reform, impeachment (1998).  
Key Point: Post-Cold War optimism accompanied by globalization, debates over role of government, and partisan realignment.

XII. 21st Century (2001-Present)  
• 9/11/2001 terrorist attacks → Global War on Terror, Afghanistan War (2001-21), Iraq War (2003-11), Homeland Security creation, PATRIOT Act.  
• 2008 financial crisis; Great Recession; Obama administration’s stimulus & Affordable Care Act (2010).  
• Social media era reshapes politics; movements such as Tea Party, Occupy Wall Street, Black Lives Matter, #MeToo.  
• Partisan polarization intensifies; 2016 election of Donald Trump, populist currents, impeachment proceedings (2019, 2021).  
• COVID-19 pandemic (2020-); 2020 election of Joe Biden; infrastructure and climate legislation; debates over voting rights, misinformation, and global leadership.

XIII. Major Constitutional Amendments & Judicial Landmarks  
• Key Amendments: 1-10 (Bill of Rights), 13-15 (Civil War), 16 income tax, 17 direct Senate election, 19 women’s suffrage, 22 presidential term limits, 24 poll-tax ban, 26 voting age 18.  
• Supreme Court: Marbury v. Madison (1803) – judicial review; McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) – implied powers; Dred Scott (1857) – denied Black citizenship; Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) – “separate but equal”; Brown v. Board (1954) – school desegregation; Miranda v. Arizona (1966) – rights of accused; Roe v. Wade (1973) – abortion rights; Bush v. Gore (2000); Obergefell v. Hodges (2015) – same-sex marriage; Dobbs v. Jackson (2022) – overturned Roe.

XIV. Enduring Themes  
1. Federal vs. state power (nullification, Civil War, civil rights, modern federal mandates).  
2. Expansion & its consequences for Native peoples, environment, foreign relations.  
3. Immigration & identity: waves of newcomers reshape society; recurrent nativism.  
4. Race & equality: slavery → segregation → civil rights; ongoing debates on systemic racism.  
5. Economic transformation: agrarian republic → industrial powerhouse → service/tech economy; cycles of boom/bust and reform.  
6. America’s role in the world: isolationism → interventionism → superpower challenges.  
7. Civic ideals vs. realities: democracy and liberty vs. exclusion and inequality; continual push for “a more perfect Union.”

Study Tips  
• Create timelines to visualize overlapping events (e.g., Civil War & technological change).  
• Compare policy eras (e.g., Reconstruction vs. Civil Rights Movement) to trace continuities.  
• Know key documents: Declaration of Independence, Constitution, Federalist Papers, Emancipation Proclamation, Gettysburg Address, “I Have a Dream.”  
• Understand cause-and-effect: how economic shifts (Depression) lead to political change (New Deal).  
• Integrate cultural history (music, literature, art) with political events to see societal mood.  
• Practice DBQ (Document-Based Question) skills: analyze primary sources for AP/IB exams.

instruction:
One or more jobs can be run automatically by a workflow. The workflows are defined in the repository as YAML files and will run if an event occurs in the repository, as well as manually, or on a certain schedule.
Bring an example of a workflow that demonstrate the CI/CD features of GitHub Actions.
decomposed_questions: Is the generated text an example of a workflow?
Does the generated text demonstrate the CI/CD features of GitHub Actions?
output:
Below is a concise GitHub Actions workflow (save it as .github/workflows/ci-cd.yml) that shows several CI/CD capabilities:

• It is triggered automatically on every push and pull-request to the main branch.  
• It can be run manually (`workflow_dispatch`).  
• It also runs every night at 03:00 UTC (`schedule`).  
• There are two jobs: build/test and deploy.  
• Deployment runs only after the build succeeds and only for the main branch, illustrating a simple CD step that publishes a static site to Netlify.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci-cd.yml
name: CI/CD pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]
  workflow_dispatch:           # manual trigger
  schedule:                    # nightly build at 03:00 UTC
    - cron: '0 3 * * *'

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      - name: Upload coverage to Codecov
        uses: codecov/codecov-action@v3
        with:
          token: ${{ secrets.CODECOV_TOKEN }}

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && github.event_name != 'pull_request'

    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      - name: Build production assets
        run: npm run build

      - name: Deploy to Netlify (production)
        env:
          NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKEN }}
          NETLIFY_SITE_ID: ${{ secrets.NETLIFY_SITE_ID }}
        run: npx netlify-cli deploy --prod --dir=dist --site=$NETLIFY_SITE_ID --auth=$NETLIFY_AUTH_TOKEN
```

This single file demonstrates:

• Multiple event triggers (push, PR, manual, scheduled).  
• A two-stage pipeline (build/test ➔ deploy) with job dependencies (`needs`).  
• Conditional deployment based on branch and event type.  
• Use of repository secrets for secure credentials.

output:
Origins and History of the Word “Oblique”

1. Proto-Indo-European Roots  
   • The ultimate ancestor of “oblique” is the reconstructed Proto-Indo-European (PIE) root *lei̯k-, meaning “to bend, turn, or wind.”  
   • From this root developed a number of words in the ancient Indo-European languages that conveyed the idea of something not straight or “off at an angle.”

2. Latin: obliquus  
   • Classical Latin formed the adjective obliquus, “slanting, sideways, indirect, evasive.”  
   • The word is built from the prefix ob- (“toward, against”) + *liquus (from the same PIE base *lei̯k- “bend”). Thus, ob-liquus literally suggests “turned toward the side.”  
   • In Latin, obliquus could describe physical angles (an “oblique” line), figurative conduct (“indirect” or “underhanded” action), and even grammatical relationships (a noun in an oblique case, i.e., any case besides the nominative and vocative).

3. Passage into Old French  
   • Vulgar and late Latin preserved obliquus, and it entered early Romance as *obliquus > Old French oblique (“slanting”) and the variant obliquier/obliqier (verb “to slant”).  
   • Through Old French courtly and scholarly usage, the term spread into Anglo-Norman legal and scholastic vocabulary after the Norman Conquest (1066).

4. Arrival in Middle English  
   • First attested in English in the late 14th century, spelled oblike, oblyke, or oblique, in medical and astronomical treatises translated from French and Latin.  
   • Geoffrey Chaucer’s translation of Boethius (c.1380) uses “oblyque” to describe the ecliptic’s angle across the celestial sphere.  
   • By the 15th century, the spelling had largely standardized as oblique, though variants (obleek, obleyk, oblyke) continued into Early Modern English.

5. Semantic Expansion in English  
   a. Geometry & Trigonometry (15th c. onward)  
      “Oblique angle,” “oblique triangle,” “oblique coordinates.” These uses retain the literal, spatial sense: not perpendicular, not parallel, slanted.  
   b. Anatomy & Medicine (16th c.)  
      Muscles such as the “external oblique” and “internal oblique” of the abdominal wall were named for their diagonal fiber orientation.  
   c. Rhetoric & Morality (16th–17th c.)  
      Figurative senses—“indirect,” “evasive,” or “underhanded”—became common. Shakespeare writes in Julius Caesar (1599): “Men may construe things after their fashion, / Clean from the purpose of the things themselves, / And turn pre-ordinance and first decree / Into the law of children. Be not fond / To think that Caesar bears such rebel blood / That will be thaw’d from the true quality / With that which melteth fools; I mean sweet words, / Low-crooked court’sies, and base spaniel-fawning. / Thy brother by decree is banished; / If thou dost bend and pray and fawn for him, / I spurn thee like a cur out of my way.” (oblique used a few lines later in some editions)  
   d. Grammar (17th c.)  
      Linguists adopted “oblique case” to translate Latin casus obliquus, covering genitive, dative, accusative, ablative, etc., in contrast to the “direct” or nominative case.  
   e. Typography & Computing (20th c.)  
      “Oblique” serves as a technical term distinct from italic: an oblique font is mechanically slanted from a Roman upright design rather than redrawn with true italic letterforms (common in sans-serif typefaces and digital font menus).

6. Pronunciation and Spelling Stabilization  
   • Modern Standard English pronunciation settled on /əˈbliːk/ (uh-BLEEK) in British English and /oʊˈbliːk/ (oh-BLEEK) or /əˈbliːk/ in North American English.  
   • The silent-e pattern helped keep the long vowel of the second syllable.

7. Derivatives and Related Forms  
   • Obliquely (adverb, 15th c.) – “slantwise; indirectly.”  
   • Obliqueness / Obliquity (both 15th c.) – “the state of being oblique; indirectness.”  
   • Oblique-angled (17th c.) – “having oblique angles.”  
   • Semi-oblique, sub-oblique (19th–20th c., anatomical and technical coinages).  
   • In fields such as crystallography, botany, ophthalmology, and military tactics (an “oblique order” of battle), the adjective generated specialized compounds.

8. Modern Figurative Use  
   • In contemporary prose, calling a remark “oblique” suggests intentional vagueness or roundabout suggestion.  
   • In film criticism, “an oblique narrative” refers to storytelling that withholds direct exposition or employs unconventional angles of interpretation.  
   • Scientists still speak of “the Earth’s obliquity” to denote the axial tilt (currently about 23.4°).

9. Cognates and Cross-Lingual Echoes  
   • French oblique, Spanish oblicuo, Italian obliquo, Portuguese oblíquo, Romanian oblic—Romance languages share almost identical forms, inherited directly from Latin.  
   • German obliquus (rare, learned) and oblique (early modern loan) can appear in medical Latin-based compound terms, though the everyday German adjective is schräg.  
   • In Sanskrit, lîna- (“bent”) comes from the same PIE root; Greek leípos (“left, remaining; slanting”) is a distant semantic cousin.

Summary  
From a PIE idea of “bending,” through Latin obliquus and Old French oblique, the English word “oblique” has traveled over 600 years, keeping its literal notion of something “slanting from the straight” while developing rich figurative extensions—indirect speech, covert motives, typographic slants, military maneuvers, grammatical cases, planetary tilts, and more. Its longevity and adaptability make “oblique” a textbook example of how a concrete spatial metaphor can permeate vast cultural and scientific vocabularies across millennia.

Is there a way of reading one single character from the user input? For instance, they press one key at the terminal and it is returned (sort of like getch()). I know there's a function in Windows for it, but I'd like something that is cross-platform.

https://code.activestate.com/recipes/134892/

output:
Answer 1: Correct.  
The referenced ActiveState recipe (commonly known as “getch” in Python) contains a short module that chooses the appropriate low-level routine for Windows (msvcrt.getch) and for Unix-like systems (termios/tty) and therefore lets you read a single character without waiting for Enter. Answer 2: Incorrect.  
input() reads a full line terminated by Enter, not a single keypress, and therefore does not meet the requirement. It also echoes the typed characters, so it is not equivalent to getch().

instruction: Give students tips on how to keep their nerves under control during class presentations.
decomposed_questions: Does the generated text include some tips?
Are the tips in the generated text aimed at students?
Are the tips in the generated text about managing anxiety?
Are the tips in the generated text useful for a class presentation?
output:
Tips for Staying Calm During Class Presentations

1. Prepare Thoroughly  
   • Know your material so well that you could explain the main points without slides or notes.  
   • Rehearse out loud several times—alone, with friends, or by recording yourself to spot areas to improve.

2. Simulate the Setting  
   • Practice standing up, projecting your voice, and using any visual aids you’ll have in class.  
   • If possible, rehearse in the actual room or a similar one to get used to the space.

3. Use Structured Notes, Not Full Scripts  
   • Create cue cards or an outline with keywords and key data.  
   • This keeps you from reading word-for-word and lets you maintain eye contact, which boosts confidence.

4. Breathe on Purpose  
   • Right before you begin, inhale for a count of four, hold for four, and exhale for six to eight.  
   • Slow exhalations signal the body to relax and lower your heart rate.

5. Establish a Grounding Routine  
   • Find a discreet “anchor” (e.g., gently pressing your thumb and forefinger together) to remind yourself to stay calm.  
   • Pair it with a silent phrase such as “I’m ready” or “I’ve got this.”

6. Reframe Nerves as Excitement  
   • Tell yourself the rush you feel is energy you can channel into enthusiasm.  
   • Research shows this simple mindset shift can improve performance.

7. Visualize Success  
   • Spend a minute picturing the room, your confident posture, classmates engaged, and the teacher nodding.  
   • Mental rehearsal primes your brain for that outcome.

8. Start Strong with a Familiar Line  
   • Memorize the first sentence or two so you can launch without hesitation.  
   • A smooth opening boosts your confidence for the rest of the talk.

9. Engage Your Audience Early  
   • Ask a quick question, show a striking image, or share a brief story.  
   • Interaction makes the presentation feel like a conversation rather than a performance.

10. Manage Body Language  
    • Stand tall, shoulders back; grounded posture reduces stress hormones.  
    • Use purposeful gestures; avoid fidgeting by lightly resting a hand on the lectern or holding a pointer.

11. Keep Water Handy  
    • Dry mouth is common when anxious. A sip of water gives you a mini-pause and prevents vocal strain.

12. Accept Imperfection  
    • Even experienced speakers stumble over words—keep going.  
    • Most classmates are focused on the content, not minor slips.

13. Debrief and Celebrate  
    • Afterwards, note what went well and one thing to improve next time.  
    • Reward yourself—confidence grows through positive reinforcement.

By combining solid preparation with simple physiological and mindset techniques, you can keep nerves in check and deliver a clear, confident presentation.

```python
def is_prime(n: int) -> bool:
    """
    Determine whether a given integer `n` is a prime number.

    Parameters
    ----------
    n : int
        The number to test for primality.

    Returns
    -------
    bool
        True if `n` is prime, False otherwise.
    """
    # Handle edge‐cases first
    if n <= 1:
        return False
    if n <= 3:        # 2 and 3 are prime
        return True
    # Eliminate multiples of 2 and 3 early
    if n % 2 == 0 or n % 3 == 0:
        return False

    # Use 6k ± 1 optimisation
    i = 5
    while i * i <= n:
        if n % i == 0 or n % (i + 2) == 0:
            return False
        i += 6
    return True


# Example usage
if __name__ == "__main__":
    for number in range(1, 21):
        print(f"{number}: {is_prime(number)}")
```

Vegan Chocolate-Peanut Butter Mousse Cups

These rich, creamy mousse cups come together in minutes and require no baking. They’re perfect for satisfying a sweet craving—no dairy, eggs, or refined white sugar needed.

Yield: 4 small cups (about ½ cup each)  
Time: 15 min active, 1 hr chill

Ingredients  
For the chocolate layer  
• 1 ripe avocado  
• 3 Tbsp unsweetened cocoa powder  
• 3 Tbsp maple syrup (adjust to taste)  
• 2 Tbsp canned coconut milk (full-fat for extra creaminess)  
• ½ tsp vanilla extract  
• Pinch of fine sea salt

For the peanut-butter layer  
• ¼ cup natural creamy peanut butter  
• 2 Tbsp maple syrup or agave nectar  
• 2 Tbsp canned coconut milk  
• ⅛ tsp vanilla extract  
• Pinch of salt

Optional toppings  
• Shaved dark chocolate (dairy-free)  
• Crushed roasted peanuts  
• Fresh berries  
• Coconut whipped cream

Directions  
1. Make the chocolate mousse:  
   a. Scoop the avocado flesh into a food processor or blender.  
   b. Add cocoa powder, maple syrup, coconut milk, vanilla, and salt.  
   c. Blend until completely smooth and airy, scraping down sides as needed. Taste and adjust sweetness.

2. Make the peanut-butter mousse:  
   a. Wipe out the processor bowl (no need to wash thoroughly).  
   b. Add peanut butter, maple syrup, coconut milk, vanilla, and salt.  
   c. Blend until smooth and fluffy.

3. Layer the cups:  
   a. Spoon or pipe a layer of chocolate mousse into the bottom of each serving glass.  
   b. Add a layer of peanut-butter mousse.  
   c. Repeat if you have extra, finishing with a swirl on top.

4. Chill for at least 1 hour to let the flavors meld and the texture firm up.

5. Serve: Garnish with shaved chocolate, crushed peanuts, berries, or a dollop of coconut whipped cream.

Tips & Variations  
• Nut-free option: Replace peanut butter with sunflower-seed butter.  
• Extra chocolatey: Fold mini dairy-free chocolate chips into either mousse.  
• Make-ahead: Cups keep well, covered, in the fridge for up to 3 days.
