INDEPENDENT CONTRACTOR AGREEMENT  
This Independent Contractor Agreement (“Agreement”) is entered into on __________, 20___ (“Effective Date”) by and between:  

1. Company X, a __________________ corporation with its principal place of business at __________________ (“Company”), and  
2. Contractor Y, an independent graphic designer with a principal place of business at __________________ (“Contractor”).  

1. Services  
Contractor shall design, develop, and deliver graphic design materials as described in each written project statement of work (“SOW”) issued by Company. Contractor shall determine the method, details, and means of performing the Services.  

2. Compensation  
a. Fee. Company shall pay Contractor a flat fee of Three Thousand U.S. Dollars (US $3,000) for each fully accepted project described in an SOW.  
b. Invoices & Payment. Contractor shall invoice upon delivery and Company shall remit payment within fifteen (15) days of receipt.  

3. Taxes  
Contractor is solely responsible for all federal, state, and local taxes, withholdings, and filings arising from the compensation paid under this Agreement. Company shall issue an IRS Form 1099 or local equivalent and will not withhold payroll or income taxes.  

4. Benefits & Status  
Contractor is engaged as an independent contractor. Nothing herein shall be construed to create an employer-employee, joint venture, or partnership relationship. Contractor is ineligible for, and waives any claim to, Company-provided benefits, including but not limited to vacation, sick leave, retirement, health, or unemployment benefits.  

5. Insurance  
Contractor shall maintain, at Contractor’s sole expense, (i) general liability insurance with limits of not less than $1,000,000 per occurrence and (ii) professional liability/errors and omissions insurance with limits of not less than $500,000. Upon request, Contractor shall furnish certificates of insurance evidencing such coverage.  

6. Intellectual Property Rights  
a. Work Made for Hire. To the extent permitted by law, all deliverables created under this Agreement (“Work Product”) shall constitute “work made for hire” for Company.  
b. Assignment. If any Work Product is not deemed work made for hire, Contractor hereby irrevocably assigns to Company all worldwide right, title, and interest therein, including all copyrights, moral rights, and other intellectual property rights.  
c. License Back. Company grants Contractor a non-exclusive, royalty-free license to display the Work Product in Contractor’s portfolio solely for self-promotional purposes, provided no confidential information is disclosed.  

7. Confidentiality  
Contractor shall not disclose or use any non-public information obtained from Company except as necessary to perform the Services.  

8. Term & Termination  
a. Term. This Agreement commences on the Effective Date and remains in effect until terminated.  
b. Termination for Convenience. Either party may terminate this Agreement or any SOW upon fourteen (14) days’ written notice.  
c. Termination for Cause. Either party may terminate immediately upon breach by the other party that is not cured within five (5) days after written notice.  
d. Effect of Termination. Upon termination, Contractor shall cease work, deliver all completed or in-progress Work Product, and invoice only for Services satisfactorily performed to date. Sections 3–7, 8(d), and 9 shall survive termination.  

9. Indemnification & Limitation of Liability  
Contractor shall indemnify and hold Company harmless from any third-party claims arising from Contractor’s negligence, willful misconduct, or breach of this Agreement. In no event shall either party be liable for indirect or consequential damages.  

10. Miscellaneous  
This Agreement constitutes the entire agreement, supersedes all prior discussions, and may be amended only in writing signed by both parties. It is governed by the laws of the State of __________, without regard to conflict of laws.  

IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the parties have executed this Agreement as of the Effective Date.  

___________________________        ___________________________

instruction: Describe the properties of water without using adjectives.
decomposed_questions: Is the generated text a description of water?
Is the generated text free from the use of any adjectives to describe the water?
output:
• Composition: every molecule joins two atoms of hydrogen with one atom of oxygen, linked through covalent bonds.

• Phases: under varied temperature and pressure, the substance can appear as ice, a liquid phase, or vapor.

• Phase change points: at standard atmospheric pressure it begins to melt near 0 °C and begins to boil near 100 °C.

• Density behavior: the density curve peaks close to 4 °C; as a result, ice remains above the underlying liquid phase.

• Molecular interactions: extensive hydrogen bonding produces cohesion, adhesion, surface tension, and capillary rise inside narrow tubes or plant vessels.

• Thermal behavior: a large amount of energy must enter or leave before the temperature shifts, and evaporation removes significant energy, moderating environmental and bodily temperatures.

• Solvent action: the substance dissolves numerous salts, gases, and organic molecules, permitting transport of nutrients and facilitation of chemical reactions.

• Electrical traits: in pure form its conductivity stays low, yet dissolved ions create solutions that carry charge readily.

• Planetary cycle: continual movement occurs through evaporation, condensation, precipitation, runoff, and infiltration, linking ocean, atmosphere, soil, and living organisms.

"To live in hearts we leave behind is not to die." — Thomas Campbell  

Introduction  
Today, we gather not in darkness, but in the warm glow of a life that lit our own.  
With gratitude in our chests, we remember a soul who showed us what it means to truly live.  

Personal Stories  
I will never forget Sunday afternoons in Maria’s kitchen, where laughter rose like bread in the oven and her grandchildren chased sunlight across the floor; she would pause mid-story, brush flour from her palms, and pull each of them close as if the embrace itself were nourishment.  
Her husband, Daniel, recalls late-night walks beneath blooming magnolias, when she would whisper plans for tomorrow—each dream cradled in tender optimism.  

Accomplishments  
Maria was a compassionate mentor, a visionary leader, a steadfast friend, an innovative thinker, and a humble servant to her community.  
She founded the neighborhood literacy program that now equips hundreds of children each year, championed sustainable gardens long before they were fashionable, and knitted blankets for every new baby on the block.  
Her gentle courage sparked change in city halls, her radiant kindness mended fractured spirits, and her tireless curiosity reminded us that learning never ends.  

Conclusion  
Though her voice is now an echo, her love remains our guiding melody.  
A good tree is known by its fruit.

instruction: Write a short fictional narrative about a journey to the Earth's core. Describe the various layers encountered along the way, ensuring each paragraph focuses on one layer and connects logically to the next from the perspective of the journey.
decomposed_questions: Is the generated text a short fictional narrative?

output:
I began my descent on a crisp autumn morning, drilling through the familiar continental crust. Granitic rock glittered around the tunnel walls, flecks of quartz catching the work lights like cold stars. Fossil-studded sedimentary layers gave way to ancient metamorphic slabs, and the comforting tremors of the surface world faded behind me. Heat rose, the air grew drier, and with a final shudder of machinery, I slipped beyond the crust’s fractured underside toward the mantle below.

The upper mantle greeted me with slow, plastic motion—solid rock that flowed like warm taffy over geologic time. Olivine crystals shimmered green beneath my headlamp, their lattice vibrating with the mounting temperature. Here, in the asthenosphere, the tunnel walls seemed to breathe, closing almost imperceptibly as convection currents whispered past. I pressed deeper, riding those molten murmurs downward, and felt the shift when pressure welded the minerals tighter, announcing my arrival in the lower mantle.

In the lower mantle, the world grew superheated and strangely serene, a kingdom of perovskite and bridgmanite squeezed into dense, unyielding configurations. My instruments registered pressures millions of times greater than at sea level; even sound traveled sluggishly in the thickened medium. Yet I pressed on, guided by seismic maps that revealed columns of subducted crust sinking like ghostly serpents. At the mantle’s base, the D'' layer flickered with pockets of partial melt—an incandescent threshold that opened into the metallic sea of the outer core.

Crossing that boundary felt like stepping into a living thunderhead. The outer core churned with liquid iron and nickel, an immense, convective ocean whose flow forged Earth’s magnetic field. My heat shields glowed white, and the electromagnetic roar hummed through every bolt of the descent capsule. Currents tugged at me, steering molten rivers that rose, cooled, and sank in an endless dance. Trusting inertia and navigation gyros, I let the capsule spiral inward until motion slowed and the liquid grew sluggish, crystallizing around me.

At last, I breached the final frontier: the solid inner core—a sphere of almost pure iron compressed into crystalline rigidity. Though hotter than the surface of the Sun, the unimaginable pressure locked the atoms in place, and my craft settled on a blindingly bright plain that rang like a bell with each faint seismic pulse from above. I stood there for a breathless moment, at the planet’s beating heart, feeling Earth’s slow vibrations echo through alloyed soles. Then, saving the memory like a spark, I turned my vessel upward, ready to retrace the layers—each now a chapter in a journey to the center of the world.

Major muscles: Chest (pectoralis major/minor), front shoulders (anterior deltoids), triceps, core stabilizers.  

EXERCISE 2 – BODY-WEIGHT SQUATS  
Sets / Time: 4 rounds × 45 s work (≈12–20 reps each round)  
Major muscles: Quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes, calves, lower-back stabilizers.  (Legs covered here.)  

EXERCISE 3 – BENT-OVER “T-RAISE” (reverse fly variation)*  
Sets / Time: 4 rounds × 45 s work (≈12–15 reps each round)  
Major muscles: Upper back (rear deltoids, rhomboids), middle trapezius, lower traps, core for anti-flexion.  
*Hold two water bottles or light dumbbells if available.  

EXERCISE 4 – WALKING OR ALTERNATING LUNGES  
Sets / Time: 4 rounds × 45 s work (≈10–12 reps per leg each round)  
Major muscles: Glutes, quadriceps, hamstrings, calves, hip stabilizers.  

EXERCISE 5 – PLANK-TO-KNEE-DRIVE (dynamic plank)  
Sets / Time: 4 rounds × 45 s work (≈16–24 knee drives total each round)  
Major muscles: Core (rectus abdominis, obliques, transverse abdominis), chest/shoulder stabilizers, hip flexors.

0:00–3:00  Warm-up  
3:00–5:00  Exercise 1, Round 1 + rest  
5:00–7:00  Exercise 2, Round 1 + rest  
7:00–9:00  Exercise 3, Round 1 + rest  
9:00–11:00 Exercise 4, Round 1 + rest  
11:00–13:00 Exercise 5, Round 1 + rest  
13:00–14:00 Water break  
14:00–24:00 Repeat the 5-exercise circuit for Rounds 2 & 3  
24:00–25:00 Water break  
25:00–29:00 Final (4th) round of all 5 exercises (shorten rest to stay on time)  
29:00–32:00 Cool-down/stretch  

Notes & Tips  
• Keep rest between exercises to 15 s; between full circuits take the 1-minute break.  
• Adjust pace or drop to knees on push-ups if needed; add jump squats or hold weights to increase squat difficulty.  
• Focus on controlled movement and full range of motion.  
• Stay hydrated and listen to your body—modify reps/time if required.

Month 6

Month 7

Vincent van Gogh’s “Starry Night” orchestrates a charged dialogue between earth and sky through a carefully balanced composition. The towering cypress anchors the foreground, its dark, flame-like silhouette bridging the tranquil village below and the ecstatic heavens above. This vertical thrust offsets the horizon’s horizontal pull, creating a dynamic equilibrium that keeps the viewer’s eye in perpetual motion.

Color amplifies the painting’s emotional tenor. Van Gogh layers deep ultramarines and Prussian blues to build a nocturnal backdrop, against which the lemon and cadmium yellows of the stars and moon blaze like embers. The complementary contrast intensifies the luminosity, transforming the night sky into a living, breathing entity. Subtle touches of viridian and ochre in the rolling hills echo the village’s muted roofs, tying the terrestrial to the celestial.

Technique is the work’s heartbeat. Thick impasto and rapidly pulsating brushstrokes carve rhythmic swirls across the canvas, suggesting cosmic turbulence and Van Gogh’s own psychological unrest. These tactile ridges catch real light, making the painted stars shimmer physically as well as metaphorically, and inviting viewers to sense, not merely see, the scene.

Together, composition, color, and technique evoke a theme of yearning—an aspiration to transcend earthly confines while acknowledging human vulnerability. “Starry Night” thus stands as a timeless testament to art’s power to translate inner turmoil into universal wonder, reshaping modern painting by championing emotion over realism and inspiring generations of artists to follow.

decomposed_questions: Does the generated text include a Punnett square?

Cross:  Aa Bb   ×   A A Bb  
Genes assort independently and each capital letter (A, B) is completely dominant to its lowercase allele (a, b).

1. Determine the possible gametes from each parent  

• AaBb → AB , Ab , aB , ab  (each ¼)  
• AABb → AB , Ab             (each ½)  

2. Set up the Punnett square  

       Parent 1 gametes  
      AB   Ab   aB   ab  
Parent 2 ┌────────┬────────┬────────┬────────┐  
gametes   │        │        │        │        │  
  AB      │ AABB   │ AABb   │ AaBB   │ AaBb   │  
          ├────────┼────────┼────────┼────────┤  
  Ab      │ AABb   │ AAbb   │ AaBb   │ Aabb   │  
      └────────┴────────┴────────┴────────┘  

(Each box represents ½ × ¼ = 1/8 of the progeny.)

3. Count the genotypes (out of 8)

• AABB … 1  
• AABb … 2  
• AaBB … 1  
• AaBb … 2  
• AAbb … 1  
• Aabb … 1  

Genotypic ratio:  
AABB : AABb : AaBB : AaBb : AAbb : Aabb  
= 1 : 2 : 1 : 2 : 1 : 1.

4. Determine the phenotypes  

Because every zygote has at least one A allele (A is dominant), all offspring show the dominant A phenotype.  
For the B locus:

• Dominant B phenotype (genotypes B–) → AABB, AABb, AaBB, AaBb = 6/8  
• Recessive b phenotype (bb) → AAbb, Aabb = 2/8  

Phenotypic ratio:  

Dominant A – Dominant B : Dominant A – Recessive b  
            3 : 1  (75 % : 25 %).

Summary  
• All progeny display the dominant form of trait A.  
• For trait B, ¾ of the offspring show the dominant phenotype, ¼ show the recessive phenotype.

Product Reviewed: Nimbus Audio “Silence Pro X” Active Noise-Canceling Headphones  
Time Used: 3 weeks (approx. 30 hours listening time)  

1. Sound Quality  
At $299, I expected premium acoustics. Instead, the Silence Pro X delivers an oddly muffled, almost “blanketed” sound signature. High-frequency detail is noticeably rolled off—cymbals and strings lose their shimmer, making classical recordings feel lifeless. The midrange is recessed to the point that vocals sit behind the instrumentation, which is particularly frustrating for podcasts or vocal-centric tracks. Bass is abundant but poorly controlled; kick drums thud rather than punch, bleeding into the lower mids. I ran the headphones through FLAC files and even tried the built-in EQ presets, but the “Hi-Fi” mode merely added a harsh, metallic edge. Ironically, the best audio I could coax out of them came from heavily compressed pop songs where the production already hides dynamic nuance.  

2. Comfort  
Nimbus touts its plush memory-foam earpads, yet the clamping force borders on vise-like. After 45 minutes, I felt significant pressure around my temples, forcing me to take breaks. The pads also trap heat—during a two-hour flight I had to remove them twice just to cool down. Adding insult to injury, the headband’s minimal padding means the top of my skull develops a hot spot relatively quickly. For context, I routinely wear competing models (Sony WH-1000XM5, Bose QC45) for 3-4 hours without fatigue, so the difference is stark.  

3. Design & Build  
Aesthetically, the Silence Pro X looks sleek in marketing photos, but in person the glossy plastic cups feel insubstantial. Within the first week, I noticed faint creaking when adjusting the yoke, and the right hinge now wobbles slightly. The gesture controls are another weak point; the touch surface is overly sensitive, pausing music whenever I brush against it to push the earcup back. The carrying case, while semi-rigid, has a zipper that snags on its own lining. All of this makes the product feel more $99 than $299.  

4. Battery Life  
Nimbus advertises “up to 35 hours” with ANC on. In real-world use at 60–70 % volume, I averaged 21–22 hours, well below the claim. Worse, there’s no quick-charge feature; a full recharge takes close to 3 hours over the dated micro-USB port (why not USB-C in 2023?). Twice, the companion app’s battery meter froze at 40 %, leaving me with a dead headset mid-commute.  

Overall Impression  
The Silence Pro X looks promising on paper but stumbles in execution. The persistent audio haze, discomfort after short sessions, flimsy construction, and subpar battery performance make it hard to recommend—especially at its premium price. Unless Nimbus issues a significant firmware update (and perhaps offers better padding), prospective buyers are better served by established alternatives from Sony, Bose, or even some budget-friendly ANC options that outperform this model in every key category.

Logic Puzzle – “All in a Line”

Six friends – A, B, C, D, E and F – are standing in a single row facing the same way (so “left” and “right” are the same for everyone).  Use the following clues to work out their exact order from left-to-right.

Clues
1.  D is standing at one of the two ends of the line.  
2.  D is somewhere to the left of B.  
3.  B is standing immediately to the left of F.  
4.  F is somewhere to the left of A.  
5.  A is somewhere to the left of E.  
6.  C is standing immediately to the right of E.  

No clue gives any person’s exact numbered place, only how each is positioned relative to the others.

-------------------------------------------------
Solution (with reasoning)

Step 1 – From clue 1 D must be at an end.  
Clue 2 says D is to the left of B, so D cannot be the right-hand end.  
Therefore D is the left-most person:

 1  D  _  _  _  _  _

Step 2 – Clue 3 says B is immediately left of F, so the string “… B F …” must occur somewhere.  
Because D already occupies the first place, the only possible adjacent pairs for B-F are positions 2-3, 3-4 or 4-5.

Step 3 – Clues 4 and 5 give a chain:  
 F is left of A, and A is left of E  ⇒  F < A < E.  
Clue 6 adds that C is immediately right of E, giving the full chain:  

 B < F < A < E < C with the extra adjacencies B–F and E–C.

Step 4 – Try to fit that whole chain next to D.

• If B–F were at 3-4, the chain would run D ? B F A E C, but this needs seven places – impossible.  
• If B–F were at 4-5, the chain would have to start somewhere to the left of D – impossible.  
• Therefore B–F must occupy 2-3.

That forces the rest of the chain:

 1  2  3  4  5  6  
 D  B  F  A  E  C

Step 5 – Check all clues:

1. D is at the left end ✔  
2. D is left of B ✔  
3. B is immediately left of F ✔  
4. F is left of A ✔  
5. A is left of E ✔  
6. C is immediately right of E ✔  

All clues are satisfied and the arrangement is unique.

Final order from left to right:
D – B – F – A – E – C

Jordan: I did what I thought was necessary to keep the company afloat.  

[Jordan reaches for his glass; his hand trembles slightly.]

Clara: Do you realize what that does to our partnership?  
Jordan: The investors demanded a prototype immediately, and your design was the only thing ready.  

[Clara leans forward, her plate untouched.]

Clara: I trusted you with my sketches, my time, and my good name.  
Jordan: I wanted to tell you, but the contract was signed before I could blink.  

[A nearby couple pauses mid-conversation, sensing tension.]

Clara: Was it really just about the money?  
Jordan: It wasn't betrayal; it was survival.  

[Clara’s eyes glisten; she steadies herself.]

Clara: Look me in the eyes and answer.  
Jordan: If I could redo the last week, I would, but here we are—so what happens next?

SWOT Analysis for an Electric Vehicle (EV) Startup

1. Strengths
• Agile R&D: As a startup, you can pivot faster than legacy automakers, implementing emerging technologies (e.g., solid-state batteries, over-the-air software updates) without the burden of legacy platforms.  
• Clean-sheet Design: No sunk costs in internal-combustion infrastructure, enabling optimized vehicle architecture (battery placement, lightweight materials, skateboard chassis).  
• Sustainability Branding: Early adoption by eco-conscious consumers and ESG-oriented investors can amplify brand reputation and attract capital.  
• Digital-First Culture: Ability to integrate connected-car ecosystems, data analytics, and direct-to-consumer sales without dealer-network constraints.  
• Strategic Partnerships: Opportunities to collaborate with battery suppliers, charging-network operators, and tech firms, pooling resources and reducing capital intensity.

2. Weaknesses
• Limited Capital & Scale: High upfront costs for battery supply contracts, manufacturing plants, and R&D; difficulty matching economies of scale enjoyed by established OEMs.  
• Supply Chain Vulnerability: Dependency on critical minerals (lithium, nickel, cobalt); potential shortages or price spikes can disrupt production timelines.  
• Brand Recognition: New entrants struggle to build consumer trust and service networks compared with well-known automakers.  
• Regulatory Complexity: Varying safety, emissions, and battery-recycling standards across regions increase compliance costs and time to market.  
• Talent Acquisition: Competition for EV-specific engineering talent (battery chemists, power electronics engineers) is intense, inflating payroll costs.

3. Opportunities
• Market Growth: Global EV sales are forecast to grow >20 % CAGR this decade, driven by falling battery costs and government incentives (zero-emission mandates, tax credits).  
• Niche Segments: Underserved categories—commercial delivery vans, affordable city cars, specialized off-road EVs—allow differentiation from mass-market players.  
• Charging Ecosystem: Offering bundled home chargers, energy-storage solutions, or subscription-based fast-charging services can create recurring revenue streams.  
• Software & Data Monetization: Advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS), in-car infotainment subscriptions, and fleet telematics can boost margins beyond vehicle sales.  
• Strategic Policy Tailwinds: Carbon-neutral pledges and ICE phase-out timelines in major markets (EU, China, several U.S. states) favor early movers in EVs.

4. Threats
• Intensifying Competition: Legacy automakers (e.g., GM, VW, Ford) are investing tens of billions in EV programs, leveraging brand loyalty, supply scale, and dealer networks.  
• Component Shortages: Semiconductor constraints and battery-grade material bottlenecks can delay production and inflate costs.  
• Price Wars: Established players may cut prices to defend market share, compressing margins for startups.  
• Technological Obsolescence: Rapid advances (e.g., next-gen batteries, hydrogen fuel cells) could render current platforms less competitive before ROI is achieved.  
• Regulatory & Incentive Shifts: Changes in subsidies, trade tariffs, or safety standards could erode financial projections; reliance on incentives is risky.  
• Macroeconomic Headwinds: Rising interest rates, inflation, or recessions could dampen consumer willingness to pay EV price premiums, tightening funding markets.

Overall, a well-focused EV startup can leverage agility and innovation to carve out a defensible position, but must aggressively manage capital, supply-chain, and differentiation risks in a rapidly evolving landscape.

Python Class Documentation
==========================

Class Name: `ShoppingCart`

Description:  
`ShoppingCart` is a lightweight utility class that helps you build and manage a virtual shopping-cart object in memory.  
It supports adding and removing items, inspecting the current cart content, and computing the running total.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Class Signature
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```python
class ShoppingCart(currency: str = "USD"):
    ...
```

Constructor Parameters  
• `currency` (str, optional) – The ISO 4217 currency code that will be used when reporting prices.  
  Default is `"USD"`.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Public Methods
--------------------------------------------------------------------

1. `add_item(name, price, quantity=1)`
   ------------------------------------------------------------
   Purpose  
   • Add a stock-keeping unit (SKU) to the cart or increase the quantity of an existing item.

   Parameters  
   • `name` (str) – A unique, human-readable identifier for the product (e.g., `"Apple"`).  
   • `price` (float) – Unit price of the product denominated in the cart’s currency.  
   • `quantity` (int, optional) – How many units to add. Must be ≥ 1. Default is `1`.

   Returns  
   • `None` – The cart is modified in place; no explicit value is returned.

   Exceptions Raised  
   • `ValueError` – If `price` is negative or `quantity` is less than 1.

2. `remove_item(name, quantity=None)`
   ------------------------------------------------------------
   Purpose  
   • Remove a product partially or completely from the cart.

   Parameters  
   • `name` (str) – The product identifier to be removed.  
   • `quantity` (int | None, optional) –  
     – If `None` (default), the item is removed entirely.  
     – If an `int`, that many units are removed. Must be ≥ 1.

   Returns  
   • `bool` – `True` if at least one unit was removed, `False` if the item was not found.

   Exceptions Raised  
   • `ValueError` – If `quantity` is not `None` and is < 1.

3. `total(include_currency=False)`
   ------------------------------------------------------------
   Purpose  
   • Calculate the aggregated cost of all items currently in the cart.

   Parameters  
   • `include_currency` (bool, optional) –  
     – If `False` (default) the method returns a `float` numeric total.  
     – If `True` the method returns a human-friendly string with the currency code appended (e.g., `"34.95 USD"`).

   Returns  
   • `float | str` – Either the numeric total or a string with currency, depending on `include_currency`.

4. `items()`
   ------------------------------------------------------------
   Purpose  
   • Retrieve a shallow copy of the cart’s current content.

   Parameters  
   • None

   Returns  
   • `dict[str, dict]` – Mapping where each key is an item name and each value is a dictionary in the form  
     `{ "price": float, "quantity": int }`.  
     Example: `{ "Apple": {"price": 0.99, "quantity": 4} }`.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Example Usage
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```python
from shopping_cart import ShoppingCart

# Instantiate a cart that reports totals in U.S. dollars
cart = ShoppingCart(currency="USD")

# 1. Add items
cart.add_item("Apple", price=0.99, quantity=4)
cart.add_item("Milk", price=3.49)          # default quantity is 1
cart.add_item("Coffee", price=8.99, quantity=2)

# 2. Remove two apples
cart.remove_item("Apple", quantity=2)

# 3. Inspect cart contents
print("Current items:", cart.items())
# -> {'Apple': {'price': 0.99, 'quantity': 2},
#     'Milk': {'price': 3.49, 'quantity': 1},
#     'Coffee': {'price': 8.99, 'quantity': 2}}

# 4. Obtain numeric total
print("Subtotal:", cart.total())           # -> 31.44

# 5. Obtain formatted total with currency
print("Subtotal:", cart.total(include_currency=True))  # -> "31.44 USD"
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Implementation (for reference)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```python
class ShoppingCart:
    def __init__(self, currency: str = "USD") -> None:
        self._currency = currency.upper()
        self._items: dict[str, dict[str, float | int]] = {}

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------
    # Public API
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------
    def add_item(self, name: str, price: float, quantity: int = 1) -> None:
        if price < 0:
            raise ValueError("price must be non-negative")
        if quantity < 1:
            raise ValueError("quantity must be >= 1")

        record = self._items.setdefault(name, {"price": price, "quantity": 0})
        # Update price in case it changed; latest price wins
        record["price"] = price
        record["quantity"] += quantity

    def remove_item(self, name: str, quantity: int | None = None) -> bool:
        if name not in self._items:
            return False
        if quantity is None:
            del self._items[name]
            return True
        if quantity < 1:
            raise ValueError("quantity must be >= 1")

        record = self._items[name]
        if quantity >= record["quantity"]:
            del self._items[name]
        else:
            record["quantity"] -= quantity
        return True

    def total(self, include_currency: bool = False) -> float | str:
        subtotal = sum(info["price"] * info["quantity"] for info in self._items.values())
        return f"{subtotal:.2f} {self._currency}" if include_currency else round(subtotal, 2)

    def items(self) -> dict[str, dict]:
        return self._items.copy()
```

Feel free to adapt or extend the class to fit your specific needs.

Vegetarian Cherry-Tomato & Cannellini Penne

Ingredient list (serves 4)
• 12 oz (340 g) penne pasta  
• 2 Tbsp olive oil  
• 3 garlic cloves, minced  
• 1 ½ cups halved cherry tomatoes  
• 1 can (15 oz / 425 g) cannellini beans, rinsed and drained  
• 3 cups loosely packed baby spinach  
• ¼ tsp crushed red-pepper flakes (optional)  
• ½ tsp salt, plus more for pasta water  
• ¼ tsp freshly ground black pepper  
• ¼ cup grated vegetarian Parmesan cheese (or other hard Italian-style cheese made with vegetarian rennet)

Five-step cooking method
1. Stockpot: Bring a large stockpot of generously salted water to a boil, add the penne, and cook until al dente (about 10 minutes).  
2. Frying pan: While the pasta cooks, warm the olive oil over medium heat; stir in garlic and red-pepper flakes, sautéing for 30 seconds until fragrant.  
3. Add cherry tomatoes to the frying pan and cook 3 minutes, gently pressing to release juices. Stir in cannellini beans; season with ½ tsp salt and ¼ tsp black pepper.  
4. Toss in spinach and cook 1 minute, just until wilted. Remove the pan from heat.  
5. When the pasta is ready, reserve ½ cup cooking water, then carefully drain the penne from the stockpot. Add pasta to the frying pan sauce, splash in a little reserved water to coat, and sprinkle with Parmesan. Toss well and serve hot.

Enjoy your quick, hearty vegetarian pasta!

The first time I realized the power of language was at a bustling train station in Tokyo. Five disparate languages were bouncing off the tiled walls, yet a single LED sign reading “Delay: 10 min” instantly synchronized hundreds of travelers. I remember marveling at how such a concise string of characters could unify people of different backgrounds, temper frustrations, and trigger a collective plan-B. That moment stayed with me, and it quietly sowed the seed of a question that has guided my academic and professional life ever since: How can we leverage computational models to harness the unifying power of language and make information universally accessible? Today, as I apply for the Natural Language Processing Scientist position at Orion AI Labs, I bring with me not only that formative fascination but also a rigorous toolkit, diverse experience, and a relentless drive to build systems that let human ideas travel freely and meaningfully.

My motivation to work in NLP stems from equal parts intellectual curiosity and social conviction. Academically, language sits at the intersection of logic, cognition, and creativity, offering a rich playground for anyone who enjoys puzzles with both concrete and human dimensions. Practically, NLP has the potential to remove barriers—be they linguistic, literacy-based, or cognitive—and I believe this democratization of information is a moral imperative in an increasingly digital world. Orion’s mission to create language tools that “speak to every user” resonates with my own commitment to inclusivity; it is precisely the environment where I want to translate curiosity into global impact.

My journey formally began at the University of Michigan, where I completed a B.S. in Computer Science with a minor in Linguistics. I gravitated toward courses like “Statistical Machine Translation” and “Computational Semantics,” ultimately graduating summa cum laude. During my senior year, I co-authored a paper on leveraging character-level embeddings to improve sentiment analysis in code-mixed social media text. Presenting that work at EMNLP 2019 was both an adrenaline rush and a masterclass in the values of rigorous experimentation and clear communication.

Following graduation, I joined BrightText, a startup building AI-powered language tutoring software. As an NLP engineer, I owned the development of a grammar-correction module that served 500k users monthly. The task required implementing a Transformer-based sequence-to-sequence model with constrained decoding to ensure pedagogically sound corrections. Over nine months, I iterated through data augmentation techniques, optimized inference pipelines with ONNX, and deployed an A/B test that cut the model’s latency by 30% while improving BLEU and GLEU scores by 4.2 and 3.8 points respectively. More importantly, user retention increased by 12%, validating that better language feedback translates into sustained learning engagement.

I then pursued an M.S. in Language Technologies at Carnegie Mellon University to deepen my theoretical grounding. My thesis focused on low-resource neural machine translation, specifically on dynamically balancing cross-lingual transfer and domain adaptation. By integrating meta-learning paradigms into universal encoder-decoder architectures, I achieved a 7-point BLEU improvement on a Swahili-English benchmark, outperforming existing baselines while reducing training time by 25%. The work now under review for ACL 2024 has already yielded a GitHub repository that over 600 researchers have starred.

Of course, the path has not been linear. During the first months at BrightText, our team discovered a high bias toward “standard English” in our grammar model, inadvertently penalizing dialectical variations like African American Vernacular English (AAVE). The issue posed a challenge both technical and ethical: we needed to correct bias without sacrificing performance on the primary user base. I spearheaded an initiative to curate a balanced corpus by collaborating with community organizations, hiring linguistically diverse annotators, and implementing bias-aware loss functions. The resulting model not only reduced disparity in false-positive rates across dialects by 60% but also taught me a lasting lesson about the responsibility that comes with deploying language technology.

Throughout these experiences, I have honed a toolbox well aligned with the requirements of this role: 

• Languages & Frameworks: Python, PyTorch, TensorFlow, Hugging Face, spaCy  
• Research & Engineering: Transformer architectures, self-supervised learning, information retrieval, MLOps (Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD)  
• Communication: First-author publications, tech talks, cross-functional collaboration with designers and product managers  

I am drawn to Orion AI Labs because of its dedication to open research, its culture of rapid iteration, and its emphasis on end-user empathy. I am particularly excited about your ongoing project to build speech-to-speech translation for under-resourced languages, an endeavor that dovetails perfectly with my background in low-resource MT and bias mitigation.

Looking ahead, my immediate goal is to contribute to Orion’s multilingual pipeline, optimizing encoder-decoders for deployment on edge devices. I also aim to mentor junior engineers, paying forward the guidance that has shaped my own career. Ultimately, I hope to help establish standards and open-source tools that lower entry barriers for researchers and developers worldwide.

Returning to that Tokyo station memory, I now see the subtlety behind those two words—“Delay: 10 min.” They were, in fact, a compact dialogue between system and human, a linguistic bridge across cultures. With Orion AI Labs, I envision building many such bridges at scale: models that listen, speak, and transform our collective experience of language. My academic rigor, applied industry success, and steadfast commitment to ethical NLP make me well suited to this challenge. I look forward to the possibility of bringing my skills and passion to your team, and to co-creating a world where every voice can be both heard and understood.

Peer Review

1. What is this paper about and what contributions does it make?  
The paper proposes “MetaFed-Adapt,” a novel framework that combines meta-learning with federated learning to enable rapid adaptation to new clients with only a handful of labeled examples (1-5 shots). The key contributions are:   
• A meta-learned optimizer that is jointly trained across clients to initialize models for fast local adaptation.  
• A theoretical convergence analysis under non-IID data assumptions.  
• An open-source simulation toolkit and two real-world case studies (mobile keyboard prediction and wearable activity recognition).  
• An ablation study showing gains over five strong baselines on three public benchmarks (LEAF, Human Activity, and a proprietary mobile typing dataset).  

2. Reasons to accept:  
• Novelty: The integration of meta-learned optimizers into a communication-efficient federated learning loop is original and timely.  
• Technical depth: Provides rigorous proofs of convergence with non-convex losses and client drift.  
• Empirical strength: Demonstrates 7-15% average accuracy improvements over baselines with only 20% of the communication rounds.  
• Open-source release: Code and detailed scripts are promised, enhancing reproducibility.  
• Societal relevance: Addresses personalization and privacy in edge devices—an important application domain.  

3. Reasons to reject:  
• Limited comparison to current self-supervised or foundation-model adaptation methods; these are briefly mentioned but not experimentally benchmarked.  
• The proprietary mobile typing dataset is not publicly shareable, hindering full reproducibility of one key result.  
• Hyper-parameter sensitivity is underexplored; the main text reports averaged results without variance or confidence intervals for several figures.  
• Ethical discussion is quite short; no systematic threat analysis regarding possible privacy leakage from meta-gradients.  

4. Questions for the Author(s):  
Q1. How does MetaFed-Adapt perform when the client participates with zero labeled samples (purely unsupervised personalization)?  
Q2. Could the authors clarify whether the meta-learned optimizer parameters are shared with the server, and if so, what privacy-preserving mechanisms are in place?  
Q3. How sensitive is the method to the number of inner-loop adaptation steps? A sweep would be informative.  
Q4. Have you considered comparing against recent parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques (e.g., LoRA, adapters) that could also be used in federated settings?  
Q5. Are there plans to release a synthetic surrogate of the proprietary dataset or a detailed data schema to aid reproducibility?

5. Soundness (score 1-5): 4  
The methodology and analysis are mostly solid, though more baselines and variance reporting are needed.

6. Excitement (score 1-5): 4  
Addresses an important and emerging problem with promising empirical gains.

7. Reviewer Confidence (score 1-5): 4  
I feel reasonably confident; I have experience in federated and meta-learning research.

8. Recommendation for Best Paper Award (Yes/No): No  
Strong paper, but missing key comparisons and deeper analysis of privacy aspects.

9. Reproducibility (score 1-5): 3  
Code availability is good, but proprietary data and some missing hyper-parameter details limit full reproducibility.

10. Ethical Concerns (Yes/No): No major concerns identified, but privacy implications of meta-gradients deserve more discussion.



Author Response

We thank the reviewer for the constructive and detailed feedback. Below we address each point and outline planned revisions.

R1. Limited comparison with self-supervised / foundation-model adaptation methods  
We agree this is important. In the revised manuscript we will add experimental comparisons with (i) FedMAE (self-supervised federated masked auto-encoding) and (ii) Federated-LoRA. Preliminary results (included in the supplementary material) show MetaFed-Adapt still outperforms these methods by 4.3% and 5.1% average accuracy respectively.

R2. Proprietary mobile typing dataset  
To improve reproducibility we will release (a) a fully anonymized, down-sampled version of the dataset that preserves token frequency statistics, and (b) a data generator script that reproduces the long-tail vocabulary distribution we observe in production.

R3. Hyper-parameter sensitivity and variance reporting  
We have rerun all experiments with 5 random seeds and will include confidence intervals (95% CI) in all plots. An appendix section will detail sensitivity to inner-loop learning rate, number of adaptation steps, and meta-batch size.

R4. Ethical / privacy analysis  
We will add a dedicated subsection on privacy, including: (1) formal argument that meta-gradient aggregation is differentially private under our DP-FedAvg noise addition; (2) empirical membrane attack simulations showing <1% membership inference gain over chance.

Responses to Questions:

Q1. Zero-shot clients: MetaFed-Adapt falls back to the shared initialization and achieves competitive performance (2-3% below full-shot) compared to FedAvg. We will include these numbers.

Q2. The meta-learned optimizer states are aggregated centrally using DP-SGD with σ=1.2, ε=2.8. We will clarify this in Section 3.2.

Q3. Sensitivity: Performance saturates after 5 inner steps; see new Figure 6.

Q4. Comparison with LoRA/adapters: Addressed in R1.

Q5. Surrogate dataset: Addressed in R2.

We hope these additions resolve the concerns and strengthen the paper.

Arts education has long been viewed as an “enrichment” rather than a core subject, yet research and practice consistently show that music, visual arts, theater, dance, and creative writing are indispensable to well-rounded learning. Through the arts, students strengthen cognitive abilities, cultivate social and emotional intelligence, and connect more deeply with their communities and cultures. In an era that prizes innovation, empathy, and adaptability, arts education is not a luxury—it is a necessity.

First, arts classes strengthen essential cognitive skills that transfer to other academic areas. Studies from organizations such as Americans for the Arts reveal that students who engage in sustained music instruction exhibit improved spatial-temporal reasoning, language development, and mathematical performance. In a middle school in Nashville, for example, administrators embedded drumming circles into daily homeroom periods; math scores subsequently rose by 15 percent because rhythmic patterns reinforced fraction and ratio concepts. By beginning with complex brain benefits and then illustrating how a real campus translated them into higher test results, it becomes clear that artistic study is a direct catalyst for academic growth.

Second, participation in the arts nurtures social and emotional learning (SEL), providing students with tools for self-expression and empathy. When learners rehearse a play or collaborate on a mural, they negotiate roles, listen actively, and interpret multiple perspectives. At Chicago’s ChiArts High School, a visual-arts cohort created autobiographical portrait projects. Students reported feeling “seen” by peers, while counselors documented a 25 percent decrease in disciplinary referrals that semester. Thus, the process of making and sharing art not only hones interpersonal skills but also fosters a positive school climate, as demonstrated by the drop in behavioral incidents at ChiArts.

Third, arts education connects students to cultural heritage and civic engagement, cultivating informed, engaged citizens. Arts curricula often spotlight diverse traditions, enabling young people to appreciate histories beyond their own. In Santa Fe, New Mexico, eighth graders partnered with local Pueblo artisans to construct clay storytellers, artifacts symbolic of oral tradition. The collaboration culminated in a public exhibition that drew families from multiple tribes and towns, sparking community dialogue about cultural preservation. This example underscores how arts instruction situates learners within broader social narratives, promoting respect, inclusion, and civic participation.

In sum, arts education sharpens cognitive faculties, advances social-emotional development, and deepens cultural and civic awareness. The Nashville drumming initiative linked music to math achievement; ChiArts demonstrated that creative self-expression curbs disciplinary issues; and Santa Fe students used clay figures to bridge cultural divides. Collectively, these outcomes confirm that the arts are not peripheral adornments but foundational experiences that equip young people to think critically, feel deeply, and engage responsibly in an increasingly complex world.

Policy Proposal: Integrated Heritage & Sustainability Framework (IHSF)

1. Community-Led Land Stewardship
   • Legally recognize indigenous territories and grant co-management authority over natural resources.  
   • Establish conservation easements that embed traditional ecological knowledge (TEK) in forest, water, and wildlife management plans.  
   • Allocate a share of green-economy revenues (carbon credits, eco-tourism fees) to tribal councils, funding cultural programs and reinforcing guardianship incentives.

   • Mandate that all public and private projects undergo Cultural Impact Assessments co-designed with indigenous experts, evaluating effects on sacred sites, languages, and livelihoods.  
   • Require free, prior, and informed consent (FPIC) as a legal threshold, with binding veto rights on developments that threaten irreplaceable heritage.  
   • Establish a national Indigenous Heritage Fund to finance mitigation, site documentation, and cultural continuity measures.

3. Sustainable Livelihood Incubators
   • Create regional incubators that pair indigenous artisans, farmers, and knowledge-holders with green-tech mentors, microfinance, and fair-trade markets.  
   • Prioritize value chains that elevate traditional crafts, agro-biodiversity, and renewable energy jobs.  
   • Monitor social and environmental outcomes jointly with indigenous evaluators, ensuring adaptive policy adjustments.

This tri-pillar approach sustains cultural integrity, empowers self-determination, and aligns development with long-term ecological resilience. (188 words)

instruction: Explain three innovative techniques presently employed in civil engineering for sustainable construction. Include real-life examples for each technique and discuss their environmental advantages.
decomposed_questions: Does the generated text provide explanations of innovative techniques currently used in civil engineering?

output:
Below are three cutting-edge techniques that civil engineers are adopting to create more sustainable buildings and infrastructure. For each technique you will find:

• A concise explanation of how it works.  
• A real-world project that already uses it.  
• The principal environmental benefits it delivers.

1. High-Performance Concrete with Supplementary Cementitious Materials (SCMs)
   • How it works  
     Ordinary Portland cement (OPC) is replaced in part by industrial by-products such as fly ash, ground-granulated blast-furnace slag (GGBS), or silica fume. These SCMs react with the calcium hydroxide in cement to form additional calcium-silicate-hydrate (C-S-H), producing a stronger, denser concrete while reducing the total amount of OPC required.

   • Real-life example  
     The One World Trade Center in New York City incorporated up to 70 % GGBS in selected concrete mixes. Similarly, the Queen’s Wharf development in Brisbane, Australia, uses fly-ash-based concrete throughout its basements and podiums.

   • Environmental advantages  
     – Lower CO₂ footprint: Cement production is responsible for roughly 7–8 % of global CO₂ emissions. Replacing 50 % of OPC with fly ash or slag can cut embodied carbon in concrete by 25–40 %.  
     – Beneficial reuse of industrial waste: Materials that might otherwise go to landfill are repurposed.  
     – Enhanced durability: Denser, less permeable concrete can last longer and resist chloride ingress, reducing the need for repairs and thereby lowering long-term resource consumption.

2. Mass Timber and Cross-Laminated Timber (CLT) Structures
   • How it works  
     Mass timber elements—glulam beams, CLT panels, and dowel-laminated timber—are engineered by bonding layers of dimensional lumber at right angles. The result is structural panels and beams that rival steel and concrete in strength-to-weight ratio while being far lighter.

   • Real-life example  
     The Mjøstårnet tower in Brumunddal, Norway, currently the world’s tallest timber building at 85.4 m, uses CLT floor slabs and glulam columns. The 25 King office building in Brisbane and the U.S. “Framework” project in Portland also showcase high-rise mass-timber construction.

   • Environmental advantages  
     – Carbon sequestration: Timber stores carbon absorbed during tree growth; using responsibly sourced wood can make the structural frame a net carbon sink.  
     – Reduced embodied energy: Manufacturing and transporting timber consumes less energy than producing steel or concrete.  
     – Lightweight construction: Lighter structures mean smaller foundations, less excavation, and reduced material use overall.  
     – End-of-life reuse: Timber panels can often be demounted and reused or recycled.

3. Smart Water Management with Blue-Green Infrastructure
   • How it works  
     Blue-green infrastructure (BGI) combines vegetated systems (green roofs, bioswales, rain gardens) with engineered water-storage (blue roofs, underground attenuation tanks) to capture, store, and slowly release stormwater. Sensors and automated valves optimize retention and irrigation in real time.

   • Real-life example  
     The “Water Square” Benthemplein in Rotterdam, Netherlands, doubles as a public plaza and a 1.7 million-liter stormwater basin, integrated with permeable pavements and bioswales. In the United States, New York City’s Cloudburst Resilience projects retrofit streets with smart sensors that open or close control structures based on rainfall forecasts.

   • Environmental advantages  
     – Flood mitigation: Temporarily storing runoff eases pressure on urban drainage systems and offsets combined sewer overflows.  
     – Urban heat-island reduction: Vegetation provides evapotranspirative cooling.  
     – Enhanced biodiversity and air quality: Plantings create habitats and filter airborne particulates.  
     – Water reuse: Captured stormwater can irrigate landscapes or flush toilets, lowering potable-water demand.

Collectively, these techniques—low-carbon concrete, mass-timber construction, and sensor-enabled blue-green infrastructure—demonstrate how civil engineering is evolving toward lower emissions, circular material flows, and resilient urban ecosystems.

output:
The Green Leather Journal of a Wayward Wanderer  
(A chance journey through Middle-earth)  

Day 1 – A Very Unlikely Crossing  
I stepped off a mist-swaddled moor in northern England and, quite without warning, found myself on the verge of an emerald downslope under a sky of impossible blue. A sweet, earthy scent—sun-warmed pipeweed?—floated on the breeze. Ahead, round-doored hobbit-holes pricked the hillside like brightly painted buttons. Their inhabitants, merry folk smaller than I, greeted me with shy curiosity. A rosy-cheeked gardener pressed a mug of frothy ale into my hands; the drink tasted of summer grain and fresh apples. My heart tumbled between disbelief and delight. If this was a dream, I begged never to wake.

Day 2 – Songs under Starlight  
By evening a westering road led me through gentle farmland to a willow-lined river. Hobbits produced fiddles and flutes, and soon a sprightly reel carried across the water. The night sky here seems closer, every star shining like a private candle. Laughter mingled with melodies about wandering and home—the first hint of how deeply song roots itself in Middle-earth. I felt the road tugging at my feet, but part of me wished to linger forever amid these soft lights and kinder hearts.

Day 3 – Among Rangers and Ruins  
Past the Shire’s hedgerows, the wild edges grew tall. I met a company of grim yet courteous Men—Rangers keeping watch on lonely ways. Cloaked in weather-beaten browns and forest greens, they spoke little, yet their silence brimmed with purpose. We camped beside the mossy bones of an ancient watchtower where once a kingdom had stood against darkness. Their campfire stories—told in low voices—hinted at sorrows centuries old. I sensed how history here lies not in books but in the land itself, breathing through stone and leaf.

Day 4 – The Falls of Bruinen  
Come dawn, silver water thundered over pale cliffs, spraying rainbows into the cool air. Elvish banners fluttered above a bridge carved finer than lace. Crossing, I entered a realm of sculpted terraces and birch-bowers: fair Imladris. Elves moved like living music, every gesture poised and graceful. A healer with starlight in her eyes tended the dusty blisters on my feet; her touch felt like moonlit water. I dared not ask how many ages her gaze had witnessed. Wonder mingled with humility—I, a mayfly beside swans.

Day 5 – Council Hall Whispers  
An invitation brought me to a vaulted chamber where maps older than my language sprawled across polished tables. Wise figures debated tidings of distant mountains and rumblings beneath the earth. To sit quietly among them was to feel time stretch, threads of past and future woven in their measured words. I learned that memory itself is currency here—and that hope, even fragile, can sway fates. Leaving the hall, I carried a hush inside me, as though my thoughts now echoed in the corridors of years.

Day 6 – Over the Misty Mountains’ Edge  
Guided by sure-footed Dwarves, I trudged a snow-laced pass. Their humor rings like hammered iron: blunt, hearty, unbreakable. They taught me to read the veins in stone—“every cliff has a tale,” said one, tapping the rock with a calloused hand. A sudden, distant roar shivered the air; clouds boiled red on the eastern horizon. The Dwarves fell silent, beards bristling. “Not our concern tonight,” they muttered, but their eyes burned with ancient grudges. My pulse quickened—some vast presence had turned in its sleep.

Day 7 – A Glimmer of Gold and Fire  
Descending to a high valley, we caught sight of a shape eclipsing the moon: wings like tarnished shields, scales glinting molten brass. The dragon wheeled far off, a living tempest. Even at that distance the mountain shuddered beneath its cry. Terror rooted me to the path, yet awe unfurled inside—how terrible beauty can be. The Dwarves spat oaths in a tongue as hard as granite, then urged haste; legends, it seems, still breathe flame.

Day 8 – Lothlórien’s Golden Silence  
Southward, the world turned to living gold. Mallorn leaves, burnished even in spring, sifted light that felt both dawn and dusk. The Galadhrim welcomed me without speech, leading me along swaying rope ladders to halls of silver wood. In that hush, thoughts loosened like petals. I dreamt of everything I had loved and lost, and woke with tears that tasted sweet, as if sadness itself were hallowed. The Lady of the Wood met my gaze only once; in it I felt the weight and mercy of eternity.

Day 9 – The River’s Long Memory  
A smooth gray boat bore me down the Great River. On either side, colossal stone sentinels—cracked but unbowed—raised their stony hands in warning or blessing, I could not tell. Wind off the water carried scents of pine and distant sea. I began to understand: in Middle-earth, each league is a lesson. Mountains teach resilience, rivers teach change, forests teach listening. And people—whether small, stern, or silver-bright—teach courage braided with kindness.

Day 10 – Returning Footfalls, Lasting Echoes  
At twilight I crossed an unseen threshold and found myself once more on the moor where my journey began. Yet nothing was the same; the very air hummed with remembered harp-strings, drake-wings, and dwarven hammers. I am filled with gratitude large enough to span ages. Middle-earth has pressed its fingerprint upon my spirit—an ink of starlight and deep earth. I close this green leather journal knowing the road remains within me, and that somewhere beyond mortal sight, Elves still sing under everlasting trees, Rangers keep their silent vigil, Dwarves strike sparks in dark halls, and a dragon’s shadow skirts the moon.

output:
Formula:  
°C = (°F − 32) × 5/9

Calculation for 375 °F:  
°C = (375 − 32) × 5/9  
   = 343 × 5/9  
   = 1715 / 9  
   ≈ 190.6 °C

So, 375 °F is approximately 190.6 °C.

Turn 1 – Patient: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having sensitivity in my lower left molar for about a week, especially when I drink something cold, and I’ve noticed a little swelling in the gum nearby. What could be going on?

Turn 2 – Dentist: Thanks for letting me know. Sensitivity and gum swelling can come from a deep cavity, a cracked filling, or early signs of an abscess. Have you had any lingering pain, fever, or bad taste in your mouth? And when was your last cleaning?

Turn 3 – Patient: No fever, but I do get a dull ache at night. Sometimes there’s a slight bad taste. My last cleaning was about nine months ago.

Turn 4 – Dentist: Understood. Based on your symptoms, I’d like to take an X-ray to check for decay beneath the existing filling and to rule out infection at the root. If it’s a simple cavity, we can replace the filling. If the nerve is involved, a root-canal may be necessary, followed by a crown. We could also prescribe an antibiotic if there’s active infection.

Turn 5 – Patient: I’m hoping to avoid a root canal if possible. How do we decide?

Turn 6 – Dentist: The X-ray will show whether the decay has reached the pulp (nerve). If it hasn’t, removing the decay and placing a composite filling should stop the sensitivity. If the pulp is affected, a root-canal is the most predictable way to relieve pain and save the tooth. Delaying treatment could allow infection to spread, which sometimes leads to swelling and tooth loss.

Turn 7 – Patient: Okay, that makes sense. While we sort this out, is there anything I can do at home to reduce the pain and protect my teeth?

Turn 8 – Dentist: Yes. 1) Use a soft-bristle brush and brush twice daily with a fluoride toothpaste formulated for sensitivity. 2) Floss gently once a day to keep the gum area clean. 3) Rinse with a warm saltwater solution (½ tsp salt in 8 oz water) three times a day to reduce inflammation. 4) Avoid very hot, cold, or sugary foods until we treat the tooth. 5) Take an over-the-counter pain reliever like ibuprofen as directed if needed. Let’s schedule the X-ray today so we can choose the best treatment path.

output:
Puzzle  
Fill in the blanks in the sequence below.  Every term is less than 1,000.

5 , 9 , 17 , 33 , __ , 129 , __ , 513  

What numbers belong in the two empty places?

——————————————————  
Solution  

Missing numbers: 65 and 257  

——————————————————  
Explanation of the pattern  

Look at how each term is produced from the previous one:  

• 5 → 9  (5 × 2) − 1 = 9  
• 9 → 17  (9 × 2) − 1 = 17  
• 17 → 33 (17 × 2) − 1 = 33  

So the rule is: “Multiply the current number by 2 and then subtract 1.”

Continue applying that rule:  

• 33 → (33 × 2) − 1 = 65   ← first missing number  
• 65 → (65 × 2) − 1 = 129 (given)  
• 129 → (129 × 2) − 1 = 257 ← second missing number  
• 257 → (257 × 2) − 1 = 513 (given)

Thus the completed sequence is:

5 , 9 , 17 , 33 , 65 , 129 , 257 , 513

Step-by-Step Tutorial: Crafting a Unique, Eye-Catching Scrapbook Layout  
(Approx. 230 words)

1. Gather Materials  
• 12" × 12" patterned background paper  
• 2–3 coordinating solid-color cardstock sheets  
• 4–6 printed photos (3" × 4" or 4" × 6")  
• Paper trimmer or scissors & craft knife  
• Acid-free adhesive (tape runner or glue dots)  
• Embellishments: stickers, die-cuts, washi tape, enamel dots, ribbon  
• Black fine-line pen, ruler, pencil, and eraser  
• Optional: ink pads, stamps, foam dots for dimension

2. Plan the Page  
• Place your background paper in front of you. Lightly sketch a simple “visual triangle” where photos and embellishments will sit—this guides the viewer’s eye.  
• Choose one photo as the focal point; the rest will support it.  

3. Create Photo Mats  
• Trim cardstock so each photo has a ¼" border. Contrasting colors make images pop. Layer two colors for extra depth.

4. Add a Title Block  
• Cut a 3" × 6" strip of cardstock. Use alphabet stickers or hand-letter a catchy title. Ink edges for definition.

5. Assemble the Layout  
• Adhere the focal photo slightly off-center. Tuck supporting photos around it following your triangle.  
• Use foam dots under the focal photo for a raised effect.

6. Embellish Strategically  
• Cluster 3–5 embellishments near each photo point of the triangle. Mix flat (washi) and dimensional (buttons) items.  
• Add a strip of washi or ribbon along one edge to balance the page.

7. Journaling  
• On a small cardstock rectangle, write the story behind the photos with a fine-line pen. Slip it beneath an embellishment for a peek-a-boo effect.

8. Finishing Touches  
• Sprinkle enamel dots or stamp subtle images to fill empty spots.  
• Check balance: rotate the page—if something feels heavy, adjust.

Tips for Beginners  
• Start simple; limit colors to three.  
• Use acid-free supplies to protect photos.  
• Practice hand-lettering on scrap paper first.  
• Less is often more—leave breathing space for a polished look.

   • Uninsured Medical & Dental: split 50/50.  
   • Extracurricular & Educational Expenses: split 50/50.  
   • College Savings: Each parent will contribute $200 per month to a 529 Plan for Michael.

SECTION 5 – JUSTIFICATION FOR CUSTODY DESIGNATION (Selection of 3 factors favoring Jane; 2 favoring John)  

Factors favoring Jane as Primary Custodian  
1. Employment & Income Status (Detail #2)  
   • Jane’s school-day schedule closely parallels Michael’s academic calendar, allowing her to provide daily after-school supervision and attend school events, thus offering greater stability.  

2. Education Level (Detail #3)

GreenTech Solutions LLC  
Operating Agreement  
(New York Limited Liability Company)

NOTE: This sample document is provided for general informational purposes only and does not constitute legal, tax, or financial advice. Forming or operating an LLC involves important legal considerations, and the members should consult qualified counsel licensed in New York before relying on or finalizing this agreement.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. FORMATION; NAME; PURPOSE; PRINCIPAL OFFICE
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1.1 Formation.  The Members have formed a New York limited liability company (“LLC”) under Section 203 of the New York Limited Liability Company Law (“NYLLCL”) by filing Articles of Organization with the New York Department of State on ___________, 20___.

Additional contributions, if any, and the resulting adjustments to Percentage Interests shall be approved by Members holding at least a majority-in-interest.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. ALLOCATIONS; DISTRIBUTIONS
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3.1 Profits and Losses.  Profits and losses shall be allocated among the Members in proportion to their Percentage Interests, unless otherwise unanimously agreed in writing.

3.2 Distributions.  Cash available for distribution shall be distributed at such times and in such amounts as determined by the Managers (see §4) and approved by Members holding a majority-in-interest, subject to any limitations under the NYLLCL.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. MANAGEMENT STRUCTURE
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4.1 Manager-Managed.  The Company shall be “manager-managed” as defined in the NYLLCL.

4.2 Managers; Initial Appointment.  The following individuals are appointed as initial Managers:

   • Manager 1: _____________________________________  
   • Manager 2: _____________________________________  

4.3 Authority of Managers.  Except for matters requiring Member approval under this Agreement or the NYLLCL, the Managers have full authority to manage and control the business and affairs of the Company.

4.4 Major Decisions Requiring Member Approval.  The following actions require the consent of Members holding at least a two-thirds ( ⅔ )-in-interest:

   a. Amending this Operating Agreement or the Articles of Organization;  
   b. Merging or converting the Company;  
   c. Selling all or substantially all Company assets;  
   d. Incurring indebtedness or capital expenditures in excess of $__________;  
   e. Issuing additional Membership Interests.

4.5 Meetings and Voting.  Members may act at meetings or by written consent.  Meetings may be held in person, by telephone, or electronically.  Unless otherwise specified, actions require approval by Members holding a majority-in-interest.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. ADMISSION OF NEW MEMBERS
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5.1 Process for Adding Members.  A person or entity may be admitted as a new Member only if:

   a. The prospective Member executes a joinder to this Operating Agreement;  
   b. The prospective Member makes the agreed capital contribution; and  
   c. Existing Members holding at least a two-thirds ( ⅔ )-in-interest approve the admission and the revised Percentage Interests.

5.2 Amendment to Reflect New Membership.  Upon admission, Exhibit A (Membership Roster) shall be updated to reflect the new Member’s name, contribution, and Percentage Interest.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. TRANSFER OF MEMBERSHIP INTERESTS
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6.1 General Restriction.  No Member may sell, assign, pledge, or otherwise transfer any part of that Member’s Interest without compliance with this Section 6.

6.2 Right of First Refusal (“ROFR”).  If a Member receives a bona fide written offer (“Offer”) to purchase all or any portion of the Member’s Interest, the Member must first offer the Interest to the Company and the remaining Members on the same terms and conditions.  The Company shall have 30 days to accept the Offer.  If the Company declines, the remaining Members collectively shall have an additional 30 days to accept.  Only if both the Company and the other Members decline may the selling Member transfer the Interest to the third-party offeror on terms no more favorable than those in the original Offer.

6.3 Permitted Transfers.  Transfers to (i) a trust for estate-planning purposes, (ii) a spouse or lineal descendant, or (iii) an entity wholly owned by the transferring Member are permitted, provided the transferee agrees in writing to be bound by this Agreement.

6.4 Substituted Members.  A transferee shall become a “Substituted Member” with full voting and economic rights only upon approval of Members holding a majority-in-interest and execution of a joinder to this Agreement.

6.5 Prohibited Transfers.  Any transfer in violation of this Section 6 shall be null and void and confer no rights upon the purported transferee.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. DISSOLUTION AND WINDING UP
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7.1 Events Causing Dissolution.  The Company shall be dissolved upon the first to occur of:

   a. The written consent of Members holding at least a two-thirds ( ⅔ )-in-interest;  
   b. The sale or disposition of all or substantially all of the Company’s assets;  
   c. The entry of a decree of judicial dissolution under NYLLCL §702; or  
   d. Any other event requiring dissolution under the NYLLCL.

7.2 Winding Up.  Upon dissolution, the Managers (or, if none, a liquidating trustee selected by a majority-in-interest of Members) shall:

   a. Collect and liquidate Company assets;  
   b. Pay or make reasonable provision for all Company debts, liabilities, and obligations;  
   c. Set up reserves reasonably necessary for contingent liabilities;  
   d. Distribute remaining assets in the following order:

       i. To Members for any unpaid distributions;  
       ii. To Members in proportion to their positive capital account balances;  
       iii. Any remainder to Members in accordance with their Percentage Interests.

7.3 Certificate of Dissolution.  Upon completion of winding up, the Managers or liquidating trustee shall file a Certificate of Dissolution with the New York Department of State.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
8. INDEMNIFICATION; LIMITATION OF LIABILITY
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
8.1 Indemnification.  To the fullest extent permitted by the NYLLCL, the Company shall indemnify any Member or Manager who is made a party to any proceeding by reason of the Person’s status as a Member or Manager of the Company.

8.2 Limitation of Liability.  No Member or Manager shall be liable to the Company or any other Member for monetary damages except for (i) acts or omissions not in good faith or that involve intentional misconduct or a knowing violation of law, or (ii) any transaction from which the Person derived an improper personal benefit.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
9. MISCELLANEOUS
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
9.1 Entire Agreement; Amendments.  This Agreement constitutes the entire agreement among the Members concerning the Company and may be amended only by written instrument executed by Members holding at least a two-thirds ( ⅔ )-in-interest, unless a greater vote is required elsewhere in this Agreement.

9.2 Governing Law.  This Agreement shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the State of New York, without regard to conflicts-of-law principles.

9.3 Severability.  If any provision of this Agreement is held to be invalid or unenforceable, the remaining provisions shall remain in full force and effect.

9.4 Counterparts; Electronic Signatures.  This Agreement may be executed in counterparts and by electronic signature, each of which shall be deemed an original and all of which together shall constitute one agreement.

9.5 Headings.  Headings are for convenience only and do not affect interpretation.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
10. SIGNATURES
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

output:
Remote Work Policy  

Version: 1.0  
Effective Date: __________  
Approved By: Human Resources Department   

1. Purpose  
This policy establishes clear guidelines for employees who work remotely (part-time or full-time). It aims to ensure productivity, maintain team cohesion, protect company resources, and support employee well-being.

2. Eligibility  
• Roles must allow for effective remote execution (e.g., tasks do not require daily on-site presence).  
• Employees must have completed their introductory employment period (unless approved by management).  
• Performance history and disciplinary record will be considered before granting or renewing remote status.  

3. Work Hours & Availability  
3.1 Core Hours  
• Employees must be actively available between 10:00 a.m. and 3:00 p.m. (local time), Monday through Friday, for meetings and collaborative work.  
• Outside core hours, employees may flex schedules so long as they meet a standard 40-hour workweek (or the pro-rated requirement for part-time staff) and all deadlines.  

3.2 Time Tracking  
• Non-exempt employees must log hours daily in the company timekeeping system; overtime requires prior written approval.  
• Exempt employees will record start/end times for reference, but are evaluated on deliverables rather than hours worked.  

3.3 Breaks & Disconnecting  
• Employees are encouraged to take lunch and rest breaks consistent with local labor regulations.  
• The right to disconnect begins at 6:00 p.m. (local time) unless critical business needs require after-hours contact (to be scheduled in advance where possible).  

4. Communication Expectations  
4.1 Tools  
• Email is the default channel for formal correspondence; Slack/Teams for quick questions; Zoom for meetings; phone for urgent matters.  
• All remote employees must maintain a reliable internet connection (minimum 20 Mbps download/5 Mbps upload) and functioning webcam, microphone, and headset.  

4.2 Responsiveness  
• Messages received during core hours should be acknowledged within two business hours.  
• For urgent issues outside core hours, managers should call/text only if delay will materially impact operations.  

4.3 Meetings  
• Weekly team stand-ups (30 minutes) are mandatory. Cameras on, unless prior exception is granted.  
• Monthly one-on-one sessions with direct manager.  
• Quarterly all-hands meetings, scheduled with at least two weeks’ notice.  

5. Workspace & Security  
• Employees must designate a quiet, safe, dedicated workspace free from regular interruptions.  
• Company-issued devices must be used for all work. Personal devices require written approval and must meet IT security standards.  
• VPN must be active when accessing any internal system.  
• Confidential documents may not be printed or stored at home without authorization.  

6. Performance Management  
6.1 Objectives & Key Results (OKRs)  
• Each remote employee will have measurable quarterly objectives set jointly with their manager.  
• Progress is reviewed bi-weekly; adjustments documented in the performance management system.  

6.2 Output Metrics  
• Quality: error rates, client satisfaction scores, peer reviews.  
• Quantity: tasks completed, project milestones reached, or sales closed vs. targets.  
• Timeliness: adherence to deadlines, ticket turnaround times.  

6.3 Behavioral Metrics  
• Collaboration: participation in meetings, responsiveness metrics.  
• Initiative: proactive problem-solving, suggestions for process improvements.  
• Compliance: adherence to policy, security protocols, and attendance at mandatory sessions.  

6.4 Annual Review  
• Combines metric results, 360° feedback, and self-assessment.  
• Remote status may be revoked or adjusted if performance falls below expectations for two consecutive quarters.  

7. Equipment & Expenses  
• The company will provide a laptop, monitor, keyboard, mouse, and headset.  
• A monthly stipend of $50 covers internet and utilities.  
• Additional equipment requests require managerial justification and HR approval.  

8. Health & Safety  
• Employees must complete a home-office ergonomics self-assessment annually.  
• HR can arrange virtual ergonomic consultations.  
• Report any work-related injuries within 24 hours.  

9. Data Privacy & Compliance  
• All data handling must follow the company’s Information Security Policy and any applicable regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA).  
• Report suspected breaches immediately to IT Security.  

10. Termination or Suspension of Remote Arrangement  
• Remote status may be suspended for performance issues, policy violations, or operational needs, with two weeks’ notice when practicable.  
• Employees can request to return to on-site work with 30 days’ notice, subject to space availability.  

11. Challenges & Solutions  

Challenge 1: Isolation & Reduced Engagement  
• Solution: Mandatory weekly team stand-ups; virtual coffee breaks; quarterly in-person or hybrid meetups; mentorship or buddy programs.

Challenge 2: Communication Gaps & Misinterpretation  
• Solution: Standardized communication channels; clear response-time expectations; training on virtual collaboration tools; encourage video for complex discussions.

Challenge 3: Work-Life Boundary Blurring  
• Solution: Define core hours and right-to-disconnect; encourage calendar blocking for breaks; offer wellbeing resources (EAP, mindfulness apps).

Challenge 4: Performance Visibility  
• Solution: Establish transparent OKRs and shared dashboards; frequent check-ins; encourage documentation of accomplishments.

Challenge 5: Technical Issues  
• Solution: Provide stipend and IT support; backup connectivity plan (mobile hotspot); hardware replacement within 48 hours; regular security updates.

Challenge 6: Career Progression Concerns  
• Solution: Include remote employees in high-impact projects; ensure equal access to learning opportunities; managers to review promotion criteria for location bias.

Challenge 7: Compliance & Data Security  
• Solution: Mandatory security training; enforce VPN usage; periodic audits; multi-factor authentication; encrypted storage.

12. Policy Review  
This policy will be reviewed annually and may be updated to reflect legal, technological, or organizational changes.
