Epic “Great Western Circuit”  
5½–6 week road adventure starting & ending in Seattle – 4,600-mile loop, 13 parks, deserts to glaciers.

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Mount Rainier National Park, Washington  
   • Recommended stay: 2 days (Paradise hikes, Sunrise, Reflection Lakes)  
   • Getting there: Seattle → Mount Rainier via I-5 & WA-7.  
     ­– Drive: 2 h / 95 mi  
     ­– No realistic air or rail options; private car or camper-van best.

2. North Cascades National Park, Washington  
   • Stay: 2 days (Cascade Pass, Diablo Lake, Ross Lake ferry)  
   • Mount Rainier → North Cascades: 3½ h / 180 mi via I-5 N, SR-20.  
     ­– Drive or book airport shuttle + rental in Sedro-Woolley (adds cost/time).

3. Glacier National Park, Montana  
   • Stay: 3 days (Going-to-the-Sun Road, Grinnell Glacier, Many Glacier)  
   • North Cascades → Glacier (West Glacier entrance): 7–8 h / 400 mi via US-2.  
     ­– Amtrak Empire Builder possible (overnight from Everett to West Glacier).

4. Yellowstone National Park, WY/MT/ID  
   • Stay: 3 days (Old Faithful, Grand Prismatic, Lamar Valley wildlife)  
   • Glacier → Yellowstone (Gardiner/North Entrance): 7 h / 380 mi via I-90 & US-89.

5. Grand Teton National Park, Wyoming  
   • Stay: 2 days (Jenny Lake, Schwabacher Landing sunrise, Taggart Lake hike)  
   • Yellowstone (South Entrance) → Grand Teton (Moose): 1–1¼ h / 60 mi.

6. Rocky Mountain National Park, Colorado  
   • Stay: 2 days (Trail Ridge Road, Bear Lake, alpine tundra)  
   • Grand Teton → Rocky Mountain (Estes Park): 8 h / 480 mi via US-191 & I-80/I-25.  
     ­– Optional one-way car rental JAC (Jackson) → DEN + Denver–Estes shuttle to reduce driving fatigue.

7. Arches National Park, Utah  
   • Stay: 2 days (Delicate Arch sunrise, Fiery Furnace tour, stargazing)  
   • Rocky Mountain → Arches (Moab): 6 h / 360 mi via I-70 W & US-191 S.

8. Canyonlands National Park, Utah  
   • Stay: 1 day (Island in the Sky mesa, Mesa Arch sunrise, or Half-day 4×4 into White Rim)  
   • Arches → Canyonlands Island-in-the-Sky district: 30 min / 32 mi.  
     ­– Same Moab basecamp, no re-packing required.

9. Bryce Canyon National Park, Utah  
   • Stay: 1½ days (Queens Garden/Navajo Loop, night-sky program)  
   • Canyonlands → Bryce: 4½ h / 260 mi via UT-24 & UT-12 (Scenic Byway 12).

10. Zion National Park, Utah  
    • Stay: 2 days (Angels Landing permit hike, The Narrows wade, Springdale cafés)  
    • Bryce → Zion: 1½ h / 85 mi via US-89 S & UT-9 W.

11. Grand Canyon National Park, Arizona (South Rim)  
    • Stay: 2 days (Desert View Drive, sunset at Hopi Point, optional rim-to-river day hike start)  
    • Zion (Springdale) → Grand Canyon South Rim: 4 h / 260 mi via I-15 S, AZ-64.

12. Yosemite National Park, California  
    • Stay: 3 days (Yosemite Valley icons, Glacier Point, Tuolumne Meadows if Tioga Pass open)  
    • Grand Canyon → Yosemite (El Portal): 9 h / 640 mi via Las Vegas, Bakersfield & CA-41.  
      ­– Tip: break night in Las Vegas or Bakersfield.  
      ­– Alternative: quick 1-hr flight LAS → FAT, then 2¾-h drive to the park.

13. Crater Lake National Park, Oregon  
    • Stay: 2 days (Rim Drive, boat to Wizard Island, sunrise at Watchman Peak)  
    • Yosemite → Crater Lake (Rim Village): 7½ h / 430 mi via CA-99 N & OR-62.

Return to Seattle, Washington  
    • Crater Lake → Seattle: 6 h / 360 mi via I-5 N.  
      ­– Amtrak Coast Starlight (Klamath Falls → Seattle) is a relaxing rail alternative (12 h).

────────────────────────────────────────
Time & distance summary  
• Nights in parks: 27.5 ≈ 28 nights  
• Pure wheel-time: ≈ 68 h ≈ 4,600 mi. Assuming 7-9 h max driving days, allocate 9 full travel days.  
• Buffer/errand/rest days: 4 days (laundry, weather, vehicle service, spontaneous detours).  

Grand total: about 41 days on the road (±1½ months).  

────────────────────────────────────────
Road-trip tips & logistics  
• America the Beautiful Pass ($80) covers entry to every park—pays for itself by the 4th park.  
• Best season: late June–mid-October for snow-free mountain passes and open Tioga/Going-to-the-Sun Roads.  
• Lodging: Mix of campgrounds (book early for popular parks), national-park lodges, and gateway-town motels/Airbnbs.  
• Vehicle prep: fresh oil, full-size spare, paper maps for cell-service dead zones, and an annual parks pass displayed on the dash.  
• Pack layers—from rainforest drizzle in the Cascades to triple-digit heat in Utah & Arizona—and bear-safety gear for Glacier & Yellowstone.  
• Download offline maps (Google Maps or Gaia) and the NPS app for trail maps & alerts.  
• Reserve any required timed-entry permits in advance (Yosemite reservation system, Angels Landing permits, etc.).  
• Add optional side quests: Antelope Canyon (Page, AZ), Monument Valley loop, Napa wineries en-route to Yosemite, Oregon Coast detour on return.  

Buckle up, cue your playlist, and enjoy six spectacular weeks of America’s most iconic wild places—ending with Mt. Rainier looming on Seattle’s horizon, right where you began!

Background: Founded in 2013 in Austin, Texas, GreenWave Solar began as a small rooftop–solar installer targeting residential neighborhoods in the Sun Belt. Initially staffed by three engineers and one sales manager, the company’s mission was to make distributed solar power as accessible and affordable as home internet service. By 2017, falling panel prices and generous state incentives spurred GreenWave to scale beyond its local market and position itself as a regional EPC (engineering, procurement, construction) provider. Key challenges: Rapid customer-acquisition costs threatened profitability, supply-chain disruptions created panel shortages, and fierce competition from national installers made differentiation difficult. In addition, utilities in several target states proposed rate changes that would reduce net-metering credits, jeopardizing the economics for prospective customers. Innovative solutions: GreenWave invested early in proprietary AI-driven design software that slashed site-assessment time from two days to 45 minutes, enabling quick quotes and lower soft costs. The firm also launched community-solar subscription models to hedge against net-metering uncertainty and partnered with local credit unions to offer zero-down financing. To secure supply, GreenWave signed long-term contracts with a U.S. panel manufacturer and warehoused critical inventory at strategically located micro-fulfillment centers. Results: Between 2018 and 2023 the company’s annual installed capacity grew from 12 MW to 190 MW, revenue expanded 15-fold to $275 million, and customer acquisition costs dropped 32 percent. More than 28,000 households now offset an average of 85 percent of their electricity use with GreenWave systems, avoiding an estimated 210,000 metric tons of CO₂ annually. The firm’s workforce has grown to 450 employees, and its community-solar program alone delivers clean power to an additional 12,000 low-income renters.

Background: WindLift Technologies, a North Sea–based start-up spun out of the University of Edinburgh in 2016, set out to commercialize airborne wind energy (AWE) systems—kite-like devices that capture high-altitude winds to generate power at lower capital cost than conventional turbines. After prototyping with grant funding, the company raised Series A capital in 2019 to deploy pilot projects on Scottish islands heavily reliant on diesel generation. Key challenges: Investors were skeptical of unproven AWE reliability, regulators lacked certification pathways, and island communities feared visual and ecological impacts. Harsh marine environments also accelerated wear on lightweight airborne components, threatening uptime targets. Innovative solutions: WindLift co-developed a digital twin platform with an aerospace partner to simulate fatigue and optimize flight trajectories, extended component life with graphene-reinforced tether materials, and embedded acoustic sensors for predictive maintenance. The team worked closely with the UK Civil Aviation Authority to draft the first provisional guidelines for AWE, simultaneously launching community consultations and offering revenue-sharing agreements to local councils. Results: The company’s 500-kW pilot array achieved 4,200 full-load hours in its first year—30 percent higher than nearby conventional turbines—cutting island diesel consumption by 1.8 million liters. A certified product line is now slated for 2025 release, WindLift’s headcount has tripled, and strategic partnerships with two European utilities position the firm to scale to 150 MW of AWE installations by 2027.

Background: BlueHarvest Tidal, established in 2011 in Halifax, Nova Scotia, was created by a group of former offshore oil engineers intent on harnessing the Bay of Fundy’s world-record tidal ranges. Their vision was to build sub-surface turbines that could withstand extreme currents while minimizing impacts on marine life, delivering predictable, zero-carbon baseload power to coastal grids. Key challenges: Early prototypes suffered mechanical failures due to cavitation and biofouling, capital expenditures were high relative to wind and solar, and public concern grew over potential harm to fisheries and whale migration routes. Financing dried up after a major device collapse in 2015, threatening insolvency. Innovative solutions: BlueHarvest pivoted to a modular, shrouded turbine design with flexible composite blades that reduce stress under peak loads. They partnered with marine biologists to integrate real-time acoustic deterrent systems and infrared imaging for wildlife monitoring, publishing data openly to build stakeholder trust. To lower costs, the firm adopted a lease-to-own model with power utilities and secured green bonds backed by Canada’s Infrastructure Bank, enabling serial production. Results: By 2022 BlueHarvest commissioned a 20-MW tidal farm feeding 25,000 homes and offsetting 60,000 tonnes of CO₂ annually. Capacity-factor data averaging 48 percent attracted $300 million in Series C funding, and the company has since broken ground on two additional 50-MW projects in the UK and South Korea. Equipment failures have dropped by 70 percent, and independent studies report negligible impact on local marine species, solidifying BlueHarvest’s position as a global leader in commercial tidal energy.

Outline of Four Key Principles of Aerospace Engineering  

1. Aerodynamics  
   • Focus: How air interacts with aircraft surfaces to create forces such as lift and drag.  
   • Core equation (lift):  
     L = ½ ρ V² S CL  
     where L = lift force, ρ = air density, V = velocity, S = reference area, and CL = lift coefficient.  
   • Design goal: Shape wings and bodies to maximize lift-to-drag ratio for the intended flight regime.

2. Propulsion  
   • Focus: Generating thrust to overcome drag and gravity.  
   • Specific Impulse (Isp) – full form: Specific Impulse.  
     After first mention, the abbreviation “Isp” is used.  
   • Key idea: Higher Isp indicates more thrust per unit of propellant mass flow, leading to improved efficiency in rockets, turbofans, and other engines.  
   • Design goal: Select engine cycles and propellants that offer high Isp while meeting mission constraints.

3. Materials  
   • Focus: Selecting substances that endure aerodynamic loads, temperature extremes, and fatigue while minimizing weight.  

   | Material        | Density (kg/m³) | Tensile Strength (MPa) | Typical Use in Aircraft/Spacecraft |
   |-----------------|-----------------|------------------------|------------------------------------|
   | Aluminum Alloy  | ~2,800          | 400–550               | Fuselage skins, wing structures    |
   | Titanium Alloy  | ~4,500          | 900–1,100             | Landing gear, engine components    |
   | Carbon Fiber-Epoxy Composite | ~1,600 | 600–1,200 | Wing spars, satellite buses         |
   | Ceramic Matrix Composite (CMC) | ~2,800 | 150–300 (at 1,200 °C) | Turbine shrouds, heat shields |

   • Design goal: Balance strength, weight, temperature tolerance, and cost.

4. Control Systems  
   • Focus: Maintaining desired flight attitude, trajectory, and stability through sensors, computers, and actuators.  
   • Real-world example: The Boeing 787’s fly-by-wire system continuously adjusts control surfaces—ailerons, elevators, rudder, and flaps—based on sensor data to keep the aircraft stable, optimize fuel burn, and enhance passenger comfort, even in turbulent conditions.

Table 1 – European smartphone market share (%)  
| Year | Apple | Samsung | Xiaomi |  
|------|-------|---------|--------|  
| 2021 | 26 %  | 32 %    | 20 %   |  
| 2022 | 25 %  | 34 %    | 18 %   |

Table 2 – Key drivers that correlate with market-share change (2021-2023)  
| Company | Product-innovation highlights | Avg. selling-price shift* | Salient marketing moves | Net share change |  
|---------|------------------------------|---------------------------|-------------------------|------------------|  
| Samsung | Galaxy S21→S23; Z Flip/Fold 3→5; 5G A-series expansion | €295→€330  (+€35) | “Awesome is for Everyone” digital blitz; Euro football sponsorships; strong carrier co-op subsidies | +3 pts |  
| Apple   | iPhone 13→15; Satellite SOS; Dynamic Island; USB-C transition | €845→€945 (+€100) | Privacy-centric ads; aggressive trade-in & instalment plans; services bundling | 0 pts |  
| Xiaomi  | Mi/12/13 flagships; Redmi Note 5G; HyperOS launch | €210→€240 (+€30) | Early influencer buzz fading; 12 % cut in EU ad spend; limited carrier presence | –6 pts |  
*Canalys/Counterpoint blended estimates for Western & Central-Eastern Europe.

400-word analysis

Over the last three years Europe’s smartphone leaderboard has been a duel between Samsung and Apple, with Xiaomi slipping after a meteoric 2020–21 rise (Table 1). Samsung’s share rose from 32 % in 2021 to 35 % in 2023. Apple oscillated narrowly, dipping one point in 2022 before regaining it in 2023. Xiaomi, by contrast, ceded six points, falling from 20 % to 14 %.

Product innovation is the first explanatory axis. Samsung broadened its appeal by pairing annual Galaxy S upgrades with genuinely differentiated foldables (Galaxy Z Flip/Fold series). The foldables are still niche, but they generated earned media and a “first-mover” halo that spilled over to the mid-range A-series, helping Samsung add three points (Table 2). Apple’s hardware changes have been more incremental, yet the company kept parity thanks to meaningful feature narratives—e.g., satellite SOS and the long-awaited USB-C port—and tight integration with its services ecosystem. Xiaomi’s innovation cadence (e.g., the 12 and 13 series) has been solid on paper, but largely spec-driven and hard to differentiate in a crowded Android space, offering limited uplift.

Pricing strategies have also diverged. Samsung nudged its European average selling price (ASP) up only €35 over three years (Table 2), preserving a clear price ladder from €200 A-series to €1,300 foldables. Apple, already commanding the highest ASP, pushed it above €900 by 2023 without losing share, proving that its upscale customers are relatively price-inelastic. Xiaomi, meanwhile, tried to offset shrinking margins by lifting ASP from €210 to €240, blurring the value positioning that originally fueled its 2020-21 surge. As carriers reinstated handset subsidies in 2023, the higher upfront cost of Xiaomi’s devices made them less attractive than subsidised Galaxy or iPhone instalment offers.

Marketing efforts completed the picture. Samsung maintained visible pan-European campaigns—football sponsorships, heavy co-op spending with carriers, and an “Awesome is for everyone” digital blitz. Apple focused on loyalty programs, trade-ins and privacy messaging, tactics that bolster retention rather than acquisition yet were sufficient to shore up share. Xiaomi reduced European marketing outlays by roughly 12 % in 2023 amid cost-cutting, and its pivot from grassroots social promotions toward more traditional channels diluted its community-driven brand equity.

Taken together, Samsung gained on the back of headline-grabbing form-factor innovation, balanced pricing, and sustained advertising. Apple kept its ground through ecosystem stickiness that shields it from both price hikes and modest innovation cycles. Xiaomi’s decline underscores how a value brand can quickly lose momentum when differentiation and marketing support wane simultaneously.

Interviewer: 1. Your latest collection has been described as “tech-artisan.” What does that term mean to you?  
Designer Aiko Marell: I’m marrying hand-loomed jacquards with moisture-wicking fibers usually reserved for sportswear. The goal is to retain the soul of craftsmanship while acknowledging that most of us live hyper-mobile, digital lives. “Tech-artisan” is simply the bridge.

Interviewer: 2. Which broader fashion trends do you think will dominate the next two years?  
Aiko Marell: We’ll see intensified “material transparency”—consumers want to know where a fiber was grown, dyed, and woven. Alongside that, I expect modular wardrobes: garments designed to zip, snap, or drape into multiple silhouettes, reducing the need to buy more pieces.

Interviewer: 3. You mentioned modular wardrobes. How do you ensure versatility without compromising aesthetics? (Follow-up)  
Aiko Marell: I start with a core design language—soft origami folds—and then engineer hidden attachment points. The trick is to use uniform hardware finishes and complementary color stories so each configuration still feels intentional rather than improvised.

Interviewer: 4. Many emerging designers struggle with sustainability costs. What practical advice can you share?  
Aiko Marell: Begin small. Replace just one conventional fabric with a certified alternative each season. Build documented supplier relationships early; transparency unlocks grants and collaborations that offset higher material costs.

Interviewer: 5. Earlier, you spoke of “material transparency.” How do you communicate those supply-chain stories to customers without overwhelming them? (Follow-up)  
Aiko Marell: Storytelling micro-tags. Each garment carries a QR code that opens a 60-second comic-style animation of the fiber’s journey. It’s engaging, not preachy, and it lives on the customer’s phone rather than in a lengthy care booklet.

Interviewer: 6. What styling advice would you give someone who wants to incorporate bold prints into a conservative wardrobe?  
Aiko Marell: Start with scale, not color. Choose a print in subdued hues but with exaggerated shapes. Pair one statement piece—say, a scarf or midi skirt—with neutrals. Once you’re comfortable, dial up the color intensity.

Interviewer: 7. Your designs often blur gender lines. Have you faced pushback from retailers, and how do you navigate it?  
Aiko Marell: Some buyers still request “men’s” and “women’s” skews. I compromise on merchandising, not design: garments are labeled by fit style—slim, classic, relaxed—so stores can rack them wherever they like. Sales data usually wins the debate.

Interviewer: 8. You spoke about hidden attachment points earlier. Could that idea extend to adaptive fashion for people with disabilities? (Follow-up)  
Aiko Marell: Absolutely. We’re prototyping magnetic closures and pull-tabs that require minimal dexterity. The research we did for modular garments maps perfectly onto adaptive needs, proving inclusivity and innovation can be one and the same.

Interviewer: 9. Looking back, what moment made you realize fashion was your calling?  
Aiko Marell: When I was ten, I turned my father’s discarded parachute into a festival tent dress for my sister. Seeing fabric transform into confidence—that feeling is addictive and, frankly, unshakeable.

Interviewer: 10. Finally, what’s one misconception about the fashion industry you wish you could correct?  
Aiko Marell: That it’s superficial. At its best, fashion is anthropology in motion, chronicling how societies feel about identity, technology, and the planet. Clothes may be material, but their impact is deeply human.

Implicit Association Test (IAT) Blueprint  
Topic: Gender–Career Stereotypes (Male ↔ Career vs. Female ↔ Family)

────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Purpose  
   • Measure the relative strength of automatic associations between  
     – Gender categories (Male, Female) and  
     – Role categories (Career, Family).  
   • Faster responses when “congruent” pairs share the same response key reveal implicit bias.

2. Stimulus Material  
   A. Gender words  
      • Male: John, Paul, Mike, Kevin, Steve, Mark, Robert, David  
      • Female: Lisa, Amy, Mary, Karen, Linda, Susan, Julie, Sarah  
   B. Role words  
      • Career: Office, Salary, Corporation, Profession, Management, Payroll, Career, Business  
      • Family: Home, Children, Wedding, Parents, Relatives, Family, Kitchen, Cousins  

3. Test Structure (7 blocks, ≈5–7 min)  

   Block 1  (Practice, 20 trials)  
     Left-key: Male  Right-key: Female  

   Block 2  (Practice, 20)  
     Left-key: Career  Right-key: Family  

   Block 3  (Practice, 20)  – “Congruent” pairing  
     Left-key: Male + Career   Right-key: Female + Family  

   Block 4  (Critical, 40) – same mapping as Block 3  
     Left-key: Male + Career   Right-key: Female + Family  

   Block 5  (Practice, 20) – switch only the Role categories  
     Left-key: Family  Right-key: Career  

   Block 6  (Practice, 20) – “Incongruent” pairing  
     Left-key: Male + Family   Right-key: Female + Career  

   Block 7  (Critical, 40) – same mapping as Block 6  
     Left-key: Male + Family   Right-key: Female + Career  

   • Within each block, words appear one by one in the screen center.  
   • Participant presses either LEFT (e.g., “E”) or RIGHT (e.g., “I”).  
   • Error: red “X” appears; correct key must be hit before next trial.  

4. Scoring (Greenwald, Nosek & Banaji, 2003 “D-score” algorithm, brief version)  
   a. Discard trials with latencies <300 ms or >10 000 ms.  
   b. Compute mean latencies for combined blocks (3+4 vs. 6+7).  
   c. Compute pooled SD of latencies across those blocks.  
   d. D = (mean Incongruent – mean Congruent) / SD.  
      – Positive D → quicker for Congruent (Male-Career/Female-Family) → stereotype-consistent bias.  
      – Negative D → quicker for Incongruent → counter-stereotypic bias.  
      – |D| ≈ 0.15 = slight, 0.35 = moderate, 0.65 = strong.  

────────────────────────────────────────────
5. Result-Recording Template

| Participant | Mean RT Congruent (ms) | Mean RT Incongruent (ms) | Pooled SD (ms) | D-score | Bias Direction | Bias Strength |
|-------------|-----------------------|--------------------------|----------------|---------|----------------|---------------|

────────────────────────────────────────────
6. Hypothetical Results (N = 10)

| Participant | Mean RT Congruent | Mean RT Incongruent | Pooled SD | D-score | Bias Direction | Bias Strength |
|-------------|------------------|---------------------|-----------|---------|----------------|---------------|
| P01         | 640              | 800                 | 220       | +0.73   | Stereotype-consistent | Strong |
| P02         | 710              | 760                 | 180       | +0.28   | Stereotype-consistent | Moderate |
| P03         | 590              | 670                 | 260       | +0.31   | Stereotype-consistent | Moderate |
| P04         | 680              | 690                 | 240       | +0.04   | None / Neutral | None |
| P05         | 720              | 950                 | 300       | +0.77   | Stereotype-consistent | Strong |
| P06         | 660              | 630                 | 210       | –0.14   | Counter-stereotypic | Slight |
| P07         | 750              | 930                 | 280       | +0.64   | Stereotype-consistent | Strong |
| P08         | 700              | 820                 | 260       | +0.46   | Stereotype-consistent | Moderate |
| P09         | 600              | 590                 | 190       | –0.05   | None / Neutral | None |
| P10         | 685              | 755                 | 210       | +0.33   | Stereotype-consistent | Moderate |

Group Summary  
• Mean D-score = (+0.31)  
• 7 of 10 participants show a positive D (stereotype-consistent).  
• 2 show near-zero (neutral).  
• 1 shows a slight counter-stereotypic bias.

────────────────────────────────────────────
7. Interpretation & Conclusions

1. Direction of Bias  
   • The positive mean D (+0.31) indicates that, on average, participants responded faster when “Male + Career / Female + Family” shared the same key, suggesting an implicit association consistent with traditional gender-career stereotypes.

2. Magnitude  
   • A mean D of 0.31 falls in the “moderate” range, implying a noticeable—though not extreme—implicit bias at the group level.

3. Individual Differences  
   • Strong stereotype-consistent bias (|D| ≥ 0.65) in 3 participants (P01, P05, P07).  
   • Majority (70 %) display at least slight stereotype-consistent bias.  
   • A minority (P06) shows slight reversal, and two participants (P04, P09) are effectively neutral.

4. Possible Explanations  
   • Cultural exposure to traditional gender roles.  
   • Personal experiences: participants with counter-stereotypic experiences (e.g., mothers in high-status careers or stay-at-home fathers) may show weaker or reversed biases.

5. Caveats  
   • Small sample; results not generalizable.  
   • Reaction-time tasks can be affected by fatigue, keyboard familiarity, or attention lapses.  
   • IAT measures relative, not absolute, associations and does not indicate deliberate endorsement of stereotypes.

6. Practical Implications  
   • Organizations may use aggregated IAT data to guide diversity training, highlighting unconscious gender–career associations.  
   • Individuals can use personal feedback to reflect on potential implicit biases and pursue bias-reduction strategies (counter-stereotypic exemplars, perspective-taking, implementation intentions).

────────────────────────────────────────────
End of design, data table, and analysis.

Flashcard 1  
Term: Protogalaxy  
Definition: A dense, gas-rich region in the early universe that collapses within a dark-matter halo. Gravity drives gas to condense, forming the first stars and laying the foundation for a young galaxy.

Flashcard 2  
Term: Hubble Sequence  
Definition: A system that arranges galaxies into ellipticals, lenticulars, spirals, and irregulars based on appearance. It helps astronomers trace morphological changes as galaxies evolve through star formation, gas consumption, and mergers.

Flashcard 3  
Question: What roles do galaxy mergers play in evolution?  
Answer: Collisions funnel gas toward galactic centers, ignite starbursts, feed supermassive black holes, and can transform spirals into ellipticals. Repeated mergers help build more massive galaxies over cosmic time.

Flashcard 4  
Term: Starburst Galaxy  
Definition: A galaxy experiencing an exceptionally high star-formation rate, often triggered by interactions or mergers. Starbursts rapidly use up gas, producing many short-lived massive stars and enriching the interstellar medium with heavy elements.

Flashcard 5  
Question: How does feedback from supermassive black holes affect galaxy growth?  
Answer: Energy and jets from active galactic nuclei heat or expel gas, suppressing new star formation. This feedback regulates galaxy mass and helps explain why the most massive galaxies are relatively old and red.

Flashcard 6  
Term: Quenching  
Definition: The process that halts or greatly reduces star formation in a galaxy. Causes include black-hole feedback, gas stripping in clusters, or exhaustion of cold gas, leading galaxies to transition from blue and active to red and passive.

Flashcard 7  
Question: Why is dark matter crucial to galaxy formation?  
Answer: Dark-matter halos provide most of a galaxy’s gravitational pull, guiding gas collapse and setting the framework for star formation. Without these invisible halos, galaxies could not accumulate enough mass to form and remain bound.

Flashcard 8  
Term: Cosmic Web  
Definition: The large-scale structure of the universe, composed of interconnected filaments of dark matter and galaxies separated by voids. Galaxies grow where filaments intersect, funnelling gas and driving hierarchical clustering.

Flashcard 9  
Question: What is the role of metallicity in galaxy evolution?  
Answer: Metallicity—the abundance of elements heavier than helium—rises as successive stellar generations enrich gas with supernova ejecta. Higher metallicity affects cooling, star formation efficiency, and the spectral properties of galaxies.

Flashcard 10  
Term: Downsizing  
Definition: Observational trend showing that massive galaxies formed most of their stars early in cosmic history, while smaller galaxies continue forming stars today. It indicates star-formation efficiency varies with galaxy mass over time.

1. Topic: Governments should substantially increase funding for projects that search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI).

   Proposition  
   • Expanding SETI budgets would accelerate technological innovation—such as improved radio-frequency receivers and data-processing algorithms—that also benefit communications and Earth-based science.  
   • Discovering extraterrestrial intelligence would have profound scientific, philosophical, and cultural impacts whose potential value easily outweighs the relatively modest cost of increased funding.

   Opposition  
   • Public resources are finite, and directing more money to SETI diverts funds from urgent, evidence-based needs like climate adaptation, public health, and education.  
   • After six decades of largely negative results, the low probability of near-term success makes additional SETI spending an inefficient investment compared with other research priorities.

2. Topic: Humanity should engage in “active SETI” (deliberately transmitting powerful, targeted messages to announce our presence to extraterrestrial civilizations).

   Proposition  
   • Proactive communication could shorten the timescale for contact, allowing us to gain knowledge from older or more advanced civilizations that might help solve global challenges.  
   • Because our planet’s electromagnetic leakage has already revealed our existence, switching to intentional, well-crafted messages offers a chance to control the narrative and showcase humanity’s peaceful intentions.

   Opposition  
   • Broadcasting our location to unknown civilizations carries existential risk, as we cannot predict or control how technologically superior recipients might respond.  
   • International consensus on active SETI is lacking, so unilateral transmissions could spark geopolitical tensions on Earth and violate principles of global democratic decision-making.

3. Topic: If microbial extraterrestrial life is discovered on another world, it should be given legal protection from human exploitation or contamination.

   Proposition  
   • Preserving alien ecosystems respects the intrinsic value of non-Earth life and prevents irreversible harm that could erase unique evolutionary information.  
   • Strict protections reduce the risk of contaminating both worlds with unfamiliar pathogens, safeguarding planetary biosafety for Earth and the host planet alike.

   Opposition  
   • Overly restrictive protections could impede scientific study needed to understand the biology, origins, and potential benefits (e.g., new medicines) of the extraterrestrial organisms.  
   • Implementing and enforcing extraterrestrial conservation laws may be impractical and prohibitively expensive, hindering exploration and the potential for resource utilization critical for future space development.

TITLE: “The Last Librarian”

Act I – Departure
1. Ordinary World  
   •  Dystopian megacity where books are outlawed; 17-year-old Jun secretly tends a hidden subway library.  
2. Call to Adventure  
   •  A smuggled micro-scroll warns that the regime will burn the Grand Archive—and all remaining books—within a month.  
3. Refusal of the Call  
   •  Jun fears capture and argues that preserving the small secret library is safer than confronting the regime.  
4. Meeting with the Mentor  
   •  Sera, an aged ex-historian, finds the hideout and reveals a map to the palace vault holding the “Index,” a catalogue of every banned text.  
5. Crossing the First Threshold  
   •  Jun abandons the tunnel refuge, following Sera beyond the city walls to seek allies and the vault.

Act II – Initiation
6. Tests, Allies, and Enemies  
   •  On the outlaw roads Jun befriends Kai, a desert courier, outwits book-burning patrols, and narrowly escapes Captain Lyron, the regime’s ruthless Archivist.  
7. Approach to the Inmost Cave  
   •  The trio infiltrates the palace catacombs; claustrophobic passages, traps, and encoded locks guard the vault.  
8. The Ordeal  
   •  Inside the vault, Lyron ambushes them. Sera stalls him, is mortally wounded, buying Jun moments to crack the final cipher.  
9. Reward  
   •  Jun secures the Index—a crystal drive containing every text—and Sera’s dying charge to “let the words breathe.”

Act III – Return
10. The Road Back  
    •  Fleeing through storm-flooded sewers, Jun drags an injured Kai while soldiers close in.  
11. The Resurrection  
    •  At the regime’s public book-burning, Jun hijacks the city’s holographic billboards, projecting pages from the Index. Faced with truth, the crowd revolts; Lyron is deposed.  
12. Return with the Elixir  
    •  A free public library rises in the old palace gardens. Jun, now Chief Librarian, mentors children beneath banners that read “Knowledge is Light,” fulfilling Sera’s last wish and transforming the world she once feared to face.

output:
Modern life rarely slows down, but meditation teaches the mind to do exactly that—and science shows it works. Training your attention for just 10–20 minutes a day can recalibrate the body’s stress response and keep emotional storms from becoming hurricanes.

Key benefits:

• Lowers cortisol. A 2013 JAMA Internal Medicine review of 47 randomized trials found that mindfulness meditation produced moderate, statistically significant reductions in the primary human stress hormone.  
• Calms the nervous system. Slow, focused breathing activates the parasympathetic “rest-and-digest” branch, easing muscle tension and steadying heart rate.  
• Sharpens emotional regulation. MRI studies from Harvard’s Sara Lazar Lab reveal thicker prefrontal-cortex tissue in meditators, a change linked to better impulse control and calmer reactions.  
• Improves sleep quality. By quieting racing thoughts, evening meditation decreases the time it takes to fall asleep and increases deep-sleep cycles—key for next-day resilience.  
• Builds long-term resilience. Carnegie Mellon researchers showed that just eight weeks of mindfulness training reduced inflammatory marker IL-6 by up to 30 %, suggesting protection against chronic stress–related illness.  

Whether you choose a guided app, a silent cushion, or a walking practice, the method matters less than the consistency. Give yourself the gift of a few mindful minutes each day; your body and mind will thank you.

Interpretation of “mid-range restaurant”  
A mid-range restaurant is one that falls between budget eateries (fast food, diners, café-style spots) and high-end or fine-dining establishments. Typical characteristics include:  
• Moderate pricing—entrées usually run roughly US $15–30.  
• Comfortable yet casual-to-smart ambiance (cloth napkins or nicer tableware, but no tuxedoed waiters).  
• Table service, a curated but not encyclopedic wine list, and a menu featuring fresh ingredients prepared to order.  
• Expectation of tipping in markets where that is customary, but not the stiff service charges of haute cuisine venues.

Suggested 18 % gratuity ……………………     9.45

(Thank you for dining with us! Grazie e arrivederci!)  

Why this qualifies as mid-range  
• Price point: With entrées in the low-20-dollar range and a full three-course meal plus beverage landing around $30–35 per person before tax/tip, the cost fits squarely between quick-service spots (<$15 per person) and fine-dining venues that often exceed $60–80 per person.  
• Amenities: Full table service, a modest but respectable wine selection, fresh house-made pasta and desserts, and a pleasant sit-down atmosphere—yet no white-glove service or degustation menu—align with mid-range expectations.  
• Experience: Patrons can enjoy quality ingredients and attentive service without the formality or premium pricing of upscale restaurants, matching the definition of a mid-range establishment.

HIGH-SCHOOL UNITED STATES & WORLD HISTORY  
16-Week Semester – 5 meetings per week – 50-55 minutes per period

────────────────────────────────────────
A. CURRICULUM-DEVELOPMENT PROCESS (ADDIE-inspired)
────────────────────────────────────────
1. Analysis  
   • Review state & AP U.S./World History standards, district pacing guides, and graduation requirements.  
   • Pre-course student survey & short diagnostic quiz to gauge prior knowledge, reading levels, interests, and learning preferences.  

2. Design  
   • Establish Enduring Understandings and Essential Questions (e.g., “How have revolutions reshaped political authority?”).  
   • Backward-map to craft measurable unit & weekly objectives that align with standards.  
   • Decide on major assessments: 2 Mid-terms (Weeks 6 & 12), DBQ Project, Comparative Civilizations Presentation, and cumulative Final Exam (Week 16).  
   • Select a mix of learning experiences—lecturettes, simulations, discussion protocols, tech-integrated tasks, fieldwork—to address multiple modalities.  

3. Development  
   • Produce lesson plans, handouts, rubrics, slide decks, formative checks (exit tickets, Kahoot!, Padlet boards).  
   • Curate diverse resources (primary-source packets, podcasts, museums’ digital archives, oral histories, documentaries, historical fiction excerpts).  

4. Implementation  
   • Launch the course, deliver instruction, collect ongoing formative data, differentiate supports (scaffolds, enrichment, ELL strategies).  

5. Evaluation & Revision  
   • Weekly reflection logs, student feedback, assessment item analyses.  
   • Post-semester data review to upgrade pacing, resources, and alignment for the next cycle.  

────────────────────────────────────────
B. WEEK-BY-WEEK SCOPE, OBJECTIVES, ACTIVITIES & ASSIGNMENTS
────────────────────────────────────────
Week 1 – Foundations of Historical Thinking  
  Objectives: Source reliability, corroboration, chronological reasoning, citation.  
  Activities: “History Mystery” artifact stations; sourcing relay race; library orientation.  
  Assignment: Source Analysis Worksheet on 3 provided artifacts.

Week 2 – Classical Civilizations: Greece & Rome  
  Objectives: Compare political systems; trace cultural legacies.  
  Activities: Senate role-play; virtual tour of the Parthenon (VR headsets).  
  Assignment: 1-page comparative reflection + primary-source discussion posts.

Week 3 – Major World Religions & Philosophies  
  Objectives: Identify origins, diffusion patterns, and core beliefs.  
  Activities: World-religions jigsaw; guest speaker (local interfaith council).  
  Assignment: Infographic summarizing one belief system.

Week 4 – Middle Ages & Islamic Golden Age  
  Objectives: Evaluate causes of feudalism, Islamic scientific contributions.  
  Activities: “Build a Feudal Manor” simulation; analyze Ibn Battuta travelogues.  
  Assignment: DBQ practice—“Impact of Trade on Medieval Societies.”

Week 5 – Renaissance & Reformation  
  Objectives: Assess humanism’s impact; political/religious upheavals.  
  Activities: Art gallery walk with QR-code audio descriptions; debate: Luther vs. Church.  
  Assignment: 500-word art critique using contextual evidence.

Week 6 – 1st MID-TERM EXAM (Units 1-4)  
  Format: 40 MCQs (60%), 1 Short-Essay (20%), 1 DBQ lite (20%).  
  Review Games: Kahoot! marathon, jeopardy, “speed dating” study pairs.  

Week 7 – Age of Exploration & Encounter  
  Objectives: Analyze motivations, Columbian Exchange impacts.  
  Activities: Map plotting using ArcGIS; Columbian Exchange marketplace simulation.  
  Assignment: Two-voice poem from perspectives of conquistador & indigenous leader.

Week 8 – Atlantic Revolutions (American, French, Haitian, Latin American)  
  Objectives: Identify revolutionary causes/effects; compare ideologies.  
  Activities: Primary-source stations; create Revolution “meme timeline.”  
  Assignment: Comparative essay outline (prep for later DBQ).

Week 9 – Industrialization & Reform  
  Objectives: Trace technological change; labor movements; economic theories.  
  Activities: Factory system assembly-line race; podcast analysis (Hardcore History).  
  Assignment: Oral history interview with a family member on work & technology.

Week 10 – Imperialism & Responses  
  Objectives: Evaluate motives; indigenous resistance; long-term impacts.  
  Activities: “Scramble for Africa” map game; analyze Kipling’s “White Man’s Burden.”  
  Assignment: Position paper: “Was imperialism inevitable?”

Week 11 – World War I  
  Objectives: Causes, trench warfare, Treaty of Versailles consequences.  
  Activities: Interactive trench letters; VR battlefield simulation; Socratic seminar.  
  Assignment: Creative diary entry + graphic organizer on causes.

Week 12 – 2nd MID-TERM EXAM (Units 5-9)  
  Format: 35 MCQs (50%), 2 Short-Essays (30%), 1 Thematic Map Analysis (20%).  
  Post-exam reflection & goal-setting conference.

Week 13 – World War II & Holocaust  
  Objectives: Examine rise of totalitarianism; genocide; global consequences.  
  Activities: Survivor testimony video; propaganda poster analysis; Axis/Allies strategy game.  
  Assignment: Annotated digital timeline of key WWII events.

Week 14 – Cold War & Decolonization  
  Objectives: Analyze ideological rivalry; proxy wars; new nations.  
  Activities: Cuban Missile Crisis crisis-room simulation; small-group case studies of Ghana, Vietnam.  
  Assignment: Position podcast (5-7 mins) on one Cold War hotspot.

Week 15 – Contemporary Globalization & Human Rights  
  Objectives: Evaluate economic interdependence; environmental & social issues.  
  Activities: Model United Nations mini-summit; data dive using Gapminder.  
  Assignment: Group presentation—“Where Are We Now?” (multimedia).

Week 16 – Review & FINAL EXAM  
  Days 1-3: Thematic review stations, practice FRQs, peer teaching.  
  Day 4: Final Exam (Cumulative)  
     • 50 MCQs (40%)  
     • DBQ essay (30%)  
     • Comparative essay (30%)  
  Day 5: Course debrief, student reflection letters, celebration.

────────────────────────────────────────
C. MAJOR ASSIGNMENTS & ASSESSMENTS
────────────────────────────────────────
1. Weekly Formative Assignments (Source analyses, reflections, short essays, infographics, etc.)  
2. DBQ Research Project (Weeks 8–10): Students craft a full 1,200-word DBQ essay using at least eight sources (half primary) on “Revolutionary Change & Continuity.” Peer-review draft + final submission.  
3. Comparative Civilizations Group Presentation (Week 15): 4-person teams create a 12-minute multimedia presentation comparing a contemporary nation’s challenges with a historical precedent studied.  
4. Mid-Term Exam 1 (Week 6)  
5. Mid-Term Exam 2 (Week 12)  
6. Cumulative Final Exam (Week 16)  
7. Class Participation & Engagement: based on discussion, simulations, collaboration, and reflection logs.

────────────────────────────────────────
D. GRADING SCHEME
────────────────────────────────────────
• Weekly Formative Assignments (12 total, drop lowest)……………… 20%  
   – Rubric: Accuracy 40%, Depth of Analysis 30%, Clarity/Mechanics 20%, Citation 10%  

• DBQ Research Project…………………………………………………………… 15%  
   – Thesis & Argument 30%, Use of Evidence 30%, Contextualization 15%, Organization 15%, Conventions 10%  

• Comparative Group Presentation……………………………………………… 10%  
   – Historical Accuracy 25%, Comparative Insight 25%, Visual/Tech Integration 20%, Delivery 15%, Collaboration/Peer Eval 15%  

• Mid-Term Exam 1…………………………………………………………………. 10%  
• Mid-Term Exam 2…………………………………………………………………. 10%

• Final Exam (cumulative)………………………………………………………… 25%

• Participation & In-Class Engagement………………………………………. 10%  
   – On-task Collaboration 40%, Discussion Contributions 40%, Reflection Logs 20%  

Total………………………………………………………………………………… 100%

Late Work & Revision Policy  
• Formative assignments accepted up to one week late at 70% maximum.  
• One optional revision allowed on DBQ Project after feedback (+up to ½ of points lost).  

────────────────────────────────────────
E. ENGAGING CLASSROOM PRACTICES & DIVERSE RESOURCES
────────────────────────────────────────
1. Simulations/Role-Plays: Senate debates, Feudal Manor economy, Cuban Missile Crisis “war room.”  
2. Project-Based Learning: DBQ research, multimedia group presentations tackling modern parallels.  
3. Technology Integration:  
   • ArcGIS story maps, Google Earth historical layers  
   • Flip (video responses), Canva for infographics, Padlet for collaborative walls  
4. Multimedia Resources:  
   • Ken Burns documentaries, Crash Course History videos, TED-Ed “History vs.” series  
   • Podcasts: “Hardcore History,” “Throughline,” “Stuff You Missed in History Class”  
   • Virtual museum tours (Smithsonian, Yad Vashem, British Museum)  
5. Primary-Source Archives: Library of Congress, National Archives DocsTeach, World Digital Library.  
6. Culturally Responsive Texts: Excerpts from “A People’s History of the United States,” indigenous oral histories, global south perspectives.  
7. Community Connections: Local historians, veterans, museum educators as guest speakers.  
8. Formative Games: Kahoot!, Quizlet Live, “Time Traveler” board games, breakout boxes.

Manifesto of the Green Horizon Movement

We gather under one universal truth: the Earth is finite, yet our collective potential is boundless. Today we pledge to defend life, restore balance, and build prosperity that endures.

Our vision is clear: a resilient planet where communities thrive without exhausting the resources that sustain them.

We commit to four achievable goals by 2035:

1. Cut greenhouse emissions in half through rapid expansion of renewable energy, efficient buildings, and electrified transport.

2. Regenerate nature by planting three trillion trees, protecting 50% of land and oceans, and restoring wetlands, soils, and coral reefs.

3. Eliminate waste: phase out single-use plastics, enact universal composting, and design products for perpetual reuse.

4. Build equitable green economies that deliver dignified jobs, clean air, and energy independence for all.

Our strategy is pragmatic:

• Mobilize one percent of global GDP annually for climate solutions.  
• Redirect subsidies from fossil fuels to solar, wind, geothermal, and storage.  
• Empower local cooperatives to own and manage microgrids, forests, and farms.  
• Embed environmental literacy in every school, workplace, and civic space.  
• Hold corporations accountable with transparent carbon audits and enforceable penalties.

We reject apathy. We reject delay. Each purchase, vote, innovation, and conversation must align with planetary boundaries.

We invite scientists, workers, farmers, artists, educators, and leaders of every community to join us.

Together we can cool the climate, revive ecosystems, and craft a just, vibrant future.

Let this manifesto be our contract with tomorrow. Rise, organize, innovate, conserve, sustain. The next generation is watching; we will not fail them.

Monday dawn. Lina Travers repositions the willow-colored guitar in her shop window, promising herself she'll learn more than three chords this time. A Post-it on the fretboard reads, “Play me if you’re lost.” She smiles at the reflection of the sleepy street, wondering who feels most lost today.

2. Mateo Cruz  
Mateo Cruz busks beneath the overpass, missing two strings but not courage. He found the green guitar by a bakery dumpster, Post-it fluttering like a dare. Coins clink, but he’s listening for his mother’s laugh in the traffic, convinced music can open the vehicles like blooming flowers.

3. Dr. Anika Voss  
Dr. Anika Voss pauses mid-rounds, hearing faint strumming from the pediatrics courtyard. The guitarist, a skinny teen with patched jeans, coaxes a lullaby. Infusion pumps hum in counterpoint. Night-shift security guard Oliver Chen confiscates the guitar after visiting hours, logging it as “found property.” Alone, he tries a C major; it rings clumsily but sincere. Cameras blink overhead like indifferent stars. Oliver imagines recording a song for his daughter, far away, password-protected behind custody papers.

5. Selene Hawke  
Selene Hawke cleans trains at dawn. She discovers the guitar abandoned on seat 7A, Post-it replaced by a paper crane. Curious, she strums one chord; the carriage lights flicker back to life. She decides to keep both instruments—stringed and folded—as unlikely tickets out of perpetual night work.

Freight conductor Priya Deshmukh notices a janitor absently humming her grandfather’s raga beside an emerald guitar. Priya offers chai, learns the instrument’s lineage of strangers and Post-its. At the coastal bonfire, Gabriel Stone receives the weathered guitar from a soot-streaked brakeman. He plays, fingers sure, voice cracked, the paper crane pinned to the headstock. output:
Individualism and collectivism form a foundational perspective for comparing Western and Eastern cultures. Western societies often emphasize personal autonomy, encouraging individuals to make independent choices and prioritize self-expression. Eastern societies traditionally place a stronger focus on communal harmony, urging individuals to consider group expectations and maintain social cohesion. The primary distinction lies in the Western celebration of personal goals versus the Eastern emphasis on collective well-being, although both systems can overlap in multicultural contexts.

Communication style provides another revealing perspective. Western culture generally values direct verbal expression, favoring clarity and openness even when discussing disagreements. Eastern culture often prefers indirect or high-context communication, stressing subtlety, nonverbal cues, and the preservation of social harmony. Consequently, Western interactions may come across as candid while Eastern exchanges may seem nuanced, yet both aim to convey respect within their own cultural frameworks.

Approaches to education further demonstrate cultural contrasts. In many Western settings, classrooms promote critical thinking and debate, encouraging students to question ideas and engage in dialogue with teachers. In several Eastern settings, education tends to highlight diligent memorization and deference to instructors, viewing the teacher as a primary authority figure. Thus, while both systems strive for academic excellence, they diverge in methods: one champions inquisitive participation, whereas the other upholds disciplined mastery.

Workplace hierarchy offers yet another lens for comparison. Western companies often adopt flatter organizational structures, where employees expect open feedback loops and relatively informal interactions with supervisors. Eastern companies commonly maintain more pronounced hierarchies, with clear lines of authority and formal respect shown toward senior staff. The difference surfaces in daily operations, as Western settings foster egalitarian collaboration whereas Eastern environments reinforce structured leadership, though globalization is gradually blending these models.

Finally, attitudes toward time and leisure reveal subtle cultural nuances. Western culture frequently frames time as a commodity, encouraging punctuality and efficiency to maximize personal and professional productivity. Eastern culture may take a more flexible, cyclical view of time, integrating pauses and communal rituals that balance work with reflection or festivity. The contrast lies in the Western focus on linear, task-oriented scheduling versus the Eastern tendency to harmonize time with social and spiritual rhythms, yet both ultimately seek a satisfying and purposeful life.

output:
Let t be time in seconds, frequency f = 5 Hz (period T = 1∕f = 0.2 s) and amplitude A = 2.  
The angular frequency is ω = 2πf = 10π rad/s.

a) Sine wave  
   s(t) = A sin(ωt) = 2 sin(10π t)

b) Square wave (±A)  
   q(t) = A sgn[sin(ωt)] = 2 sgn(sin(10π t))

c) Triangle wave (linear rise & fall between ±A)  
   r(t) = (2A/π) arcsin[sin(ωt)] = (4/π) arcsin(sin(10π t))

d) Sawtooth wave (linear ramp from –A to +A each period)  
   w(t) = 2A [(t mod T)/T – ½]  
   or, equivalently,  
   w(t) = 4[(t ∕ 0.2 – ⌊t ∕ 0.2⌋) – ½] = 4[(t mod 0.2)/0.2 – 0.5]

All four expressions produce waves with frequency 5 Hz and peak amplitude 2.

1. Ionic Bonds  
   • What happens: One atom gives up one or more electrons and another atom accepts them. The “giver” becomes a positively charged ion, the “taker” becomes a negatively charged ion, and the opposite charges hold the two together—much like the attraction between opposite poles of magnets.  
   • Key idea: Usually forms between a metal (which loses electrons) and a non-metal (which gains them).  
   • Everyday examples:  
     – Table salt (sodium chloride, NaCl): Sodium donates an electron to chlorine, creating Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that lock together in a crystal.  
     – Road salt/de-icer (calcium chloride, CaCl₂): Each calcium atom donates two electrons—one to each of two chloride ions—producing Ca²⁺ and two Cl⁻ ions that attract one another.

2. Covalent Bonds  
   • What happens: Two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons so that each “feels” as if it has a full outer shell. Picture two people holding the same rope—neither gives it up, they simply share it.  
   • Key idea: Common between non-metals; the shared electrons form a stable link.  
   • Everyday examples:  
     – Water (H₂O): Each hydrogen shares an electron with oxygen, forming two O–H covalent bonds that give water its famous bent “Mickey-Mouse” shape.  
     – Methane (CH₄): One carbon shares four pairs of electrons—one with each of four hydrogen atoms—creating a stable, lightweight fuel.

3. Metallic Bonds  
   • What happens: Metal atoms pool (or “delocalize”) their outer electrons into a communal “sea.” Positive metal ions sit in an orderly lattice, while the free-to-move electrons flow around them, holding the structure together.  
   • Key idea: The roaming electrons explain why metals conduct heat and electricity well and can be bent or drawn into wires.  
   • Everyday examples:  
     – Copper wire (Cu): The sea of electrons lets electricity travel easily through the wire to power devices.  
     – Aluminum foil (Al): The same type of bonding makes aluminum both lightweight and able to conduct heat, ideal for cooking wraps.

```python
# Import PyTorch's neural network (nn) module
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class TwoHiddenLayerNN(nn.Module):
    """
    A simple feedforward neural network with:
      • An input layer
      • Two hidden layers (using ReLU)
      • An output layer
    Hidden-layer sizes are chosen between 32 and 128 units to keep the model
    reasonably small yet expressive.
    """

    def __init__(self, input_size: int, output_size: int,
                 hidden_size1: int = 64, hidden_size2: int = 32):
        """
        Args:
            input_size  (int):  Number of input features
            output_size (int):  Dimension of the network output
            hidden_size1(int):  Neurons in the first hidden layer (default=64)
            hidden_size2(int):  Neurons in the second hidden layer (default=32)
        """
        super(TwoHiddenLayerNN, self).__init__()

        # First linear transformation: input -> first hidden layer
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(input_size, hidden_size1)
        # Second linear transformation: first hidden -> second hidden layer
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(hidden_size1, hidden_size2)
        # Final linear transformation: second hidden -> output layer
        self.out = nn.Linear(hidden_size2, output_size)
        # ReLU activation function (reused for both hidden layers)
        self.relu = nn.ReLU()

    def forward(self, x):
        """
        Forward pass through the network:
          1) Input -> fc1 -> ReLU
          2) -> fc2 -> ReLU
          3) -> out
        """
        x = self.relu(self.fc1(x))  # Pass through 1st hidden layer + ReLU
        x = self.relu(self.fc2(x))  # Pass through 2nd hidden layer + ReLU
        x = self.out(x)             # Output layer (no activation here; apply externally if needed)
        return x
```

output: “One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.”  Beauvoir’s 1949 assertion powerfully exposed how society, not biology, assigns feminine roles, yet its focus on a universal “woman” now shows limits.  Mid-century France largely centered white, Western, cisgender, heterosexual experiences; Beauvoir’s framework underplayed how race, colonialism, class, disability, and sexuality create divergent womanhoods.  Intersectional feminism later demonstrated that gender cannot be isolated from these axes of power, and queer and trans scholars have further complicated the binary on which her sentence rests.  Moreover, the premise that one “becomes” a woman by internalizing oppression risks overlooking agency and the diverse ways people actively redefine gender today—from non-binary identities to digital spaces that enable new solidarities.  While the line still galvanizes critiques of social construction, contemporary discourse demands a broader lens that acknowledges plural, fluid identities and structural inequalities beyond gender alone.  Thus Beauvoir’s insight remains seminal but requires expansion to fit a more complex twenty-first-century reality.

Plate Tectonics: The Moving Puzzle Beneath Our Feet
--------------------------------------------------

Imagine Earth as a giant jigsaw puzzle. Instead of cardboard pieces, the puzzle is made of huge slabs of rock called tectonic plates. These plates fit together to cover Earth’s surface, and they are always moving—although so slowly that we don’t feel it in our daily lives. Plate tectonics is the study of how these plates move, interact, and reshape our planet. The movement of plates is the main cause of both earthquakes and volcanic eruptions.

1. What Are Tectonic Plates?
   • Tectonic plates are large sections of Earth’s outer layer, the lithosphere.  
   • Pieces can be as large as entire continents or oceans.  
   • They “float” on a softer, semi-melted layer beneath them called the asthenosphere.

2. Why Do Plates Move?
   • Heat from Earth’s core causes convection currents in the mantle (the thick layer beneath the crust).  
   • Hot material rises, cool material sinks, and this slow churning pushes the plates around—usually just a few centimeters a year, about as fast as fingernails grow!

3. Types of Plate Boundaries
   When two plates meet, the edge between them is called a plate boundary. How they interact determines the geologic activity we see.  
   a. Divergent Boundaries: Plates move apart. Magma (melted rock) rises, cools, and creates new crust. Example: the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.  
   b. Convergent Boundaries: Plates collide. One plate may dive beneath another in a process called subduction. This can form deep ocean trenches, mountain ranges, and volcanoes.  
   c. Transform Boundaries: Plates slide past each other sideways. They don’t create or destroy crust, but they can cause powerful earthquakes. Example: the San Andreas Fault in California.

4. How Plate Tectonics Causes Earthquakes
   • Plates are rough and often get stuck while trying to move. Stress builds up until the rocks suddenly snap free.  
   • This sudden release of energy sends waves through the ground—an earthquake!  
   • The point inside Earth where the quake starts is the focus; the spot directly above on the surface is the epicenter.

5. How Plate Tectonics Creates Volcanoes
   • At divergent boundaries, magma rises through gaps and erupts, forming volcanic ridges.  
   • At convergent boundaries, the subducting plate melts, and the molten rock can rise to the surface, creating chains of volcanoes like the Andes.  
   • Some volcanoes also form over “hot spots,” where plumes of hot mantle material melt through a plate, such as in Hawaii.

6. Why It Matters
   Understanding plate tectonics helps scientists predict where earthquakes and volcanic eruptions are most likely to happen. This knowledge guides building codes, emergency plans, and early-warning systems, helping keep people safe.

Quiz Time!
----------

Multiple-Choice (circle the correct answer)

1. What layer do tectonic plates “float” on?
   A. Outer Core  
   B. Asthenosphere  
   C. Inner Core  
   D. Biosphere  
   Answer: B

2. Which type of plate boundary is most likely to create strong earthquakes by plates sliding past each other?
   A. Divergent  
   B. Convergent  
   C. Transform  
   D. Subduction  
   Answer: C

3. Volcanoes commonly form at convergent boundaries because:
   A. Plates are sliding sideways.  
   B. One plate melts as it sinks beneath another, producing magma.  
   C. Plates are spreading apart, letting water in.  
   D. The crust is too thick to break.  
   Answer: B

True-False (write T or F)

4. Plates move at speeds similar to how fast your fingernails grow.  
   Answer: T

5. All earthquakes start at Earth’s epicenter.  
   Answer: F (They start at the focus; the epicenter is on the surface above the focus.)

The downpour drums on a corrugated roof.

Overview
The human circulatory system is a closed-loop network that transports blood, nutrients, gases, hormones, and waste products throughout the body.

Main components and their roles
1. Heart – Muscular pump with four chambers.
   • Right atrium: receives oxygen-poor blood from the body.  
   • Right ventricle: pumps this blood to the lungs.  
   • Left atrium: receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs.  
   • Left ventricle: pumps oxygen-rich blood to the body.

2. Blood vessels  
   • Arteries: carry blood away from the heart under high pressure.  
   • Arterioles/capillaries: thin vessels where nutrient and gas exchange occur with tissues.  
   • Venules/veins: return blood to the heart.

3. Lungs – Site of gas exchange; blood releases carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen (pulmonary circulation).

4. Systemic tissues – Organs and cells that receive oxygen/nutrients and release carbon dioxide/waste (systemic circulation).

Flowchart (direction of blood flow)
Body veins / Venae cavae  
   -> Right atrium  
   -> Right ventricle  
   -> Pulmonary arteries  
   -> Lungs  
   -> Pulmonary veins  
   -> Left atrium  
   -> Left ventricle  
   -> Aorta / Systemic arteries  
   -> Body capillaries (systemic tissues)  
   -> Body veins / Venae cavae (cycle repeats)

Topic 1: Schrödinger Equation  
• Central non-relativistic wave-equation that governs the time evolution of a quantum state.  
• States are represented by wave-functions 𝜓(𝐫,t); physical information is encoded in |𝜓|², the probability density.  
• Time-dependent form (single particle in potential V):  
  \( i\hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\,\psi(\mathbf{r},t)=\left[-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\nabla^{2}+V(\mathbf{r},t)\right]\psi(\mathbf{r},t) \)  
• In stationary situations (V independent of t) we separate variables, 𝜓(𝐫,t)=φ(𝐫)e^{-iEt/ħ}, leading to the time-independent form:  
  \( \left[-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\nabla^{2}+V(\mathbf{r})\right]\phi(\mathbf{r})=E\phi(\mathbf{r}) \)  
• Hermitian Hamiltonian guarantees real energy eigenvalues and unitary time evolution.  
• Superposition principle: general solution is linear combination of eigenfunctions, enabling quantum interference.  
• Boundary conditions (normalizability, continuity) quantize energies in bound systems (e.g., particle in a box, hydrogen atom).  

Topic 2: Dirac Equation  
• Relativistic wave-equation for spin-½ particles; reconciles quantum mechanics with special relativity.  
• Predicts intrinsic spin and g≈2 magnetic moment naturally; led to prediction of antimatter.  
• Covariant form (ℏ = c = 1 units):  
  \( (i\gamma^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}-m)\,\psi(x)=0 \)  
  where γ^μ are 4×4 Dirac matrices satisfying {γ^μ,γ^ν}=2η^{μν}.  
• In Hamiltonian form (standard representation):  
  \( i\hbar\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\psi = \left[c\,\boldsymbol{\alpha}\!\cdot\! \mathbf{p}+ \beta mc^{2}\right]\psi \)  
  with α⃗ and β matrices encoding spin and particle/antiparticle components.  
• Solutions are four-component spinors; positive-energy components describe particles, negative-energy components describe antiparticles.  
• Conserved probability current:  
  \( j^{\mu}=\bar{\psi}\gamma^{\mu}\psi \), where \( \bar{\psi}=\psi^{\dagger}\gamma^{0} \).  
• Non-relativistic limit (via Foldy–Wouthuysen or Pauli reduction) reproduces Schrödinger/Pauli equations, linking g-factor and spin-orbit coupling.

Physics equation (uniformly-accelerated motion):
s = u·t + ½·a·t²

Where  
s = displacement (m)  
u = initial velocity (m s⁻¹)  
a = constant acceleration (m s⁻²)  
t = time (s)

Assigned values  
u = 12 m s⁻¹  
a = 3 m s⁻²  
t = 5 s  

Calculation  
1. u·t = (12 m s⁻¹)(5 s) = 60 m  
2. ½·a·t² = ½(3 m s⁻²)(5 s)²  
   = 0.5 × 3 m s⁻² × 25 s²  
   = 1.5 m s⁻² × 25 s²  
   = 37.5 m  
3. s = 60 m + 37.5 m = 97.5 m

Result  
The object travels a displacement of s = 97.5 m.

Page 1

NON-DISCLOSURE AGREEMENT

This Non-Disclosure Agreement (“Agreement”) is entered into as of ________ (“Effective Date”) by and between Party A and Party B (each a “Party,” and collectively the “Parties”) in connection with a software development project (“Project”).

1. Purpose  
The Parties wish to exchange proprietary data solely to evaluate, design, develop, test, and support the Project and desire to keep such data confidential.

2. Definitions  
2.1 “Confidential Information” means any tangible or intangible information disclosed by one Party (“Discloser”) to the other (“Recipient”), in any form, that is marked or reasonably understood to be confidential, including without limitation source code, algorithms, designs, documentation, business or marketing plans, customer or supplier data, and trade secrets.  
2.2 “Disclosure” means any act of communicating, transmitting, or otherwise making available Confidential Information.  
2.3 “Recipient” means the Party receiving Confidential Information, including its affiliates, officers, directors, employees, contractors, and advisers who are bound by obligations no less protective than those set forth herein.

3. Confidentiality Obligations  
The Recipient shall: (a) use Confidential Information only for the Project; (b) restrict access to persons with a need to know for that purpose; and (c) protect such information with at least reasonable care.

4. Term  
These confidentiality obligations commence on the Effective Date and continue for five (5) years after the last Disclosure under this Agreement, regardless of earlier termination of the Project or this Agreement.

-----
Page 2

5. Return or Destruction  
Upon the earlier of (a) completion or abandonment of the Project, (b) the Discloser’s written request, or (c) termination of this Agreement, the Recipient shall, within ten (10) business days, return or, at the Discloser’s option, irreversibly destroy all Confidential Information and every copy, summary, analysis, or derivative, in any form, and certify such action in writing. Backup media may be overwritten during normal archival rotation, provided the data remains protected under Section 3 until eradicated.

6. Exceptions  
Section 3 does not apply to information the Recipient can prove: (a) is or becomes public without breach; (b) was lawfully in its possession before receipt; (c) is obtained from a third party without duty of confidence; or (d) is independently developed without use of Confidential Information. If compelled by law or court order to disclose Confidential Information, the Recipient shall give prompt notice to the Discloser and cooperate in seeking a protective order or other remedy.

7. Breach and Remedies  
Any breach of this Agreement will cause the Discloser irreparable harm not fully compensable by money damages. The Discloser is entitled to injunctive and equitable relief, in addition to all other legal remedies, including recovery of direct damages, lost profits, reasonable attorneys’ fees, and costs. The breaching Party shall indemnify and hold harmless the non-breaching Party from all third-party claims arising from such breach.
